# Gateway release notes

What changes, release by release, for the people who call the gateway and
the people who run it: what changed, who notices, and what to do. Entries use ids or descriptive names, and
[Proof](#proof) names the tests that show the documented behaviour. A behaviour with
no test is not listed here as a feature.

## Unreleased

### MCP tool-span content capture

Full-content capture exports tool inputs and outputs to your organization's
collector and masks known credential formats. Other sensitive content may still
be exported. Off by default; only an organization Owner or Admin can enable it.
Enabling and disabling are audited.

MCP body export requires all of: the operator's `otel.include_bodies`, explicit
organization consent `privacy.trace_content: true`, resolved content mode `full`,
and retention that permits bodies. Without explicit organization consent, new
organizations and workspaces export no tool-span bodies. Consent is organization
scoped and applies to its workspaces. The Security tab shows the disclosure
beside the opt-in; Save persists it. The existing audit record stores actor, organization, old/new value
and timestamp, including changes through config activation. An audit failure
rolls back the change. This does not configure a collector or qualify real SIEM
delivery; collector provisioning and routing remain separate.

With capture off or any closed-body policy, spans carry no tool inputs or
outputs. Approved scalar dimensions must match a bounded identifier shape;
nonconforming or known credential-shaped values become a fixed placeholder.
Ordinary identifiers remain unchanged. Full capture masks known credential field
aliases, header records and folded headers, URL credentials, private JWK members,
and bounded textual Base64/percent encodings, including adjacent MCP text chunks.
Depth and size bounds fail closed. This is format-based masking, not a guarantee
about arbitrary sensitive content.

Regression coverage: `TestIndependentPrivacyContent`,
`TestIndependentPrivacyCollector`, `TestIndependentPrivacyStreamedCollector`,
`TestW5IndependentCollector`, `TestScalarPrivacyCollector`,
`TestTraceCaptureExplicitOrgConsent`, and `test_span_capture_consent.py`.

Every upstream try is now recorded as an attempt with its own cost and
outcome. `model: "auto"` picks a model from the providers your key can
reach (N2). Keys, request metadata and
org-config saves are checked more strictly. An org config's infrastructure
secrets (cache, A2A, audit, alerting and MCP credentials, and alert channel
URLs that carry a credential) are stored encrypted and shown to no reader
(F12, F22), and the model hub's provider keys,
custom-model credentials and dataset secrets are stored encrypted instead of
base64-encoded (F21). Stored objects, MCP sessions and
the response cache are scoped to the caller's organization. Checks on the
request read the input of every API, not only chat's (C35), and the
arguments of a request's tool calls, which a mask rewrites (C36);
prompt-injection reads a tool's result and the system prompt (C37); and the
checks on the request run before the response cache, so a cached answer is
served only to a request they pass (C38). Async requests
from organization API keys are refused (C16). One timeout ceiling,
`server.max_request_timeout`, now holds every request outside MCP, chat
completions included, while async jobs keep their own cap (C23); a default
request timeout above it stops start-up (U9). Deepgram's and Cartesia's
streaming speech APIs are relayed for internal keys, and for any caller
when request auth is off (N12). Managed models,
managed tools and the console pages that are not finished ship switched off
or hidden (see
[Present but switched off](#present-but-switched-off)). What this means on
FutureAGI's hosted gateway is in
[On FutureAGI's hosted gateway](#on-futureagis-hosted-gateway).

This release makes no speed claim. Its only performance measurements are
in-process benchmarks of the chat-completion handler with a mock upstream
on 127.0.0.1. They are not end-to-end latency, overhead or throughput, and
none of those was measured. On an n2d-standard-8 VM that ran only the
release gate's benchmark job, this release's
`BenchmarkChatCompletionNonStreaming` median is 248,921 ns per request
against 235,190 ns for the dev baseline it merges, both
built with go1.26.10: 5.8% (about 14 µs) more. It allocates 311 objects
per request against dev's 304, within the release's pinned budget of at
most 7 more.
The figures, the machine and the command that reproduces them are in
[`agentcc-gateway/README.md`](../../agentcc-gateway/README.md#-benchmarks).

### Provider type defaults before validation

**PROVIDER-PRESET-ORDER-1.** A config.yaml provider's `type` now fills preset
fields before required-field validation, at startup and reload. Previously,
validation rejected type-and-key entries before the registry could apply their
defaults.

- `groq`, `mistral`, `together`, `fireworks`, `deepinfra`, `perplexity`, `cerebras`,
  `xai`, `huggingface`, `anyscale`, `replicate` and `openrouter` fill an empty
  `base_url` with that type's existing preset URL, an empty `api_format` with
  `openai`, and an unset `api_path_prefix` with `/v1`. The exact URLs are in the
  [provider type defaults table](../../agentcc-gateway/README.md#provider-type-defaults).
- `azure` fills only an empty `api_format` with `azure`. It still requires a
  resource-specific `base_url`, and does not fill a path prefix.
- Explicit URL, format and prefix values are unchanged, including an explicitly
  empty prefix. Existing endpoint overrides remain necessary: Perplexity Sonar
  uses `api_path_prefix: ""`, and DeepInfra's OpenAI-compatible endpoint uses
  `/v1/openai`. This change does not alter any preset URL or prefix.
- Type names are exact lowercase matches, independent of the provider map ID.
  An unknown or absent type still requires both URL and format. Errors name the
  provider ID, its nonempty type, and the missing field.
- Type does not fill a key, models, `managed`, or tenant policy. Organization
  upstream overrides remain independent; inheriting organizations still use
  their own credentials and may override the prefix, including with `""`.
- The hosted deployment profile (`AGENTCC_DEPLOYMENT_PROFILE=hosted`) resolves
  types first too, so a type-and-key entry loads there with its preset HTTPS
  URL, at startup and reload. The hosted transport checks run on the resolved
  URL. An explicit `base_url`, `skip_tls` or `local` still overrides the preset,
  and the hosted profile still refuses it when it is insecure.

Proof: `TestProviderPresetLoadBeforeValidation`,
`TestProviderPresetValidateBeforeRequiredFields`,
`TestProviderPresetExplicitFieldsAlwaysWin`,
`TestProviderPresetMissingFieldsNameType`,
`TestProviderPresetUnknownExplicitConfigUnchanged`,
`TestProviderPresetDoesNotBypassManagedFormatValidation`,
`TestProviderPresetLoadThenRegistry`,
`TestProviderPresetExplicitRegistryUnchanged`,
`TestProviderPresetTenantOwnUpstreamUnchanged`,
`TestHostedProfileProviderPresetShorthandLoads`,
`TestHostedProfileProviderPresetReload` and
`TestHostedProfileProviderPresetKeepsExplicitInsecureRefusals` in the
gateway's config and providers packages. Upstream request checks use synthetic local servers, not
vendor APIs.

### Router availability

Router models (automatic model selection) aren't available with Future AGI credits yet. Choose a specific model.

The six router listings previously included in CAT-2 stay unavailable on credits,
with CAT-2 OFF or ON. Direct IDs and fallbacks cannot enable them. Their existing
own-key routes remain available under the same policy and pricing. Image/music
activation and CAT-2's five-piece ON requirement are unchanged; router exclusion
is an additional integration requirement, not a replacement for any piece.

### Managed accounting and availability

These guarantees apply when managed models are explicitly enabled; this change
activates no provider, billing configuration or console feature.

- Model denials include listed variants of the denied base. An exact allowlist
  entry does not grant additional variants. `managed_models.allow_free: false`
  refuses free offers; leaving the field unset retains its existing default,
  `true`. Model lists and access offers use the serving policy, including
  provider locks and endpoint restrictions.
- An upstream failure before usable output is not an estimated generation.
  Reported usage still counts. A client cancellation after upstream acceptance,
  or an interruption after output, can be settled using an estimate. SSE error
  objects are errors, not successful empty answers.
- Successful nonstreamed text or tool answers without usage use the same
  estimate as streams: the reservation input estimator (messages, tools and
  structured-response schema) and about four output bytes per token. Estimated
  attempts are marked as such; the request is marked estimated if any billed
  attempt used an estimate. A billable retry needs another atomic credit hold
  before dispatch. Holds remain estimates, not guarantees about an upstream's
  eventual reported token count or charge.
- Token-priced cards must explicitly quote both prompt and completion prices;
  explicit zero is valid. A per-request-only quote remains a separate supported
  shape. Historical persisted catalogues remain readable for audit but cannot
  restore an older parser's pricing classification into serving.
- Expired and policy-denied offers are not advertised as callable. A free-only
  model's access row names its callable `:free` ID. Unknown dated model names
  are refused rather than silently served as an undated model. Historical
  `-latest` and `-turbo` grouping aliases are not serving aliases unless the
  exact requested ID is listed.

**Availability limits:** all 32 bundled Gemini listings contain unsupported
per-image pricing and remain unavailable on Future AGI credits. Gemini requires
your own provider key until that accounting dimension is supported. The seven
dynamically priced router listings are also refused. `/v1/models` exposes token
rates only; it has no field for a per-request fee. The existing catalogue-access
`pricing.request` field retains that fee. No new pricing response shape is
introduced here.

The managed guarantee is not a claim of routing parity for
`/v1/messages/count_tokens` or caller-defined fallback controls. Native Anthropic
and Gemini early-stream acceptance and the console/browser flows still require
integration proof; local upstream stand-ins do not establish vendor behavior.

Regression sources:
`managed_policy_consistency_test.go`, `managed_accounting_failure_test.go`,
`managed_accounting_attempt_test.go`, `managed_billability_bundled_refusal_test.go`,
`pricing_dimensions_test.go`, `pricing_restore_test.go` and
`pricecard_dimensions_test.go` under `agentcc-gateway/internal/`.

### W4: your own MCP accounts

The Integrations page's **Your accounts** panel lists only the signed-in
person's accounts. Connecting is an explicit action; Disconnect asks for
confirmation. Readiness uses stored state, not vendor discovery: a missing
organization app remains **unknown**, because CIMD or dynamic registration
may still be supported. Disabled servers, unusable expired tokens and
unavailable catalogue sign-ins do not show as connected.

Personal account list, start and disconnect require an individual principal.
Browser bearer sessions and person-owned `user`/`mcp` API-key pairs remain
supported; keys require an existing active organization membership.
Organization/system, ingest and synthetic service credentials are not a
personal sign-in. These routes do not create workspace access. The public
start-link redirect still requires no credential and starts nothing; the
callback requires the cookie and state issued by an individual-authenticated
start. In-flight starts created before this change must be restarted.

Generic credential reads include shared metadata and only the caller's
user-scoped metadata. Generic DELETE refuses personal OAuth rows without
changing them: use `/agentcc/mcp/connect/{server_id}/` for complete cleanup.
DELETE accepts validated `mode=user|shared` (default `user`); shared mode keeps
its Owner/Admin check. Unknown and repeated selector fields are refused.

A disconnected account stops new token delivery, but local revocation is not
proof of upstream revocation or cache eviction. `gateway_synced` reports cache
purge confirmation; `cleanup_pending` keeps a retry action visible across
reloads until supported upstream revocation and cache cleanup finish. An issuer
without a revocation endpoint cannot be made to invalidate its tokens here.
Older revoked personal rows without a cleanup receipt receive a retry action.

Coverage: `test_mcp_personal_boundary.py`, `test_mcp_connections.py`, the
neighbouring upstream/shared OAuth tests, and
`IntegrationsSection.my-connections.test.jsx` exercise mock HTTP and component
behavior. This is not an end-to-end OAuth acceptance or catalogue-wide enablement
claim. Browser consent/cookies, runtime egress, offline assets and literal
EE-linked contract checking remain release gates.

#### W4 shared credential rollout: gateway and Django together

Shared bearer/API-key grants now carry a push-only `revision`. **Deploy the
matching gateway and Django/backend-worker versions as one coordinated change,
not independent rolling upgrades.** Complete the reviewed `prism` migration
`0063_mcp_credential_grant_revision` (after `0062_mcp_cleanup_receipts`) before
new Django writers run, after old shared-credential writers have drained.
Do not overlap the backfill with old-version credential creation or rotation:
those writers do not assign revisions. It numbers existing shared grants;
zero is not a valid distributed grant revision. Verify no active shared-static
row still has revision zero before refreshing configs. This does not enable
MCP or managed tools.

If the deploy cannot be atomic, upgrade **all gateway replicas first**, then
immediately Django and its workers, and refresh all active org configs through
the new Django push/bulk-sync payload. Verify the refreshed revisions on every
replica before declaring shared-static service ready. There is an intentional
fail-closed interval: a new gateway with Redis refuses old unrevisioned pushed
grants. Conversely, an old gateway strictly rejects the new `revision` field,
so deploying Django first can reject the entire org-config sync. Neither mixed
state is a supported steady state or a compatibility window.

Every serving replica needs the revision-capable credential resolver and the
same Redis revision authority. The current wiring supplies it through the MCP
Django credential channel; without that channel, do not claim distributed
shared-static revocation readiness. A revisioned purge on a replica without
that authority returns `501 revision_revocation_unsupported`, not confirmation.
Django retains its durable pending obligation until a capable replica confirms.
Generic config saves, activation/rollback, and server deletion retire removed
shared-static references transactionally and request eviction after commit;
read-only bulk sync carries the resulting active config, never resurrecting the
removed grant. Personal and unrelated grants retain their own lifecycles.

Register `agentcc-mcp-shared-evictions-retry` with the existing Temporal schedule
registration at the coordinated deploy: **every minute**, SKIP overlap, at most
20 slots and 3 per org per tick, no new slot after 60 seconds, and a no-op when
nothing is pending. It retries only existing shared-static eviction obligations;
it does not enable a feature or connect an account. Registration creates the
schedule unpaused, as for the other schedules; this code change registers
nothing by itself. In-request opportunistic retries are capped at 3 additional
slots; deferred obligations remain pending for the schedule.

Do not roll either component back alone. Preserve migration 0063, credential
revision numbers, pending obligations and Redis revocation state. A rollback
must use a compatible gateway/Django pair and refresh every active config;
rolling back to pre-revision binaries loses the revocation guarantee and is
not a supported live rollback. An older config version cannot reactivate a
credential retired by its removal: explicitly regrant it with a newer revision.
See the [deployment pre-flight checklist](../../deploy/README.md#pre-flight-checklist).
Synthetic regression gates do not replace hosted multi-replica acceptance.

### On FutureAGI's hosted gateway

H1 to H4 describe the hosted gateway's deployment settings, not this
release's code: each gives its current state and any prerequisites for
enablement. Enabling a setting in the hosted config requires the owner's
approval. H5 to H8 describe this release's code.

- **H1. One key for every model (Future AGI credits).** Off in the shipped
  hosted config. Enablement requires verified gateway and Django billing
  behaviour on the combined code, passing end-to-end checks, a non-evicting
  Redis, a coordinated gateway and Django deploy, and the owner's approval.
  Credits apply only where your gateway offers Future AGI credits: if
  Gateway > Models shows the Future AGI credits card, turn credits on there.
- **H2. Response cache.** Off on the hosted gateway. The hosted config
  sets the gateway's `cache.enabled: false`, which overrides any
  organization's own cache setting. Enablement requires a cross-org
  cache-key isolation check and the owner's approval.
- **H3. A2A.** Off on the hosted gateway; `/a2a` answers 404. Its
  end-to-end validation and security review are incomplete. A2A is
  self-hosted only.
- **H4. MCP and connectors (org-wide MCP and the app catalogue).** Off
  on the hosted gateway; `/mcp` answers 404. Enablement requires hosted MCP
  validation, revocation checks, and the owner's approval. Connectors work
  where MCP is enabled for your gateway.
- **H5. Async requests from console keys are refused.** Every API key the
  console creates is an organization key, and this release answers a chat
  completion sent with `x-agentcc-async: true` from an organization key
  with 400 `deferred_run_unavailable` (C16). Send it synchronously.
- **H6. The console hides what is not finished** (N7).
- **H7. Checks on the request read every API, and refuse what they cannot
  read** (C35). An organization whose checks on the request include one in
  block mode, or one that masks or redacts, gets 403 `request_unavailable`
  on every transcription, translation and OCR request and on embeddings
  sent as token ids, before the provider is called. Set those checks to
  warn or log to serve such requests unread.
- **H8. Checks on the request read an agent's tool calls and tool
  results** (C36, C37). An organization's PII, secrets, keyword blocklist,
  content moderation, topic and input-validation checks in block mode now
  refuse a request whose tool calls' arguments hold what they block, and
  its prompt-injection check in block mode refuses an injection in a tool's
  result. A check that masks or redacts rewrites the arguments too, and a
  check that rewrites the request and does not finish within its timeout
  refuses the request (C39). Such checks also refuse, with 403
  `request_unavailable`, a request whose tool calls' arguments are nested
  more than 64 levels deep, or whose body holds a value they read nested
  more than 64 levels deep, which they cannot read (C36). The response cache
  is off on the hosted gateway (H2), so C38 changes nothing there.

### Before you upgrade a self-hosted gateway

**U1. Admin tokens must be strong, or the gateway will not start.** The
gateway exits at start-up when either token below is empty, shorter than 32
characters, has fewer than 8 distinct characters, contains a value published
in this repository (such as `agentcc-admin-secret` or the compose default
`local-dev-only-admin-token-replace-me`), or is a placeholder:

- `admin.token` (`AGENTCC_ADMIN_TOKEN`), whenever admin auth is configured;
- `control_plane.admin_token` (`AGENTCC_CONTROL_PLANE_TOKEN`), whenever a
  control-plane URL is set.

The error names the setting, never the value. Django's gateway admin
endpoints refuse the same tokens with 403. Generate one value with
`openssl rand -hex 32` and set it as both variables, on the gateway and on
Django. Setting only `AGENTCC_ADMIN_TOKEN` is not enough when a config file
holds a literal `control_plane.admin_token`. For local development only,
`AGENTCC_ALLOW_INSECURE_ADMIN_TOKEN=1` (read from the environment, never
from a config file) lets the gateway start anyway.

**U2. MCP needs a state key.** With `mcp.enabled: true`, the gateway refuses
to start until `AGENTCC_MCP_STATE_KEYS` (or `mcp.state_keys`) is set:
comma-separated keys, the current key first, each at least 32 bytes. Use one
value from `openssl rand -hex 32` per environment. To rotate, put the new
key first and keep the old one second.

**U3. IP rules read the TCP peer unless you name your proxies.** Every IP
rule (`ip_acl`, an org's `ip_acl`, a key's `allowed_ips`) now checks the TCP
peer address. `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Real-IP` are ignored unless
`server.trusted_proxies` (or `server.trusted_hops`) is set, because a caller
can write any address into them. Behind a load balancer or ingress, every
request then appears to come from the balancer: an allow list refuses
everyone and a deny list stops no one. List the balancer's addresses in
`server.trusted_proxies` before you rely on an IP rule. The `server` section
of `agentcc-gateway/config.example.yaml` explains both settings. The gateway
logs a warning at start-up when IP rules are on and neither is set.
`ip_acl.trusted_proxies` was never read, and still is not.

**U4. Scheduled routing stops start-up.** `routing.scheduled.enabled: true`
is refused: "scheduled jobs are not org-scoped, not billed and not
attributed in this build".

**U5. FutureAGI guardrail rules need their own credentials.** A
`provider: futureagi` rule in the gateway's config file with no `api_key`,
no `secret_key`, or no `eval_id` / `eval_ids` stops start-up. An unset
`${VAR}` counts as missing. The gateway no longer falls back to the
`FI_API_KEY` and `FI_SECRET_KEY` environment variables. Org-config checks
are covered by C3.

**U6. Plan the database migrations.** This release adds `prism` (the
`agentcc` app) migrations 0029 to 0045 and `usage` 0030. `prism` 0046 gives
the three new `agentcc_org_config` columns (`managed_models`, `tools`,
`identity`) a database default of `{}`, so a Django pod still running the
old code can save an org config during the deploy. 0030 adds 37 columns to
`agentcc_request_log` (36 nullable, and `attempt_count` with a database
default of 1) in one transaction, and it holds that table's lock while it
runs. 0031 and 0041 build their indexes concurrently. Nobody has measured
the lock time on a large request log, so run the migrations in a quiet
window. `usage` 0030 creates the managed-credit ledger tables, which stay
empty while managed models are off.

**U7. The response cache starts cold once.** Every response-cache key
changes, because each key now includes the caller's organization (C15).

**U8. Agent-signal keys in Redis are prefixed and shorter-lived.** With
Redis configured, the outcome and affinity keys (`aout:*`, `aff:*`) carry
the gateway's Redis prefix: `redis.prefix`, else `agentcc:`. The per-request
outcome record is kept for one hour, and only for agent-tagged traffic or a
request a managed attempt served. Keys written under the old names are not
read after the upgrade, and they expire on their own. For a request that was
neither agent-tagged nor served by a managed attempt, or one older than an
hour, `POST /v1/feedback` answers 404 `generation_not_found`.

**U9. A default request timeout above the request ceiling stops start-up.**
This release adds `server.max_request_timeout`
(`AGENTCC_MAX_REQUEST_TIMEOUT`), the longest a request may run (C23). Unset,
it is `server.write_timeout`; a value above `write_timeout` is kept, and the
gateway moves each response's write deadline to that request's own deadline,
so a request that runs past `write_timeout` still gets its answer, a timeout
included. The gateway refuses to start when
`server.default_request_timeout` (`AGENTCC_DEFAULT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT`) is
above that ceiling, and the error names both values, for example
"server.default_request_timeout (10m0s) is above the ceiling
server.max_request_timeout (5m0s)". `config.example.yaml` sets
`write_timeout` and `max_request_timeout` to 300 s and
`default_request_timeout` to 60 s. Before you upgrade, check
`default_request_timeout` against the other two in the config and the
environment you deploy.

**U10. Organization guardrail settings that hold `${VAR}` stop working.**
Earlier releases resolved a `${VAR}` in an organization's guardrail config
from the gateway's own environment (F5). This release does not: a
`futureagi` check whose `api_key`, `secret_key` or `base_url` holds `${`, or
an external-provider check with `${` in any top-level setting, makes no call,
and with action `block` every request of that organization gets 403
`content_blocked`. Before you upgrade, find such values in organization
configs and guardrail policies and replace each `${VAR}` with the value
itself. The console shows a stored credential as `__encrypted__`, so a
`${VAR}` saved there cannot be seen: re-enter every credential of a
`futureagi` or external-provider check that was set to a `${VAR}`. After the
upgrade the console refuses such a value with a 400 that names the field. It
also refuses to switch on such a check, to change anything else about it
while it keeps the value (its endpoint, provider or action, say), or to
activate a version that has one switched on: through the Guardrails page's
switch and edit, update-config and version activation, whatever the stored
shape. The guardrail policy API is the exception (below).

Switching such a check off is never refused for the value it holds. Where
you switch it off depends on how the organization's guardrails were last
written:

- **By the Guardrails page's rules editor, update-config or
  update-guardrail** (stored as a `rules` list): the on/off switch
  (toggle-guardrail) switches it off.
- **By an older console save** (stored as a `checks` map): the on/off
  switch (toggle-guardrail), update-guardrail with `enabled: false` and the
  rules editor's save (update-config) each switch it off, and the section
  stays a checks map (F4).
- **By a guardrail policy** (stored as a `checks` list: every policy
  create, update, delete, apply or sync rewrites the section from the
  organization's active global policies): the on/off switch
  (toggle-guardrail), update-guardrail with `enabled: false` and
  `PATCH /agentcc/guardrail-policies/{id}/` with that check's
  `enabled: false` each switch it off in the policy it came from, so it stays
  off through later syncs (F15). Deactivating or deleting the policy also
  works, the last policy that holds a check included: the gateway then gets
  an empty guardrails section (F14).

Two limits remain. A rules-editor save of a section a guardrail policy wrote
switches the check off only until the next policy sync puts it back; switch
it off with the on/off switch instead. And the guardrail policy API does not
check a value already held in a policy's encrypted credentials:
`PATCH /agentcc/guardrail-policies/{id}/` that switches such a check on
answers 200, and the gateway refuses the check without making a call (F5),
so with action `block` every request of the organization gets 403. `${VAR}`
in the gateway's own `config.yaml` is unchanged (U5).

**U11. Scrub the credentials earlier releases stored in the request log,
and rotate the keys it names.** Earlier releases stored some credential
headers in the request log in clear (F6) when it kept request headers
(`include_bodies: true` and content mode `full`). Once this release runs,
run `python manage.py agentcc_scrub_request_log_credentials` on the
platform. It reads every stored request-log row, soft-deleted ones too, and
reports by organization and key id, never by value: each gateway key a row
held, and whether that key still authenticates, and how many rows held
another credential header, by header name. Rotate every active key it
names: whoever could read the request log could read it. Then run it again
with `--apply` to mask those headers in the stored rows. `--org <id>` limits
it to one organization. A hosted Django runs management commands only in
its operator bootstrap job; this command is on that job's list.

**U12. On a self-hosted gateway, list any private guardrail or alert
endpoint before you upgrade.** This release dials an organization's guardrail
webhooks, external guardrail services and alert channels through the gateway's
guarded egress path (F10, F11). If an organization relies on a guardrail or
alert endpoint on a private, LAN or loopback address — a self-hosted
guardrail service, an in-cluster collector — add that address to
`mcp.egress.private_allow` (a CIDR, or a `host[:port]`) before you upgrade.
Until it is listed, those checks return a call failure (a blocking check then
refuses the request) and those alerts are not delivered. A guardrail or alert
endpoint on a public address needs nothing. FutureAGI's hosted gateway sets no
`mcp.egress.private_allow`, so after this release any hosted org check or alert
channel pointing at a private, LAN or loopback address is refused — the
intended outcome on a multi-tenant gateway. Cloud-metadata addresses are never
reachable, listed or not.

The FutureAGI eval check (`futureagi-eval`, `provider: futureagi`) is covered
too. The platform fills an org check's `base_url` with its own `BASE_URL`
(`http://localhost:8000` unless you set it). A check whose `base_url` is
unset, or is `https://api.futureagi.com` (the platform's default `BASE_URL`
on FutureAGI's cloud), goes to the gateway's `FI_BASE_URL` as before, with
nothing to list. When your `BASE_URL` is a private, LAN or loopback address,
do one of these before you upgrade: set the gateway's `FI_BASE_URL` to exactly
the same URL (the gateway trusts its own `FI_BASE_URL` and nothing else on
that host; a check naming `https://api.futureagi.com` is then sent there too,
as it already is wherever `FI_BASE_URL` is set), or list its `host:port` in
`mcp.egress.private_allow` (which opens that address to every org callback,
not only this check). Until then the check returns a call failure. The
gateway also adds the comma-separated entries of
`AGENTCC_MCP_EGRESS_PRIVATE_ALLOW` in its environment to that list, checked
as the config file's are. The Standalone install (`docker-compose.yml`) sets
it to `localhost:8000,127.0.0.1:8000` for its gateway, the API in the same
container and only its port, so there an org FutureAGI eval check whose
`base_url` is the default `BASE_URL` keeps reaching the API with guardrails
on, whatever config file is mounted.

**U13. Rotate the org-config infrastructure secrets stored before this
release.** Earlier releases stored each org's cache-backend credentials
(Redis password, S3 secret access key, Azure connection string and SAS token,
and the semantic cache's vector-store API keys), its A2A agent tokens, its
audit-sink and alert-channel webhook headers, its alert channel URLs that
carry a credential (a Slack incoming webhook, a token in the path or query),
and its MCP server auth in clear in the org config, where every member of the
org — a Viewer included — could read them (F12, F22). This release stores them
encrypted, and migrations `prism` 0047, 0050 (the same secrets saved under
the gateway contract's other spellings, such as `secretAccessKey`) and 0051
(the alert channel URLs) encrypt the ones already stored, in every version of
every org. Run all three before the new release serves traffic. After the
deploy, treat those secrets as exposed and rotate them at their source (the
S3/Azure/GCS account, the Redis instance, the vector DB, the A2A agent, the
SIEM or alert webhook, the Slack or other chat webhook, the MCP server), then
enter the new value in the console — the field is write-only and keeps the
old one until you do. Each migration is idempotent and reversible. Each
commits in batches of 500 rows, each in its own transaction, rather than
holding the whole table in one: if it stops part way, the batches already done
stay encrypted, and running `migrate` again finishes the rest.

**U14. A rule that rewrites the request refuses it when it does not finish,
and only logs in async mode.** A rule in the config file, or an
organization's check, that rewrites the request (`pii-detection` with
`remediation` `mask`, `redact` or `hash`, or the action `mask`) and times
out or fails now refuses the request with 403 `remediation_unavailable`,
with `guardrails.fail_open` on (the default) or off (C39). Raise the rule's
`timeout` (or `guardrails.default_timeout`) if requests are refused this
way. Such a rule in `mode: async` never rewrites the request: it only logs
what it finds.

**U15. Model-hub keys are encrypted by migration `model_hub` 0125 when
`INTEGRATION_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is set; check the result after the deploy.**
Earlier releases stored the model hub's provider keys, custom-model
credentials and dataset secrets base64-encoded (F21). Migration `model_hub`
0124 changes the two key columns to `text` (on PostgreSQL a catalog change, no
table rewrite), and 0125 encrypts every stored key with
`INTEGRATION_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, soft-deleted rows included; each key reads back
as the earlier release read it (a value that release could not read at all is
encrypted as it was stored). It commits in batches of 500 rows, each in its
own transaction, and a re-run finishes what is left.

- **The key must be set and kept.** FutureAGI Cloud sets
  `INTEGRATION_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, the Helm chart generates and keeps it, and the
  installer fills it; `deploy/setup.sh` does not generate it. Keep it with the
  database backups: a new value cannot read keys stored under the old one.
  Without it, on a local install (where `settings.py` makes one up per
  process), or with a value Fernet refuses (a placeholder such as
  `your-fernet-key`, or a key of the wrong length), nothing is encrypted: 0125
  says how many rows stay in the old encoding and what is wrong with the key
  (never its value) and leaves them, and keys saved later are stored that way
  too, so they keep working as before. A malformed key is also named in a
  warning when each process starts and on every save of a key. Set a valid
  key, restart, and run `python manage.py model_hub_keys_at_rest --encrypt`.
- **After the deploy, check.** `python manage.py model_hub_keys_at_rest --check`
  counts rows still in the old encoding and rows holding no key this
  deployment can read, never a value, names `INTEGRATION_ENCRYPTION_KEY` when
  it is not a valid Fernet key, and fails while any row is not encrypted;
  `--encrypt` encrypts the rest. Read both counts: a process running with a
  different or malformed key reports every encrypted row as one it cannot
  decrypt. A hosted Django runs management
  commands only in its operator bootstrap job; this command is on that job's
  list.
- **While the earlier release still serves.** The Helm chart migrates in a
  pre-upgrade hook, before the new pods start. Until they replace the earlier
  release's pods, those pods cannot read an encrypted key. They read it as no
  key, and the LLM library they call then takes a provider key from the
  process environment when one is set there (`OPENAI_API_KEY` and the like),
  so a call can run on the deployment's own key. A key one of those pods
  re-saves (a provider key, or a custom model's cost or metric edit) is lost:
  `--check` counts such rows, `--encrypt` names each by row id, and its
  organization must enter the key again. Keep that window short, or, where you run migrations yourself, run
  0125 once the new release serves.
- **Rolling back.** First run
  `python manage.py model_hub_keys_at_rest --to-legacy --confirm`, which stores
  the keys in the old encoding again; `migrate model_hub 0124` refuses to go
  back while any key is encrypted.
- **Exposure before this release.** Anyone who could read the database or a
  backup of it could decode those keys. If that access was wider than you
  intend, rotate the keys at their providers and enter the new ones.

**U16. An organization's IP rules, budgets, tool policy and alert rules
take effect on every gateway that receives org configs.** Before, an org's
`ip_acl`, `budgets`, `tool_policy` and `alerting` sections did nothing
unless the gateway's own switch for each (`ip_acl.enabled`,
`budgets.enabled`, `tool_policy.enabled`, `alerting.enabled`) was on, and
every shipped config leaves them off. A gateway with `control_plane.url` or
`admin.token` set now builds those four plugins whatever its switches say,
so a section an org saved earlier, and still has enabled, starts to apply on
the first request after the upgrade: an `ip_acl` allow list refuses callers
outside it, a hard budget refuses requests past it, a tool policy strips or
refuses tools, and alert rules send to the org's channels. Before you
upgrade, review the org configs you hold (Gateway > Org Config) and turn
off a section you do not want enforced. An org's `ip_acl` takes effect
only on a gateway that sets `server.trusted_proxies` or
`server.trusted_hops` (below). An org that set none of these
sections sees no change and causes no extra Redis command beyond the
organization-level spend count every organization has (F33). The node
switches still add the gateway's own rules on top.

An org's `ip_acl` applies to the model calls of chat and text
completions, `POST /v1/responses`, `/v1/messages`, `/v1beta`, embeddings,
images, audio, rerank, OCR, search and async jobs. The key-gated routes that make no model call
(the models list, files, videos, scheduled jobs, async-job and
stored-response reads, MCP, and the A2A request itself) apply it too. The
items of an admin batch (`/-/batches`) are judged by the address that
submitted the batch, resolved as for any request, by the gateway's rules
and the org's. An A2A task's model call (with `a2a.enabled`) is judged by
the address of the A2A request that started it, as the caller's chat call
is. Calls the app's backend makes with an org's key, such as the Test
Playground and console batch jobs, come from the backend's address: an org
allow list, or the gateway's own, that leaves it out refuses them. An org's
`ip_acl` needs `server.trusted_proxies` (or `server.trusted_hops`): without
either, a gateway cannot tell a caller from the load balancer in front of
it, so with the gateway's own `ip_acl.enabled` off it does not enforce an
org's `ip_acl` at all. `GET /-/config` then leaves `ip_acl` out of
`org_sections_enforced` and reports `org_sections_not_enforced:
{"ip_acl": "client IP unknown (trusted_proxies not set)"}`, the console's
Security tab and Settings say the same, and a start-up warning names the
fix. Set it before an organization relies on an IP list. With
`ip_acl.enabled` on, the gateway's and each org's rules apply to the
address the gateway resolves, as before (the TCP peer without a trusted
proxy, U3).

An org's budget starts from the spend the control plane recorded for the
current period when the gateway started. An org that turns budgets on
while a gateway runs is counted from that moment; after the gateway's next
restart it is counted from the start of the period, so a request its
budget allowed before the restart can be refused after it.

An org's `cache` section still needs the gateway's `cache.enabled`, and
its `rate_limiting` section `rate_limiting.enabled` (on by default). With
more than one replica, keep `redis` on: budget spend, RPM and org TPM
counters are then shared; without it each replica counts its own. A
config-file key's own `rate_limit_tpm` remains replica-local even with
Redis (C75, Known limits). `GET /-/config` lists what a gateway enforces
in `org_sections_enforced` (N8).

**U17. `prometheus.path` and `assistants.enabled` are read.** Both were
parsed and ignored. If your config sets `prometheus.path`, the metrics
endpoint moves there from `/-/metrics` on upgrade (a leading `/` is added
when missing; unset keeps `/-/metrics`; it still needs the admin token):
point your scraper at that path or remove the setting. If it sets
`assistants.enabled: false`, every assistants, threads and vector-stores
route now answers 404 `assistants_disabled` and sends nothing upstream
(before, they were proxied). The default stays `true`.

**U18. Register the alert and webhook schedules, and run prism 0048.**
Email alerts and webhook retries now run on two Temporal schedules:
`agentcc-alerts-evaluator` (every minute) and `agentcc-webhook-delivery`
(every 30 s). Run `python manage.py register_temporal_schedules` after the
deploy, as for every new schedule; until it runs, request-level alert
emails and a console Retry are still sent when Temporal accepts the start,
but threshold alerts, alerts held by a cooldown and webhook retries wait.
`prism` 0048 adds four columns (the email alert's dispatch state,
`last_error` and `last_error_at`, and the webhook's sent budget keys), each
an ADD COLUMN with a constant database default, so a pod still running the
old code can save an alert or a webhook during the deploy.

**U19. A Redis response cache now uses its `tls` and `mode`.** Before, the
gateway ignored `cache.redis.tls`, `mode` and all but the first of
`addresses`: it dialled one node in plaintext and sent the password in
clear (F39). Now:

- `tls: true` makes every connection TLS 1.2 or later, verified against the
  system's CA roots for the host of the address dialled. A Redis that does
  not speak TLS, or whose certificate does not verify, stops the gateway at
  start-up; nothing is sent in plaintext.
- `mode: cluster` uses Redis Cluster, found from `addresses` (and
  `address`). `db` must be 0: a cluster has no other database.
- `mode: sentinel` reads `address` as the master set's name (the name in the
  sentinels' `sentinel monitor <name> ...`) and `addresses` as the
  sentinels. The password goes to the master only; the sentinels are asked
  without one. A `host:port` in `address` is refused with an error that says
  so.
- `mode` unset or `single`: the node at `address`, else the first of
  `addresses`, as before (a warning says how many addresses it ignores).
- Any other `mode` stops the gateway at start-up.

Check `cache.redis` before you upgrade. A config that set `tls: true` for a
Redis without TLS, or `mode: cluster` or `sentinel` for a single node, ran
before (in plaintext, on one node) and now stops at start-up with an error
naming the cause.

**U20. Register the batch schedule, and run the batch-jobs migration.**
Console batch jobs are now reported and their keys revoked by a Temporal
schedule, `agentcc-batches` (every minute). Run
`python manage.py register_temporal_schedules` after the deploy, as for
every new schedule; until it runs, a batch whose page is open in the console
is still reported when it ends, and every other one waits. Migration `prism`
0048 (`0048_r7_batch_jobs`) adds the `agentcc_batch_job` table; it only
creates a table. Batches submitted from the console before the upgrade are
not in it and answer 404 afterwards (none of them could run: every item
ended `invalid_api_key`, F40).

**U21. Deploy the gateway before the platform, and roll them back together.**
The platform now pushes an alert rule's `severity` (C68) to the gateway, and
a rule saved earlier from Monitoring > Create Rule already holds one. A
gateway built before this release decodes an org config strictly and answers
such a push 400 `invalid_json`, so that organization's whole config (its
providers, guardrails and budgets included) stops syncing until the gateway
is upgraded. Upgrade the gateway first, then the platform; never roll the
gateway back alone past this release.

**U22. The gateway names the config keys it does not read.** When it loads
its config file, a key that no setting reads (a misspelt key, or one an
earlier release read) is named in one warning, `config: keys the gateway
does not read were ignored`, and the gateway starts as before. Such a key
has no effect, so check the log after upgrading. The warning carries key
names only: a `${VAR}` reference is shown as `$VAR`, never its value, and a
value that a missing space joined to its key (`{api_key:...}` in a flow
mapping) is left out.

**U24. The MCP servers in the config file serve keys with no
organization.** With MCP on, the gateway serves an organization's keys
that organization's own servers (N13). The servers in its config file
(`mcp.servers`) are served to keys that carry no organization, as before,
and no longer to an organization's keys. To serve them to one
organization as well, set `mcp.static.org_id` to its id: that
organization's keys then get the config file's servers together with its
own, a server it saved shadows a config-file server of the same id, and
keys with no organization get no config-file server. The MCP admin routes
answer for one organization each (C81).

**U25. Run migrations `prism` 0052 to 0057, then check the MCP secrets.**
0052 adds the tables of Omega EE's provisioning API, and 0053 to 0055 the
agent-key policy, its expiry backfill and mint idempotency (scoped agent-key provisioning). 0056
moves every MCP server secret an organization config holds (F12) into the
MCP credential vault, and leaves a reference to it in the config (N14).
It rewrites the config versions in place and pushes nothing to the
gateway. 0057 binds each stored MCP server credential that the active
config version sends to the origin (scheme, host and port) of its server's
URL there, where the gateway sends it today. Any other credential is bound
to none: it is sent nowhere until its secret is entered again with its
server (F13). An organization with MCP servers in a config version created
before migration `prism` 0035 also gets `mcp.access.default: allow` on its
active version, unless that version states a default, so every key of the
organization reaches its servers as before. Then run
`python manage.py agentcc_mcp_migrate_secrets --check`: it exits 0 when
nothing is left to migrate. When it exits 1, it names what is left (the
organization, the config version and the path), never a value; run it
with `--apply` to move a value a pod on the previous release wrote during
the rollout.

**U26. Give the platform the gateway's public URL.** Omega EE's
scoped agent-key provisioning API hands out each virtual server's address as
`<AGENTCC_GATEWAY_PUBLIC_URL><AGENTCC_GATEWAY_MCP_ENDPOINT>/v/<id>`. Set
`AGENTCC_GATEWAY_PUBLIC_URL` on the backend to the gateway's public HTTPS
origin, and `AGENTCC_GATEWAY_MCP_ENDPOINT` to the gateway's
`mcp.endpoint` when it is not `/mcp`. While that address is not a public
HTTPS URL, provisioning answers 503 `gateway_url_not_public` and writes
nothing. The Helm chart sets it from the LLM gateway's route
(`gatewayApi.llmGateway`); with the gateway exposed another way, set it
in `config.extraEnv`.

**Omega EE upgrade compatibility. Upgrade Omega EE with this release or before it.** An Omega EE
deployment attaches to this gateway through the `omega-ee-attach/v1` scoped agent-key contract,
whose fixtures and spec carry the set digest
`sha256:317a7cae83d55fe710ae3dacbd0d6f80ef644706668f5ffd835a8f77ae9fd9a8`.
Deploy the Omega EE build that speaks it together with this release, or
first.

**U28. With request auth off, `/mcp` still serves a request with no key,
and now checks a key that is sent.** With request auth off
(`auth.enabled: false`), a request with no key on `/mcp` is served the
servers in the gateway's config file with no key, as before, while
`mcp.static.org_id` is unset. A key that is sent is now checked there too:
an unknown, revoked or expired key gets 401, and a valid key reaches the
servers U24 gives it. A request with no key gets 401 on a virtual server's
address (`/mcp/v/<id>`), and on `/mcp` once `mcp.static.org_id` binds the
config file's servers to an organization. A client that sends a
placeholder key to such a gateway gets 401: remove the key, or turn request
auth on and give the client a gateway key. `mcp.allow_anonymous_dev`, which
serves every request with no key, is for tests only.

### Changes callers can see

**C1. A key's `allowed_providers` is enforced on every endpoint.** Before,
it was not enforced on chat or completions. It now applies before the
provider is called, on every endpoint that routes to a provider: chat,
completions, messages and count tokens, Gemini `generateContent`,
embeddings, images, the audio routes, rerank, responses, search, OCR, the
assistants and vector-store routes, and realtime. An organization's API key
that may not use the resolved provider gets 403 `permission_denied`, "API key
does not have access to provider: \<id\>". On realtime,
C43 refuses every key but an internal one before a provider is resolved, so
such a key gets C43's 403 `permission_denied` there instead. If you set
`allowed_providers` on a key, check that it names every provider the key
really uses.

**C2. `/mcp` and `/a2a` need a key, and only canonical paths are served.**
With request auth on, every method and subpath under the MCP endpoint and
`/a2a` needs a valid API key, as `/v1` already did. An invalid key on `/mcp`
is a 401; before, it was a 200 JSON-RPC error. A route spelled
non-canonically (`//v1/...`, a trailing `/`, dot segments, an encoded `/`)
is refused: 401 without a key, and 404 `non_canonical_path`, naming the
canonical path, with one. Every 401 carries
`WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="agentcc-gateway"`.

**C3. An incomplete FutureAGI evaluation check now blocks.** An org-config
`futureagi-eval` check with no API key, no secret key or no eval id used to
be skipped, so requests passed unchecked. Now, with action `block`, the
request gets 403 `content_blocked`, and the message names the check and the
missing field. No call is made to the evaluation API. On this platform,
Django fills in the org's own keys when the check's `base_url` is the
platform's, so the eval id is usually what is missing.

**C4. Video, scheduled, search and realtime routes answer 501.** With no
video provider configured (no provider adapter that ships with this release
is one), every `/v1/videos` route answers 501 `endpoint_not_configured`. So
does every `/v1/scheduled` route. No shipped adapter serves search or
realtime either: `POST /v1/search` answers 501 `not_supported`, and
`GET /v1/realtime` answers 501 to an internal key (any other key gets 403
first, C43). The gateway README says so wherever it names these routes.

**C5. Org-config saves refuse routing keys the gateway does not run.** A new
or changed `routing.scheduled`, `routing.access_groups` or `routing.mirror`
value gets 400 `unsupported_routing_key`, with `param` naming the key. A
value the active config version already holds is saved unchanged, with a
warning. Removing or clearing one is never refused. `routing.conditional_routes`
and `routing.default_model` are stored with a "not enforced yet" warning.
Default model and conditional routes are not available on this release: the
console no longer offers them (the Fallbacks page, Org Config > Routing), and a
value already stored is kept as it is.
Every write path applies these rules, update-config included, and the
response carries the warnings.

**C6. Reserved names in key metadata and request metadata.**

- Creating or updating an API key with any of these metadata names gets 400:
  `org_id` (other than the key's own org), `access_groups`, `type`,
  `key_type`, `role`, `allow_policy_override`, `team`, `id`, `name` and
  `owner`. `log_content` is set through its own field, not through
  `metadata`. `rate_limit_rpm`, `rate_limit_tpm` and `allowed_ips` are
  refused either way (C22). `type`, `name` and `team` are plausible labels of
  your own: rename them.
  At the next key sync, the gateway drops reserved entries that keys already
  hold.
- The gateway admin route `PUT /-/keys/{id}` answers 409
  `reserved_metadata` to a change to a reserved entry. `POST /-/keys` and
  the key sync: C41.
- Request metadata, in the `x-agentcc-metadata` header or the body's
  `metadata` field, now also drops keys that start with `auto_`, `managed_`,
  `agent_`, `omega_`, `run_`, `step` or `ledger_`, and these exact keys:
  `cost_base`, `cost_markup_percent`, `billing_mode`, `usage_estimated`,
  `model_alias_requested`, `routing_options`, `upstream_provider_object`,
  `billing_alert`, `source_choice`, `outcome_class`, `ocr_pages`,
  `search_units`, `response_status`, `counted_tokens` and
  `usage_unreadable`. Keys that start with `rbac_` are dropped too: the budget
  plugin reads `rbac_team` as the key's team. The request still runs; the
  dropped key just does not reach your logs. A key named `step_count` or `run_label` is dropped too,
  so rename such dimensions. An object under `metadata.agent` or
  `metadata.omega` is read as the request's agent context, not as a
  dimension. C40 reserves more names.

**C7. Agent context headers.** Chat completions, embeddings, rerank and
capability calls read an agent context from request headers named
`x-agentcc-<field>` (each also accepted as `x-omega-<field>`) and from the
body object `metadata.agent` (or `metadata.omega`) under the field's
snake_case name (`run-id` is `run_id`). The gateway records it in the
request log and never sends it upstream. The fields and the values each
accepts:

- `agent-id`, `agent-version`, `run-id`, `parent-run-id`, `task-id`,
  `trace-id`, `workflow`, `attempt-id`, `budget-scope` (also `ledger-id`)
  and `workspace-id`: 1 to 128 characters of `A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ : @ / -`.
- `user-id`: 1 to 255 bytes of printable characters (letters, marks,
  numbers, punctuation, symbols and the space), so `jane+tag@example.com`,
  `user 42` and a 200-character id are accepted. Control characters (tab,
  newline, NUL, DEL), invisible characters (zero-width characters, spaces
  other than U+0020, the byte-order mark, line separators) and invalid UTF-8
  are refused. When the call sends neither `x-agentcc-user` nor a body
  `user`, it is the request's user in the request log.
- `env` and `framework`: 1 to 32 characters of `A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ : @ / -`.
- `step`: one of `plan`, `act`, `tool`, `extract`, `verify`, `reflect`,
  `memory`, `coordinate`, `summarize`, `final`, `other`.
- `turn`: an integer from 0 to 100000.
- `budget-usd`, `budget-remaining-usd`, `max-cost-usd`: a decimal number of
  US dollars from 0 to 1000000 (C50).
- `deadline-ms`: an integer number of milliseconds from 1 to 3600000 (C50).
- `route-hint`: `cost`, `balanced`, `quality` or `latency`; `require`: a
  comma-separated list of `tools`, `json_schema`, `vision`, `reasoning`,
  `audio`, `long_context`; `prev-outcome`: `ok`, `empty`, `verify_failed`
  or `retried`.

The session id is `x-agentcc-session-id` (also `x-omega-session-id`): any
value of at most 255 bytes. A longer `x-agentcc-session-id` gets 400
`session_id_too_long`, a longer `x-omega-session-id` 400
`agent_header_invalid`. `x-session-id`, the body's `session_id` and
`metadata.session_id` are read only when neither header is sent, and only
when they are at most 255 bytes.

Two errors refuse an agent context, both 400 with `error.param` naming the
header or body key:

- `agent_header_invalid`: a value its field does not accept;
  `error.message` states the field's rule (for example
  `x-agentcc-user-id must be 1 to 255 bytes of printable characters: ...`).
  A body field of the wrong JSON type and an `x-agentcc-user` longer than
  256 characters get it too.
- `agent_header_conflict`: the same field sent twice with different values
  (a header and its `x-omega-` alias, or a header and the body).

By default the gateway's CORS list lets a browser send three agent
headers, `x-agentcc-user-id`, `x-agentcc-session-id` and
`x-agentcc-trace-id`, and none of the others. A
`cors.allowed_headers` list replaces the default one, so an operator who
allows more headers lists every header browsers send.

**C8. Embeddings.**

- `input_type` must be `query`, `document`, `classification` or
  `clustering` (400 `invalid_input_type`).
- On a provider with no such parameter (OpenAI, Azure and Bedrock
  embeddings), any `input_type` gets 400 `input_type_unsupported`; before,
  it was dropped silently. Cohere and Gemini take it.
- An embedding request makes exactly one upstream attempt, with no failover
  to another host and no model fallback, because vectors from another model
  or host live in another vector space. A failed target returns its own
  error. The response header `x-agentcc-embedding-space` names the vector
  space.
- When Gemini reports no usage, the gateway logs an estimate marked
  `usage_estimated`.
- Cohere rerank is billed by its `search_units`.

**C9. Image models past their shutdown date answer 410.** From a model's
shutdown date, a request for it gets 410 `model_expired`, naming the
replacement. The calendar is `agentcc-gateway/catalog/deprecations.json`.
Nine entries were already past on 2026-10-18: `dall-e-2` and `dall-e-3`
(replacement `gpt-image-2`); `gemini-2.5-flash-image` and
`imagen-3.0-generate-002` (replacement `gemini-3.1-flash-image`); and, on the
Gemini API, `imagen-4.0-generate-001`, `imagen-4.0-fast-generate-001`,
`imagen-4.0-ultra-generate-001` and `gemini-3.1-flash-image-preview`
(replacement `gemini-3.1-flash-image`) and `gemini-3-pro-image-preview`
(replacement `gemini-3-pro-image`). Next: `gpt-image-1` on 2026-10-23;
`gpt-image-1-mini`, `gpt-image-1.5`, `gpt-image-1.5-2025-12-16` and
`chatgpt-image-latest` on 2026-12-01. Azure keeps some of these longer, and
its own dates are in the file. There is no switch to turn this off.

**C10. A non-chat request never takes a model fallback.** A non-chat request
(embeddings, rerank, images, audio and the rest) for a model that no
provider serves gets that model's own error, even when the config names a
fallback model for it. A route that overrides the model still serves a
non-chat request with the route's model (gateways built before 2026-10-14
answered such a request with 500). On `/v1/images/generations`, `/v1/ocr`,
`/v1/audio/speech`, `/v1/audio/translations` and `/v1/audio/transcriptions`
the gateway also reports that model (`x-agentcc-model-used`, and
`resolved_model` in the request log) and prices the request on it: the cost
estimate, which budgets count, is that model's. If the gateway has no price
for the route's model (a deployment name, say), it prices the request on the
requested model instead, as it does on chat, and `cost_source` names where
that price came from (`modeldb`, for example) rather than `unpriced`. Either
way, a per-model budget counts the request under the requested model.

**C11. Native server tools are costed and checked.**

- On BYOK `/v1/messages` and Gemini `generateContent` calls, the cost
  estimate now includes server-tool fees: Anthropic web search and web fetch
  counts, and Gemini grounding. Such an attempt is marked `usage_estimated`,
  because the fee is the gateway's estimate of your own provider's bill.
- A request with a server tool, pinned to a provider that cannot run it,
  gets 403 `model_not_permitted` with `metadata.reason`
  `server_tool_unsupported`, and no upstream is called.
- Gemini grounded responses are never stored in the response cache, because
  the Gemini API terms forbid it.

**C12. The circuit breaker is per model.** One failing model opens its own
circuits, not its provider's, so the provider keeps serving its other
models. A request whose every target has an open circuit gets 503
`all_providers_unavailable` without reaching an upstream.

**C13. Anthropic-dialect usage on `/v1/messages`.** When `/v1/messages` is
served by a provider that is not Anthropic's own API (Bedrock Claude, for
example), the usage follows Anthropic's format, streaming or not:
`input_tokens` no longer includes cached tokens, and
`cache_read_input_tokens` and `cache_creation_input_tokens` are reported on
their own. Token counts you read from `input_tokens` will be lower for
cached prompts.

**C14. Cache hits do not return the original charge.** A response served
from the cache no longer carries `usage.cost_details`, `usage.is_byok` or
the stored response's upstream `provider`. Token counts are unchanged. A
cache hit is not charged and has no `x-agentcc-cost` header: it is absent,
not `0`. The cache boundary is the execution path, not the provider's API
format. It covers non-streaming requests executed through the canonical/chat
pipeline: `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/completions` (see Known limits for
one provider path), and `/v1/messages`, including Messages requests routed
or retried through an Anthropic-format provider. For Messages, only the
native pass-through path bypasses the cache; a provider speaking Messages
natively does not by itself imply pass-through. Gemini `generateContent`
is cached when translated for a provider that does not speak that API;
its native pass-through path bypasses the cache. It never covers streams
(they bypass both the exact and semantic tiers on every deployment),
embeddings or the Responses API. Native pass-through `/v1/messages` and
`generateContent` requests report `x-agentcc-cache: skip`. On every
deployment, only a request whose organization has turned its own cache on
is cached (see the README's Response cache section).

**C15. Stored objects, A2A tasks and MCP sessions belong to their org.**

- Files, stored responses, async jobs, video jobs and A2A tasks are scoped
  to the organization of the key that created them. Another organization's
  id gets the same answer as an id that does not exist (404; for A2A, the
  JSON-RPC error `task not found` at HTTP 200), and the object is left
  untouched. Scheduled jobs cannot be created in this build (C4, U4).
- Keys with no organization, and every request when request auth is off,
  form one no-org tenant: they no longer see organizations' objects, and
  organization keys no longer see theirs.
- An MCP session belongs to the key that opened it. Another key, even one in
  the same organization, gets 404 for its session id. After you rotate a
  key, the client must initialize a new session (MCP clients do this on a
  404).
- Response-cache entries are never shared between organizations (U7).

**C16. Async requests from organization API keys are refused.** A chat
completion (`/v1/chat/completions`, the only route that reads the header)
with `x-agentcc-async: true`, sent with an organization's API key, gets 400
`deferred_run_unavailable`: "async inference is not available for
organization API keys yet; send the request synchronously". This covers
every key that is not an internal service key, managed requests included.
No job is stored and no provider is called. Before, the job was queued.

Internal service keys, and every request on a gateway with request auth
off, can still queue async jobs, with these changes:

- Jobs run on the routing the request resolved when it was sent.
- One organization runs at most `async.max_workers_per_org` jobs at once
  (by default half of `async.max_workers`, so 5 of 10) and queues at most
  half of the queue's 1,000 slots. Every request on a gateway with auth off
  counts as one tenant, so a gateway that used all 10 workers now gets 5
  unless you raise the cap.
- A job's run time is capped at `async.max_job_timeout`. By default this is
  the longest timeout in the config.
- A job that cannot be queued is refused at once, with 429
  `async_org_queue_full` or 503 `async_queue_full`, and is not stored.
  Before, it was accepted with 202 and stored as `failed`.
- `DELETE /v1/async/{id}` cancels the running provider call.
- A request authorized by a license token gets 400 `async_not_supported`.

**C17. IP rules are checked on every route a key opens.** A key's
`allowed_ips` and the global and per-org `ip_acl` used to be checked only by
the request pipeline, so routes that skip the pipeline (files, video,
responses, async and scheduled jobs, MCP and A2A) did not check them. The
key gate now applies the same rules on every route it gates. It checks the
client address described in U3, so a rule means what that address means:
behind a proxy, set `server.trusted_proxies` first. Automation that reached
those routes from outside its allow list now gets 403. A key's
`allowed_ips` applies only to keys in the gateway's config file: the
platform's API does not offer it (C22).

**C18. The guardrail policy header needs permission.** When the gateway has
any guardrail rule in its config file, `X-Guardrail-Policy` from a key
without `allow_policy_override` gets 403 before the provider is called, and
an invalid value gets 400. Before, on a gateway whose rules were all on the
output, the header could skip those rules. Every route a check on the
request reads (C32) now reads the header, as `/v1/chat/completions` and
`/v1/completions` do: `/v1/messages` and its `count_tokens`, `/v1beta`
`generateContent`, `streamGenerateContent` and `countTokens`, and
`/v1/responses`, streamed, not streamed or in the background, whether the
request is passed through to the provider's own API or translated. A key
with `allow_policy_override` gets `log-only`, `disabled` and `strict` there
as on chat, and a key without it that sends the header gets 403 before the
provider is called. Before, those routes ignored the header: a permitted
override changed nothing, and a key without the permission was not
refused. The routes in C35 read it too, the same way: `/v1/embeddings`,
`/v1beta` `embedContent`, images, the audio routes, rerank, search, OCR,
`/v1/videos`, the Assistants API and vector store search.

**C19. Deleting a key revokes it on the gateway.** Deleting a key in the
console now revokes it on the gateway too; before, the delete only marked
it in Django, and the gateway dropped it at its next key sync. If the
gateway cannot revoke it, the delete answers 503, and the key is left
revoked and listed. A revocation reaches every replica that shares the
gateway's Redis at once, and the others at their next key sync. A key
created on that replica stays there until a key sync that starts at least
`control_plane.key_sync_grace` (30 seconds by default) after the key was
created. A key the gateway has revoked stays revoked even when a key sync
that read the key list just before the revocation lands just after it.

**C20. A user removed from every organization sees nothing.** Such a user's
session used to reach other organizations' gateway keys, request logs and
configs through the shared list views. Those views now return nothing for a
request with no organization.

**C21. The MCP admin API tells "MCP is off" apart from a failing gateway.**
On the platform's gateway admin API:

- `GET /agentcc/gateways/{id}/mcp-status/` reports
  `reason: gateway_mcp_disabled` for every organization when the gateway runs
  with MCP off, including organizations with no MCP server.
- `mcp-tools/`, `mcp-resources/` and `mcp-prompts/` answer 404 with code
  `gateway_mcp_disabled` when MCP is off, and 502 with code
  `gateway_unreachable` when the gateway fails or cannot be reached. Before,
  both answered 200 with an empty list.
- `test-mcp-tool/` answers 404 `gateway_mcp_disabled` when MCP is off.
- An unreachable gateway still reads as `mcp-status` 200 with
  `reason: gateway_unreachable`.
- This release's gateway answers each organization's MCP status with
  `org_enabled` (N13). Against a gateway whose MCP status has no
  `org_enabled` (one that keeps a single registry from its own config
  file), `mcp-status` reports `reason: gateway_not_org_scoped` for every
  organization, `mcp-tools/`, `mcp-resources/` and `mcp-prompts/` answer
  an empty list, and `test-mcp-tool/` answers 400 as for an organization
  with no MCP server, without running the tool.

**C22. API keys no longer accept `rate_limit_rpm`, `rate_limit_tpm` or
`allowed_ips`.** The gateway does not yet enforce per-key rate limits or IP
allow lists for platform-managed keys, so creating or updating a key with
any of them, as a field or as a `metadata` name and with any value (`null`
included), now fails with 400 `key_limit_not_enforced`, which names the
fields, and nothing is saved. Before, a key could carry them in its
`metadata`, where the gateway never applied them. Reads no longer show the
three names in a key's `metadata`; a value stored before stays in the row,
unused.

**C23. One timeout ceiling holds every request.**
`server.max_request_timeout` (unset: `server.write_timeout`, 300 s by
default; U9) is the longest a request may run, whatever its timeout header
or model timeout asks for.

- Chat completions is held at it. Before, the request deadline skipped
  `/v1/chat/completions`, so a chat request's upstream call ran to whatever
  its timeout header or model timeout asked for, even past `write_timeout`,
  where its response could no longer be written.
- A route that resolves no timeout of its own (the gateway's admin routes,
  `/v1/models`, files and the like) used to end at
  `server.default_request_timeout`, 60 s by default. It now ends at the
  ceiling.
- On a route that resolves its own timeout (embeddings, rerank, images,
  audio and the rest), a model timeout above `default_request_timeout` now
  holds, up to the ceiling. Before, the request deadline cut it at the
  default.
- A timeout header (`x-agentcc-timeout` or `x-agentcc-request-timeout`)
  still sets a request's timeout, but only up to the ceiling: a longer value
  is held at it. Before, a header could ask for any length, on every route.
- Three things are not held at it. The MCP endpoint and its OAuth metadata
  have no request deadline, so the MCP event stream stays open. An async
  job (C16) runs to the timeout its request resolved before the ceiling,
  and `async.max_job_timeout` caps it. A relayed speech session
  (`GET /deepgram/...`, `/cartesia/...`) keeps relaying past the ceiling once its
  WebSocket is open, until either side closes it or the relay's own idle and
  session limits end it.

**C24. `x-agentcc-timeout-ms` reports the limit that applied.** The
response header now carries the shorter of the timeout the gateway resolved
for the request and the client timeout of the provider instance that served
it, when that provider states one. Before, it carried the resolved timeout,
even when the provider's own client timeout ended the call sooner. On chat
it reads the instance that served the response, after any retry or
failover.

**C25. A blocked chat answer gets 403 `content_blocked`, and its log entry
says so.** When a guardrail on the output blocks the answer to a
`/v1/chat/completions` request, the request gets 403 `content_blocked` (type
`guardrail_error`), and the message names the check. Before, a rule in the
gateway's config file answered 500 `internal_error` ("no response from
provider"), which SDKs retry, and an organization's output check in block
mode did not block at all: the answer was served with 200 and only
`X-Agentcc-Guardrail-Triggered: true`. Of an organization's checks, only
`data-leakage-prevention` and `hallucination-detection` read the answer; the
others read the request only. An answer from a cache hit that the output
check blocks gets the same 403, for a streaming request too (it got 500).
The request log records status 403, the error and
`guardrail_action: blocked`; it recorded status 0 for a rule in the config
file and 200 for an organization's check. The other routes are in C26. On a
stream:

- A streamed answer that a blocking check reads is held until the check
  passes, so it starts when the answer is complete. A blocking check is a
  rule in the config file at the post stage whose action is `block`, an
  organization's check on the answer in block mode, or the streaming
  checker with `failure_action: stop`. The response's status and headers
  go out at once; its body waits. The checks read the answer the gateway
  assembles for them (C30). A passing answer then goes out chunk for chunk
  as the provider sent it, with its usage as C79 says.
- A blocked one carries none of the answer and ends with the guardrail's
  error event: `content_blocked`, or `stream_blocked` from the streaming
  checker, then the usage chunk when the request asked for usage, then
  `[DONE]`. When the streaming checker stops the stream before the
  provider's stream ends, its error event is the whole stream. The log
  entry records 403 and `guardrail_action: blocked`, and the response
  cache never stores the blocked answer.
- A held stream that ends before the provider's stream does (the
  request's deadline, a client gone, or a provider error mid-stream) is
  checked on the part it read, and goes out or is refused the same way.
  The streaming checker's final check reads the text after its last
  check. Every check runs to its end, within its own timeout, even when
  the request's deadline fires while a check is running; only a check's
  own timeout or failure counts for `guardrails.fail_open`.
- The streaming checker runs the config file's rules under the policy the
  other checks use: the organization's, with the key's overrides on top.
  An organization's override that makes a rule block holds and blocks a
  chat stream, and one that makes a blocking rule warn holds nothing.
  Before, the checker read the key's policy only.
- A held stream buffers at most 10 MiB, the size the gateway reads of a
  provider's answer. A stream over it, or an answer the checks cannot read
  whole, is refused the same way, with `answer_unavailable` naming the
  check.
- With the streaming checker in disclaimer mode and no other blocking
  check on the answer, the stream is not held: the answer goes out as it
  comes, the disclaimer follows it, and no error event follows. A request
  with no blocking check on the answer streams as it comes.

**C26. A blocked answer is withheld on the other routes too.** What C25 says
for `/v1/chat/completions` now holds on `/v1/messages`, `/v1beta`
`generateContent`, `/v1/completions` and `/v1/responses`, whether the
gateway translates the request for the provider or passes it through to the
provider's own API, and for async jobs, batch items and A2A tasks. The
request gets the guardrail's 403 in that API's own error format: Anthropic's
`permission_error`, Google's `PERMISSION_DENIED`, or `content_blocked` (type
`guardrail_error`) on the OpenAI-format routes, and the request log records
the same status. An async job fails with the guardrail's error, a batch item
is an error that names the check, and an A2A task fails with the guardrail's
error (`Pipeline error: content_blocked: …`), never as a provider that sent
no answer. Before, the blocked answer was
served with 200, except that a rule in the config file got 500
`internal_error` (which SDKs retry) on `/v1/completions` with a provider
that is not OpenAI-compatible, on an answer from a cache hit and in an async
job, and a batch item reported success with no response. A stream on these
routes that a blocking check reads is held as C25 says, translated or passed
through: a blocked one carries none of the answer, not in a delta, a done
event or a completed event, and ends with the guardrail's error event in
the route's own format: on `/v1/completions` the error event, then the
usage chunk when the request asked for usage, then `[DONE]`; on
`/v1/messages` an `error` event; on `streamGenerateContent` a data frame
that holds the error; and on `/v1/responses` an `error` event. The checks
read the answer on all of these routes (C30); where the gateway cannot, a
check that would block refuses the request (C31).

**C27. A `/v1/completions` stream request keeps a refusal's status.** A
streaming `/v1/completions` request refused before its stream starts, for
example by a guardrail on the request, gets the refusal's own status and
error (403 `content_blocked` for a guardrail), as on every other route.
Before, it got 500 `internal_error`, which SDKs retry.

**C28. A guardrail's refusal on a translated `/v1/messages` or `/v1beta`
request is a permission error.** When the gateway translates such a request
for a provider of another format, a guardrail's 403 now carries Anthropic's
`permission_error` or Google's `PERMISSION_DENIED`, as the pass-through
routes already did. It carried `api_error`, Anthropic's type for its own
internal failures, and `UNAVAILABLE`, Google's status for a transient
failure.

**C29. A translated `streamGenerateContent` stream ends when the provider's
does.** A `/v1beta` `streamGenerateContent` request served by a provider of
another format stayed open after its last event until the request's
timeout, and its cost and log entry were recorded only then. It now ends
with the provider's stream.

**C30. A check on the answer reads it on every route that returns one.** A
check that reads the answer's text (an organization's
`data-leakage-prevention` or `hallucination-detection`, or a rule in the
gateway's config file at the post stage) now reads the answer the client
gets on `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/completions`, `/v1/messages`, `/v1beta`
`generateContent` and `streamGenerateContent`, and `/v1/responses`: passed
through to the provider's own API or translated, streamed or not, whether or
not the request log keeps bodies. A block then works as C25 and C26 say. The
answer is withheld (403 in the route's format) when it is not a stream. A
streamed answer that a blocking check reads is held until the check passes,
so it starts when the answer is complete; a blocked one carries none of the
answer and ends with the guardrail's error event. The log
records 403 and `guardrail_action: blocked`. Before, the checks were given
only the answer's usage on a request passed through to the provider's own API
(`/v1/messages` to an Anthropic-format provider, `/v1beta` to a
Google-format provider, and `/v1/responses`). They read a stream's text only
on chat and completions, and only when the request log or OpenTelemetry kept
bodies. So the blocked answer was served with 200 and logged as a success.
This is the path Claude Code traffic to Claude models takes. Every choice is
read: every choice of a `/v1/completions` answer (`n` above 1, or a list of
prompts), every candidate of a Gemini answer, and each choice of a stream on
its own. On `/v1/completions` to an OpenAI-compatible provider, which gets
the request as the client sent it, the checks used to read the first choice
only, so a blocked answer in a later choice was served with 200 and logged as
a success; the request log's `response_body`, when the log keeps bodies, now
holds every choice of such an answer, where it held the first. A stream with
two choices or candidates used to be read as one string with their text
interleaved, so a statement split by the other choice's text was never read
whole, even with bodies kept. With the streaming checker on, a chat stream
is assembled for an organization's checks only. The checker already reads
the stream for the config file's rules as it goes. Where a check reads the
answer of a request passed through to the provider's own API, the request
log's `response_body`, when the log keeps bodies, now holds that answer as a
chat answer, where it held only the usage.

**C31. When no check can read the answer, a check that would block it
refuses the request.** A `/v1/responses` request with `background: true` is
answered later, and its answer never passes through the gateway. When a
check on the answer would block, the request is now refused before the
