provider is called, with 403 (type `guardrail_error`, code
`answer_unavailable`). The message names the check and says that a
background response's answer does not pass through the gateway. Send the
request without `background` to have it checked. A 200 answer the gateway
cannot read (not the API's JSON) on `/v1/responses`, or on `/v1/messages` or
`/v1beta` passed through to the provider's own API, is withheld with the
same error when such a check would block it. "Would block" means a rule in
the config file at the post stage whose action is `block` after the key's
policy and `X-Guardrail-Policy`, or an organization's check that reads the
answer in block mode. With such checks only in warn or log mode, or none,
these requests run as before. The request log records the refusal as a
guardrail block, with `answer_unavailable` in its metadata. Before, a
background response was sent and served unchecked.

**C32. A check on the request reads it on every route that sends one to a
chat model.** A check that reads the request (an organization's PII,
prompt-injection, keyword blocklist, secrets, topic, language, system
prompt protection or other check that runs before the provider, or a rule in
the gateway's config file at the pre stage) now reads the request on
`/v1/messages` sent to an Anthropic-format provider, on `/v1beta`
`generateContent` and `streamGenerateContent` sent to a Google-format
provider, and on `/v1/responses`, streamed, not streamed or in the
background. It also reads the prompt the provider gets to count its tokens,
on `/v1/messages/count_tokens` and `/v1beta` `countTokens` (as `contents`,
or as a `generateContentRequest`). `/v1/messages/count_tokens` to an
Anthropic-format provider now goes through the gateway's pipeline as
`/v1/messages` does, as `/v1beta` `countTokens` already did: rate limits,
request quotas and budgets apply to it, and it is logged, so each call is
metered as a gateway request. Counting tokens therefore counts against the
key's and the organization's rate limits, request quotas and budgets on
both count routes, as any other request does. Each count is logged with the
status the client got (the provider's own when the provider refused the
count) and with the count the provider returned, under `counted_tokens` in
the entry's metadata. The entry's token counts stay 0: counting is free at
the provider and consumes no tokens, so the count is never priced as the
request's usage. A `/v1beta` `embedContent` is logged with its status the
same way. Before, `/v1/messages/count_tokens` was neither logged nor
metered, and a logged count recorded status code 0.
The gateway passes these requests through to the provider's own API as the
client sent them, and before, no check on the request read them: every such
check passed them, whatever they held. This is the path Claude Code traffic
to Claude models takes. A request a check in block mode refuses is now
refused before the provider is called, with the guardrail's 403 in
the route's own error format (Anthropic's `permission_error`, Google's
`PERMISSION_DENIED`, `content_blocked` of type `guardrail_error` on
`/v1/responses`); a stream is refused before it starts. The request log
records 403 and `guardrail_action: blocked`. The checks read such a request
as the gateway's translators give it to a provider of another format: the
system prompt (Anthropic's `system`, Gemini's system instruction, the
Responses `instructions`), every turn's text, tool results and tool calls,
and the tools by name. They also read a document's and a search result's
text on `/v1/messages`, Gemini function responses and code execution
results, and Responses tool outputs and a stored prompt's variables. The
output of a tool the provider runs is read too: a command's `stdout` and
`stderr` (Anthropic code execution and bash code execution results,
Responses `shell_call_output`), a text editor result's file text and changed
lines, the page a web fetch result holds, a search result's title, an
`apply_patch_call_output` and a code interpreter's logs. A Gemini function
response is read as Google decodes it before the model reads it, so text a
client wrote with JSON escapes (`\u002d`, or the escapes Python's
`json.dumps` writes for non-ASCII letters) is read as the characters it
stands for. Gemini fields are read under either name Google's API takes
(`systemInstruction` or `system_instruction`, ...), and a repeated field
given as one object (`"contents": {...}`, `"parts": {...}`, as Google's own
examples send them) is read as a list of one. A check on the tools (an
organization's Tool Permissions check) reads each tool by one name: a
function by its name, a tool the provider runs by its type (Responses
`web_search`, `file_search`, ...; Anthropic server tools by their `name`)
or, on Gemini, by its field in snake_case (`google_search`,
`code_execution`, `url_context`, whichever spelling the request uses), and
an MCP server as `mcp:<its name>` (Anthropic `mcp_servers` and
`mcp_toolset` tools, the Responses `server_label`), so `mcp:*` matches
every named MCP server. The checks at the post stage read the same request, as they read
a chat request. When the gateway cannot read such a request (it does not
have the shape its API defines), the request is refused before the provider
is called with 403 `request_unavailable` (type `guardrail_error`, or the
route's own format) if a check on the request would block it or rewrite it
(C33), and the message names the check and says why. "Would block" means a
rule in the config file at the pre stage whose action is `block` after the
key's policy and after `X-Guardrail-Policy`, which every route here reads
(C18), or an organization's check that reads
the request in block mode. "Would rewrite"
means such a rule, or an organization's check, whose remediation rewrites
the request, in any mode: its rewrite could never be applied. Otherwise the
request goes on unread, with `request_unavailable` in the log's metadata.
The same holds on native `/v1/completions` for a prompt of token ids, which
the provider decodes and the gateway cannot read.

**C33. A check's rewrite of the request reaches the provider on every
route.** `pii-detection` with remediation `mask`, `redact` or `hash`
rewrites the text it reads. On `/v1/chat/completions` the provider gets the
rewritten request. The gateway now writes the rewrite into the body it sends
on the routes that pass the request through as the client sent it, where
the provider got the text the check meant to hide:

- `/v1/messages` to an Anthropic-format provider: into the system prompt,
  text blocks, tool results (the provider's own tools' output included) and
  documents' text.
- `/v1beta` `generateContent` and `streamGenerateContent` to a
  Google-format provider: into the system instruction, text parts, function
  responses (their JSON text as Google decodes it) and code execution
  results.
- `/v1/messages/count_tokens` and `/v1beta` `countTokens`, as on the routes
  above, so the provider counts the tokens of the request it would get.
- `/v1/responses`, streamed, not streamed or in the background: into the
  instructions, input text and refusal parts, tool outputs and a stored
  prompt's variables.
- `/v1/completions` to an OpenAI-compatible provider, which gets the prompt
  as the client sent it: into the prompt, or each prompt of a list.

Each rewritten text goes back to the place it was read from, as do the
rewritten arguments of a tool call (C36). Everything else in the body
(`cache_control`, a tool call's name and id, other fields) is sent as the
client sent it, apart from white space between the fields of the objects and
lists that hold a rewritten text or rewritten arguments. When a masked match runs across two text blocks
of one turn, the two blocks are merged into the first. When the rewrite
cannot be written (a match that runs across two fields of one content block
or two prompts of a `/v1/completions` list, or a Gemini function response
the rewrite makes other than JSON, as a mask inside a number does), the
request is refused before the provider is called with 403
`remediation_unavailable`, naming the check, and the log records the block.
A request the gateway cannot read at all is refused before any check runs
(C32), as is a `/v1/completions` prompt of token ids. On the routes that
translate the request for a provider of another format, the provider gets
the rewritten request, as before.

**C34. An organization's check takes the action `mask` where it can rewrite
the request.** The console offered `mask` as the action of every
organization check, and the gateway read it as `log`: an organization that
chose it on `pii-detection` got neither a block nor a mask, and the provider
got the text the check matched. Now an organization's `pii-detection` with
the action `mask` replaces each match in the request with `***` and lets
the request through, as in log mode (no warning header), on every route in
C33. Where the gateway passes the request through as the client sent it, it
writes the mask into the body it sends, and it refuses the request before
the provider is called, as C32 and C33 say for a check that rewrites the
request, when it cannot read the body (`request_unavailable`) or cannot
write the mask into it (`remediation_unavailable`). A `remediation` of
`redact` or `hash` in the check's config rewrites that way instead: the
action turns the rewrite on, and the remediation says how. The request log
records the check with the action `mask`. The console offers `mask` only
for a check whose type can rewrite the request it reads, which is
`pii-detection` (`pii-detector` in a section stored as rules); every other
check offers block, warn and log, in the Rules tab and in the Overview's
edit dialog. On a check of any other type the gateway still reads `mask` as
`log` (see [Known limits](#known-limits)): a dialog that opens on such a
stored action shows it, disabled, as "runs as Log", and a save that changes
nothing keeps it. Which checks take which actions is in
`api_contracts/gateway/guardrail-check-actions.json`, which the gateway's
test and the console's test both read.

**C35. A check on the request reads every other API's input.** Before, a
check on the request (an organization's check that runs before the
provider, or a rule in the gateway's config file at the pre stage) read only
the chat-shaped routes of C32: on every other API it passed whatever the
request held, and the provider got it; the Assistants API, vector store
search and `/v1/videos` ran no guardrail at all. Now each of these is read:

- `/v1/embeddings`: the input, a string or each string of a list.
- `/v1beta` `embedContent`: the content's text parts and the title.
- `/v1/images/generations`: the prompt.
- `/v1/audio/speech` and `/v1/audio/speech/stream`: the input text.
- `/v1/audio/transcriptions` and `/v1/audio/translations`: the prompt.
- `/v1/rerank`: the query and each document.
- `/v1/search`: the query, a string or each string of a list. No provider in
  this release serves search, so the route answers 501.
- `/v1/videos`: the prompt, before the job is stored. No provider in this
  release serves video, so the route answers 501.
- The Assistants API: an assistant's instructions and tools (create and
  update), a thread's messages, a message, a run's instructions, additional
  instructions, additional messages and tools, the thread and run of
  `/v1/threads/runs`, and each tool output a run is given. A message is read
  as its text or its text parts; an image URL is read as an image.
- `/v1/vector_stores/{id}/search`: the query, a string or each string of a
  list.

The rules of C32, C33 and C34 hold on every one of them. A request a check
in block mode refuses gets the guardrail's 403 `content_blocked` naming the
check (Google's `PERMISSION_DENIED` on `/v1beta`) before the provider is
called, and a refused video request stores no job. A request log entry of
a refused request records 403 and the block. A check's rewrite (`mask`,
`redact`, `hash`) goes into the field the provider reads, keeping the
input's shape (a string stays a string, a list keeps its other items), or
the request is refused with 403 `remediation_unavailable`. The gateway reads
the request it sends, not the body as spelled: a field written in another
case or twice is read as the provider gets it. An organization's Tool
Permissions check reads the tools an assistant or a run offers, by name (a
function by its name, `code_interpreter` and `file_search` by their type).
`X-Guardrail-Policy` applies on all of them (C18). A request log entry
records the result of each check that triggers and the action taken
(`guardrail_action`). The other requests of the Assistants, Vector Stores
and Files APIs run the pipeline C80 describes. An Assistants API body sent
empty (`POST /v1/threads` with no body creates an empty thread) holds
nothing to read, and goes on as `{}` does.

**Behaviour change: input the checks cannot read is refused when a check
would block or rewrite it.** Embeddings given as token ids, the document of
an OCR request (a document or image URL, inline data, or a file at the
provider) and the audio file of a transcription or translation are not text
the checks can read. When a check on the request would block the request
or rewrite it (C32's "would block" and "would rewrite"), such a request is
refused before the provider is called, with 403 `request_unavailable` (type
`guardrail_error`) naming the check and saying why, for example "Request
blocked by guardrail: pii-detection — it checks the request, and the
gateway cannot read this request: its audio file is not text the checks
can read". This holds even when a transcription's prompt passes: the prompt
is read, the audio is not. It holds for any check on the request in block
mode, whatever its type: an organization whose only such check is Tool
Permissions, which could never match audio or a document, is refused too.
An organization with a check on the request in block mode, or one that
masks or redacts the request, therefore cannot transcribe, translate or run
OCR through the gateway until it sets those checks to warn or log (without
a remediation); a key with
`allow_policy_override` can send `X-Guardrail-Policy: log-only` to run the
config file's rules as log (C18; an organization's checks ignore the
header). Without such a check the request goes on, with
`request_unavailable` in the log's metadata, and a check in warn or log mode
still reads a transcription's or translation's prompt: the response
carries `x-agentcc-guardrail-triggered: true` on a match, and the log
records it as logged or warned. Images, audio and files inside a chat,
Messages, Gemini or Responses request stay as C32 says: not read, and not
refused.

The console's Guardrails page (Overview, "Requests Before LLM checks read")
lists every route a check on the request reads, what it reads there and what
it refuses unread. The list is
`api_contracts/gateway/guardrail-request-routes.json`, which the gateway's
test and the console's test both read; the gateway's test checks that every
POST route the gateway registers under `/v1`, `/v1beta` and `/a2a`, and the
batch API, is in it, either as a route a check reads or as one that sends
no text a model reads (`/v1/files`, which the gateway keeps;
`/v1/count_tokens`, which it counts itself; the metadata-only Assistants and
vector store writes; `/v1/scheduled`, refused; `/v1/feedback`; the test
capability). This gateway has no route for `/v1/moderations`,
`/v1/images/edits` or `/v1/images/variations`: they answer 404, and no
provider gets the request.

**C36. A check on the request reads the arguments of the request's tool
calls, and a rewrite rewrites them.** Before, every check on the request
read a message's content only (internal security assessment 1, POL-2): a
value in the arguments of a tool call an assistant turn made passed every
check in block mode, reached the provider and stayed in the request log.
The arguments are a chat request's `tool_calls[].function.arguments`, an
Anthropic `tool_use` block's `input`, a Gemini `functionCall`'s `args`, and
on `/v1/responses` a `function_call`'s or `mcp_call`'s `arguments`, a
`custom_tool_call`'s `input`, a shell call's `action`, an
`apply_patch_call`'s `operation` and a code interpreter call's `code` (a
string, or, where a client sends another JSON value in its place, that value
as JSON). Now
`pii-detection`, `secret-detection`, `keyword-blocklist`,
`content-moderation`, `topic-restriction`, `input-validation`'s deny and
require patterns, and the external and FutureAGI checks (in the text they
send) read them, on `/v1/chat/completions` and every route of C32. Arguments
that are JSON are read value by value, up to 64 levels of nesting, with JSON
escapes decoded (`\u002d` is read as `-`). Each member is read with its key, as
`key: value`, so a pattern that needs a keyword matches it
(`secret-detection`'s password pattern matches `{"password": "..."}`); a
member whose value is an object or a list is read by its key, and what it
holds in turn. Arguments that are not JSON (a custom tool's free text) are
read whole. A tool call's name is not read. `input-validation`'s length
rules still count each message's content only. `topic-restriction` now also
reads text given as content parts (a tool result as parts), which it
skipped.

Arguments nested more than 64 levels deep (an object or a list inside 64
others) are not read: they are input the gateway cannot read, recorded as
`request_unavailable` in the request log, and a check on the request that
would block or rewrite the request refuses it before the provider is
called, 403 `request_unavailable`, as for embeddings sent as token ids
(C35); under a check that only warns or logs the request goes on.
Arguments that begin with more than 64 `[` or `{` are refused the same way,
free text included: the depth is checked before the gateway knows whether
they are JSON, and the refusal says "nested more than 64 levels deep or
begin with more than 64 [ or { brackets". The
gateway reads each tool call's arguments in one pass over their bytes,
once for all the checks on the request, before they run (and once more for
the checks on the answer that read the request); a check that outlives its
timeout stops reading.

A body is read up to 64 levels deep too. Where the gateway reads a body it
passes through (C32) or proxies as sent (C35) by walking a value on its own
(an item, content part or block of a type it does not know, the result of
a tool the provider runs, a Gemini `functionResponse`, a block inside an
Anthropic tool result, search result or document), it reads that value up
to 64 levels deep: an object or a list inside 64 others is not read. Such a
request is input the gateway cannot read in full: a check on the request
that would block or rewrite it refuses it before the provider is called,
403 `request_unavailable` naming the check and saying where (for example
"Request blocked by guardrail: pii-detection — it checks the request, and
the gateway cannot read this request: input[1] holds a value nested more
than 64 levels deep"), with `request_unavailable` in the request log; under
a check that only warns or logs the request goes on, and the checks read
the rest of it. Values the gateway does not walk (a tool's JSON schema,
metadata) are not limited. The gateway reads a body in one pass over its
bytes (it finds where each object and list ends, then decodes each once),
writes a check's rewrite back the same way, and stops reading at its next
step once the request's deadline passes or the client goes away (checking
the body is JSON, and decoding one long string, are single steps). Before, it decoded a
value again at every level of its nesting: one Responses item nested 9000
deep took seconds to read, four took past the client's deadline while the
read went on, and a body read in time went to the provider unread. The prompt a prepaid `/v1/responses` stream is charged
for when its last event cannot be read (F3) is estimated from the body
read the same way, whether or not the client is still connected.

`pii-detection` with `mask`, `redact` or `hash` rewrites each match in the
arguments where it is: in a value, or in a key that matches; a match that
starts in a key and runs into its value (a passport keyword and its number)
rewrites the value's part. Arguments that are JSON stay JSON, a rewritten
number is written as a string (with `redact`, `{"card":4111111111111111}`
becomes `{"card":"[REDACTED:credit_card]"}`), and arguments with no match
keep their bytes; a rewrite keeps every byte inside the arguments' JSON
value that it does not rewrite, white space and escapes included (white
space before and after that value is not kept). On `/v1/chat/completions`
and the translated routes the provider gets the rewritten arguments; on the
routes that pass the body through they are written back where they were
read, as JSON into a JSON value and as a string into a string, or the
request is refused with 403 `remediation_unavailable` when they cannot be
(a rewrite that is not JSON where the body holds a JSON value), as in C33.
The request log records the rewritten arguments. Two matches that overlap
(a URL whose credentials look like an email address) are rewritten as one;
before, `pii-detection` panicked on such a message, and with
`guardrails.fail_open` (the default) the request went on with that message
as sent.

**C37. prompt-injection reads a tool's result and the system prompt.**
Before, the check read the user's messages only (POL-3), so an injection in
a tool's result, the usual way text someone else wrote (a web page, a
document, an email) reaches an agent, or one spliced into a system prompt,
was never read. Now it reads a tool's result (a `tool` or `function`
message, an Anthropic `tool_result`, a Gemini `functionResponse`, a
Responses tool output) with every pattern, as it reads a user message. It
reads the system and developer messages (Anthropic's `system`, Gemini's
system instruction, the Responses `instructions`) for the signs of text
someone else wrote: a chat-template token or a fake role tag
(`<|im_start|>`, `[INST]`, `<system>`, `[system]`), a JSON message that
claims the system or developer role, a jailbreak persona ("you are now
DAN", "jailbreak mode", "developer mode enabled", "do anything now") and a
request to decode hidden text (base64, rot13, hex). The wording a system
prompt states its own rules in ("ignore previous instructions", "never
reveal your system prompt", a `### Instructions` heading, "users cannot
override your instructions") does not count there, so such a system prompt
scores 0 and is refused at no threshold. An assistant message, the model's
own earlier turn, and its tool calls' arguments are not read. The patterns,
the sensitivity levels and the score are unchanged.

**C38. The checks on the request run before the response cache.** Before,
the response cache answered before the guardrails (POL-4): a cache hit
skipped every check on the request, so an entry stored before an
organization turned a check on, under a key whose `X-Guardrail-Policy`
turned the config file's rules off, for a request only like this one (a
semantic hit), or under a caller-chosen `x-agentcc-cache-key` was served to
a request the checks block. Now the checks on the request run first: a
request they refuse gets their 403 and no cached answer, and carries no
`X-Agentcc-Cache-Status`. The checks on the answer already read a cached
answer (C25). The cache keys an entry by the request as the checks left it,
so two requests that differ only in what `pii-detection` masks share one
entry, and neither the entry's key nor its semantic vector is built from
the masked value. The checks on the request now run after authentication,
RBAC and the request quota, and before the response cache and the budget:
a cache hit waits for them; an organization paused or over its request
limit is refused with 429 before any check reads its request, as before;
a request over budget is read by the checks before the budget refuses it,
so one that is also blocked gets the check's 403 rather than the budget's 429.
On the answer the order is the same: the checks on the answer run before
the cache stores it and before the budget records its cost. An answer a
check rewrites (`pii-detection` masking the answer) is stored as the check
left it, so a request the check does not apply to (one sent with
`X-Guardrail-Policy: disabled`, for example) is served the masked answer on
a hit; an answer a check withholds is not stored. Before,
a cache backend that writes an answer when it stores it (Redis, disk, an
object store) stored the raw answer and served it raw to such a request,
and a withheld answer was stored. The response cache is off on FutureAGI's
hosted gateway (H2).

**C39. A check that rewrites the request and does not finish in time
refuses it.** A check runs with a timeout (a rule's `timeout` or
`guardrails.default_timeout`, an organization's `timeout_ms`). Before, a
check that rewrites the request (`pii-detection` with `mask`, `redact` or
`hash`, or an organization's check with the action `mask`) and outlived its
timeout kept rewriting the request after the gateway stopped waiting for
it, while the request was being sent, so the provider could get it
rewritten, partly rewritten or as sent. Now such a check runs
on a copy of the request's messages, which becomes the request only when
the check finishes in time. When it times out or fails, its rewrite was
never applied, and the request is refused before the provider is called
with 403 `remediation_unavailable` naming the check and saying why, with
`guardrails.fail_open` on (the default) or off: letting it through would
send the text the check was set to hide. Other checks keep their timeout
behaviour, and each reads its own copy of the request's fields, so one that
outlives its timeout reads the request as it was when it started, not a
later check's rewrite or what the gateway sets after the checks. A rule in
`mode: async`, which the request does not wait for, runs on a copy of what
it reads: a rewriting rule there only logs, and never rewrites the request
(U14).

**C40. Request metadata cannot set the gateway's own keys.** Request
metadata (the `x-agentcc-metadata` header and the body's `metadata` field)
shares one map with the keys the gateway writes for billing, cost,
telemetry, routing and identity, and a caller could set many of them.
`audio_seconds` priced a transcription or translation of an upload the
gateway cannot measure (anything but a WAV) on the caller's number, and the
budget counted that cost. `model_alias` applied the operator's
`cost_tracking.alias_cost_factors` to the request's price (managed credit
excepted). Routing evidence such as `routing_strategy` came back as the
gateway's own `x-agentcc-*` response headers and reached the request log.
Now every name the gateway writes into or reads out of request metadata is
reserved unless it is listed below as yours, and a test reads the
gateway's source and fails on any name written there (a literal or a
constant) that is neither. A reserved name is
dropped from both channels, in any letter case: the request still runs,
your other dimensions still land, and the dropped name does not reach your
logs. Rename a dimension of your own that uses one.

- Newly reserved: keys that start with `route_reason.`, and `a2a_context_id`,
  `a2a_task_id`, `access_group_matched`, `access_groups`,
  `answer_unavailable`, `assistants_operation`, `audio_seconds`,
  `completion_tokens`, `complexity_original_model`, `complexity_override`,
  `complexity_provider`, `complexity_score`, `complexity_source`,
  `complexity_tier`, `edge_cache`, `edge_cache_control`, `edge_cache_etag`,
  `edge_cache_vary`, `endpoint_format`, `endpoint_type`,
  `failover_attempts`, `failover_original_provider`, `fallback_model`,
  `fallback_provider`, `images_generated`, `input_characters`,
  `input_token_warning`, `input_tokens`, `model_alias`, `model_deprecated`,
  `model_map_matched`, `model_map_provider`, `model_max_output_tokens`,
  `no_perf_disclosure`, `original_model`, `original_provider`,
  `output_tokens`, `privacy_mode`, `privacy_redacted`, `prompt_tokens`,
  `provider_lock_target`, `provider_locked`, `quality`, `race_winner`,
  `request_unavailable`, `response_content_type`, `response_size_bytes`,
  `routing_rule`, `routing_strategy`, `routing_strategy_applied`,
  `tools_filtered`, `tools_requested`, `translation_drops`,
  `vector_stores_operation` and `x-guardrail-policy`. C6 lists the names
  reserved before.
- Still yours, although the gateway uses them too: `provider_lock` (the
  metadata form of `x-agentcc-provider-lock`, checked like the header),
  `if_none_match` and `edge_cache_opt_in` (edge-cache requests about your
  own response), and `customer_id`, `license_id`, `instance_id`,
  `thread_id`, `message_id` and `assistant_id`. The gateway sets those six
  itself only under license authentication or on an Assistants route whose
  URL names one, and there its value replaces yours.
- `privacy_mode` in request metadata no longer changes how the request log
  or a trace export redacts the request. To keep less of a request in the
  log, send the `x-agentcc-log-content` header (N4).
- `X-Guardrail-Policy` is read only from its header (C18). Before, the same
  value in request metadata reached the guardrail plugin too, and on
  `/v1/messages` and `/v1/responses` it replaced the header's (still only
  for a key with `allow_policy_override`).
- A transcription or translation of an upload the gateway cannot measure
  is unpriced, whatever the request's metadata holds: no
  `x-agentcc-cost`, no cost in the request log, and no budget counts it. A
  WAV is priced on its own length, as before.

**C41. The gateway admin API refuses reserved key metadata on create.**
`POST /-/keys` (behind the gateway's admin token) stored every metadata
name it was sent, while `PUT /-/keys/{id}` refused a change to a reserved
one (C6). Now `POST /-/keys` answers 400 `reserved_metadata`, naming them,
to a key whose metadata holds `access_groups`, `role`, `team`, `type`,
`key_type`, `id`, `name` or `owner`, and makes no key. `org_id` and
`allow_policy_override` stay settable there, because the platform sets
them: it binds every key it makes to its organization, and its guardrail
playground key may override a policy. Both key-sync paths (`POST
/-/keys/sync` and the gateway's pull of the platform's keys) drop those
eight names from a key and keep the key. The platform never sends them, so
keys made in the console are unchanged. On a self-hosted gateway driven
through the admin API directly, give a key a role, a team or access groups
in `config.yaml` (`auth.keys[].metadata`), and rename a label of your own
that uses one of the eight names.

**C42. `/v1beta` checks the key before any handler.** With request auth on,
the native Google GenAI API (`/v1beta`) is gated at the edge as `/v1` is
(C2). A request with no key or an invalid one gets 401 `invalid_api_key`;
before, the handler ran first and answered 403 "model ... is not available
for this API key", or 400 for an unsupported action. The key is read as
the GenAI handler reads it: the `key` query parameter, then
`x-goog-api-key`, then a `Bearer` Authorization header. `x-api-key` is not
read on `/v1beta`, as before. With license authentication on, a managed
service token gets 403 on `/v1beta` (it is valid only for `POST
/v1/chat/completions`), and a token that fails verification gets 401, both
before any handler.

**C43. `/v1/realtime` refuses every key but an internal one.** The realtime
route resolved the model in the gateway's own provider registry for any
key, so an organization's key would have reached the operator's realtime
provider and credentials, outside the organization's budget, credits,
guardrails and request log. No provider in this release implements
realtime, so the route answered 501 to every key. Now a key other than an
internal service key gets 403 `permission_denied` ("model ... is not
available for this API key") before a provider is resolved or a session
slot is taken. An internal key, and a gateway with request auth off, still
reach the gateway's own provider and get 501 in this release. Realtime
through an organization's own providers is not in this release.

**C44. File ids are random.** A file id is `file-` and 24 hexadecimal
digits from a cryptographic random source (96 bits). Before, it was
`file-<unix seconds>-<n>`, where `n` counted every organization's uploads
since the gateway started, so an id told its holder how many files other
organizations had uploaded. Treat a file id as opaque.

**C45. An organization's `default_max_tokens_estimate` is at least 1024.**
`managed_models.default_max_tokens_estimate` is the output a managed
request that sends no `max_tokens` is held for. Its minimum was 1, so such
a request could be held for one output token and still run to the model's
maximum output. The minimum is now 1024, a quarter of the gateway's 4096
default (`managed.reserve_default_output_tokens`), so an organization can
still lower its holds fourfold. A save below it (in `managed_models`, or a
rollout's) is refused with 400 naming the field. A value stored before this
release is pushed to the gateway as 1024 (the stored row is not changed),
and the gateway reads any lower value as 1024. A request that sends
`max_tokens` is held for that, with no floor. Managed models are switched
off in this release (Present but switched off).

**C46. An organization's own price for a model applies to the model that
served an own-key request, in either form.** An organization key's request
for `<provider>/<model>` that the organization's own provider serves now
reaches that provider's host as the id the organization registered,
`<model>`; before, the host was sent `<provider>/<model>`. The
organization's own price for a model (`cost_tracking.custom_pricing`)
applies to such a request whether it is keyed by the id asked or by the id
registered; when both are keyed, the id asked wins. A price keyed
`<provider>/<model>` now also prices a bare `<model>` request that provider
serves, where before that request took the listed price. It does not price
the model when another provider serves the request, with one exception,
unchanged here: when a request asked for as `<provider>/<model>` fails over
to another provider, the failover takes that price if its host answers
naming the id it was sent, and its listed price if its host answers with a
dated id. A key that is both an id one of the organization's providers
registered and `<provider>/<model>` (`anthropic/claude-sonnet-4` registered
on an Anthropic-format router, say) prices both. A model fallback hop, an
auto-routed request's runner-up included, is priced on the organization's
price for its own model, in either form, or else at its listed price, or
unpriced when the catalog does not list it; never at the price of the model
asked for. Before, a hop whose host answered naming the id it was sent
could be charged the organization's price for the model asked for or, with
no such price, that model's listed price. So, as an intended change, such a
hop on a model the catalog does not list now goes unpriced (no
`x-agentcc-cost`, `cost_source` `unpriced`) where a bare `<model>` request
charged it the listed price of the model asked for; in a
`<provider>/<model>` request on an Anthropic-format host it was already
unpriced before this change. This changes the cost estimate
(`x-agentcc-cost`, with `cost_source` `org_custom`, `modeldb` or
`unpriced`) of own-key requests only: a managed request never takes the
organization's prices.

**C47. An organization's API keys get its routing, over its own providers.**
A key limited to its organization's providers (every key made in the
console) now gets the organization's retry, provider failover, circuit
breaker and routing strategy. Before, it made one call to the first of the
organization's providers that listed the model, whatever the organization
had configured. Now:

- `round_robin`, `weighted` (each provider's `weight`), `least_latency`,
  `cost_optimized` and adaptive routing choose among the organization's
  providers that list the model. With no strategy, the first of them in
  provider-id order serves, as in C48.
- Retry (`routing.retry`) retries the provider the request went to.
- Provider failover (`routing.failover.enabled`) moves a failed request to
  another of the organization's providers that lists the model, on
  `routing.failover.on_status_codes`. The model fallback switch alone does
  not move a request across providers; it moves it down its chain (C49).
- Circuit breakers (`routing.circuit_breaker`) are the organization's own:
  one circuit per provider and model. No other organization's failures and
  none of the gateway's own circuits can open them, and they open none of
  the gateway's. While every one of the organization's providers for the
  model has an open circuit, the request gets 503 without an upstream call.
- Strategy, retry, provider failover and circuit breakers keep such a key
  on the organization's own providers and keys. A model fallback is the
  one exception: when the organization turned managed models on, the next
  model of a chain can be a managed model, served by the gateway and
  billed to the organization's credits (with the managed credit check).
  With managed models off, a fallback also stays on the organization's
  providers.

A key of the gateway's own (`key_type: internal`) still fails over across
the gateway's providers. Two things change for an internal key of an
organization: the model map applies to it (C48), and when the
organization has chains and never set `fallback_enabled`, it runs the
organization's failover settings (C49).

**C48. The model map applies to every key of an organization.** A model
name the organization's `model_map` maps to one of its own providers
(enabled, with a key) goes only to that provider, as the organization's
own instance with the organization's credentials. This holds for an
internal key too: before, an internal key's mapped name went to the
gateway's provider of the same id with the gateway's key, under the name
it was sent. When that provider lists exactly one model and not the
requested name, the request is sent as that model, so a map entry can be
an alias. A map entry that names any other provider is not used for a key
limited to its organization's providers. A model with no map entry goes
to the first of the organization's providers that lists it in provider-id
order, unless, for a key limited to its organization's providers, a
strategy (C47) chooses among them; before, it went to whichever provider a
map iteration reached first, and an alias answered 403 to such a key. A
chat request sends an alias as that model. Embeddings, images, audio, rerank, OCR,
search, `/v1/completions` and `/v1/responses` take a mapped provider only
when they can send the requested name unchanged.

**C49. Model fallback chains run unless the organization turned them off.**
An organization whose `routing.model_fallbacks` holds a chain and that never
set `routing.fallback_enabled` now has its chains tried, on the failover
status codes (429, 500, 502, 503 and 504 unless it set others), as the
Fallbacks page always showed. `fallback_enabled: false` keeps them off: they
stay stored and are never tried. The Fallbacks page and Org Config >
Routing show the same value for the switch, and the Provider Failover
switch, the timeout switches and the default status-code lists show what
the gateway runs when they are unset. A chain is looked up by the
requested name first, so a `model_map` alias's own chain runs, streamed
or not. An internal key of an organization that has chains and never set
the switch now runs the organization's failover settings (its
`routing.failover`, else 3 attempts on the default status codes) across
the gateway's providers, as with `fallback_enabled: true`; before, it ran
the gateway's own failover.

**C50. Run budgets, per-call cost caps and deadlines are enforced.** Before,
`x-agentcc-budget-usd`, `x-agentcc-budget-remaining-usd`,
`x-agentcc-max-cost-usd` and `x-agentcc-deadline-ms` were checked and then
ignored. Now, on chat completions:

- **Run budget.** A call names its run with `x-agentcc-budget-scope` (or
  `x-agentcc-ledger-id`), else `x-agentcc-run-id`. `x-agentcc-budget-usd`
  sets that run's budget, shared by every call of the run in the same
  organization; a lower value sent later lowers it, a higher one is
  ignored. Before routing, each call holds its worst-case cost at the
  model's price (its prompt plus its `max_tokens`; with none, 4096 output
  tokens, or the model's maximum output when that is lower) and settles at
  what it cost. A call whose worst case is over what the budget has left
  has its `max_tokens` lowered to fit, as under a per-call cap (below);
  when not even 256 output tokens fit, or the budget is spent, it gets 402
  `agent_budget_exhausted` and is never sent upstream. `error.metadata`
  names the run (`scope: "run:<id>"`). Each call in a run with a budget
  answers `x-agentcc-budget-remaining-usd`, what the budget has left. A
  run's budget is kept in Redis
  for 24 hours after its last call (the org's
  `routing.agents.budget_scope_ttl_seconds`). A call that sends
  `x-agentcc-budget-usd` without a run id has a budget for that call alone.
  A retry that repeats the call's `x-agentcc-attempt-id` reuses its hold.
  Embedding and rerank calls that name a run count what they cost toward
  its budget too.
- **Per-call cap.** `x-agentcc-max-cost-usd` and
  `x-agentcc-budget-remaining-usd` cap one call, in a run or not; the lowest
  of them and the run's remaining budget applies. When the worst case is
  over the cap, `max_tokens` is lowered to the largest value that fits and
  the response says so in `x-agentcc-max-tokens-clamped`; when not even 256
  output tokens fit, the call gets 402 `agent_call_cap_exceeded` and is
  never sent. A model with no price cannot be held under a cap or a budget:
  402 `call_cap_unenforceable`, unless the org sets
  `routing.agents.unpriced_under_cap` to `allow`. A cap needs no Redis.
- **No Redis.** A run budget needs the gateway's Redis. Without it, a call
  that sends a run budget gets 503 `budget_state_unavailable`; with Redis
  configured but unreachable, every call that names a run gets it. An org
  that sets `budgets.fail_mode` to `open` is served instead, with nothing
  held.
- **Deadline.** `x-agentcc-deadline-ms` (also `x-omega-deadline-ms` and
  `metadata.agent.deadline_ms`) is counted from when the gateway received
  the call. On a non-streaming call every upstream attempt runs under it:
  an attempt still running at the deadline is cut and its upstream
  connection closed, and the call gets 504 `gateway_timeout`; an attempt
  that would start after the deadline is never sent and is logged as
  skipped (reason `deadline`).
  When no attempt could start before the deadline, the call gets 504
  `deadline_exceeded`, and every response the deadline ended carries
  `x-agentcc-deadline-exceeded: true`. A retry's wait never runs past the
  deadline: the call ends at it with the last attempt's error. A stream
  whose first chunk has not arrived by the deadline is answered the same
  way; a stream that has started is cut at the deadline and ends with a
  `gateway_timeout` error event and no `[DONE]`.

**C51. `GET /v1/capabilities` and `POST /v1/feedback` have fixed shapes.**
Both answer any valid key. Their field names and JSON types are pinned by
contract tests; a later release may add fields but does not rename, remove
or retype these. What `/v1/capabilities` lists (endpoints, providers and
their values) depends on the gateway's and the organization's providers.

- `GET /v1/capabilities` returns `generated_at` and `endpoints`, each with
  `endpoint`, `launch_tier` and `providers` (by provider id: `status`,
  `credential_type`, `features`, `managed_allowed`, `source`, `qualified`,
  `qualified_at`, and `price` when the provider has one: `sku`,
  `usd_per_unit_billed`, `markup_percent`). `features` holds the booleans
  `stream`, `tools`, `json_schema`, `vision`, `audio_input`, `reasoning`
  and `prompt_caching`. `GET /v1/capabilities?model=<id>` returns
  `generated_at`, `model` and `providers` (by provider id:
  `credential_type`, `source`, `flags` (the same booleans),
  `context_length`, `max_output_tokens`, `modalities` with `input` and
  `output`, and `endpoints` by endpoint with `status` and
  `managed_allowed`).
- `POST /v1/feedback` takes one JSON object of at most 4 KB:
  `generation_id` (the call's `x-agentcc-request-id`, at most 256 bytes),
  `outcome` (`ok`, `bad` or `verify_failed`) and an optional numeric
  `score`, and no other field. It answers 200
  `{"data": {"generation_id", "outcome", "event_id"}}`. Any other body gets
  400 `invalid_feedback`. An unknown generation, another organization's,
  one older than an hour, or one the gateway did not keep (a BYOK call
  with no agent headers) gets 404 `generation_not_found`.

**C52. Provider key rotation changes the key the gateway sends.** Before,
`POST /-/admin/providers/{id}/rotate` and `.../rotate/promote` answered 200
and showed the new key as primary while every upstream call kept the old
key, and `drain_period` was ignored. Now, for a provider in the gateway's
config file with `rotation.enabled`:

- The promote first makes one upstream call with the new key: `openai` and
  `azure` providers list models; other formats, and an OpenAI-compatible
  server whose models endpoint answers 404 or 405, send a one-token chat
  completion to the first of the provider's `models`. A key the provider
  refuses answers 422 and stays pending; nothing changes. The answer gives
  the provider's status, type and code, never its message, since a provider
  may repeat the key it refused. A validation call that gets no answer
  (nothing listening, a TLS error, the provider's timeout) also answers 422
  and stays pending, saying the call got no answer and the key was not
  checked.
- From the promote on, every new call and every retry sends the new key.
  A call already in flight finishes on the old one, whose idle connections
  close after the provider's own `drain_period` (default 30 s). An async
  job (`x-agentcc-async: true`) queued before the promote and started after
  it sends the new key.
- With `redis` on, the promote reaches every replica over Redis pub/sub,
  the key sealed with a key derived from the admin token; nothing is
  stored. A replica that is not subscribed at that moment keeps its key.
- Rollback cancels a pending rotation. A promoted key already serves every
  call, so rolling it back answers 409. To go back, wait for the drain to
  end (`drain_until` in `GET .../rotation` and in the 409) and start a new
  rotation with the previous key; a rotation asked for while one drains
  answers 409 naming `drain_until`. An unknown provider, or one without
  `rotation.enabled`, answers 404.
- The rotation lives in the gateway's memory, and a restarted or newly
  rolled-out replica starts with the key in its deployment config: update
  the deployment config with the new key before the next restart or
  rollout. Every rotation answer and `GET .../rotation` say so
  (`applies_until: "restart"` and `note`).
- Each promote writes one log line naming the provider, where the key came
  from, how it was validated and the drain period; no log line carries a
  key or part of one.
- Bedrock providers are not rotated this way (they sign with AWS
  credentials); `rotation.enabled` on one is ignored with a warning.

**C53. Budget refusals name their level; Throttle has its own code.** Every
budget refusal (429 `org_budget_exceeded`, `budget_exceeded` or the new
`budget_throttled`) now carries, in the request log's metadata,
`budget_exceeded_level` (`org`, `team:<team>`, `user:<user>`,
`key:<key name>` or `tag:<key>:<value>`), `budget_period` (`daily`,
`weekly`, `monthly` or `total`), `budget_period_start` (RFC 3339, UTC) and
`budget_action` (`block` or `throttle`). A value the caller sent for any of
the four is overwritten. A Throttle budget past its limit answers 429
`budget_throttled` with `Retry-After` (F28).

On the OpenAI-compatible chat API, a blocking refusal's body is an `error`
object with `type: "rate_limit_error"` and a `message` explaining the
budget. Its `code` is `org_budget_exceeded` for an organization's budget
(hosted included), or `budget_exceeded` for the gateway's config-file
tracker. These 429 refusals are distinct from credit and agent-run-budget
402 errors; native API routes may translate the error into their own shape.

**C54. A per-user budget is the request's user's.** The user level of an
organization's budgets now counts the request's user: `x-agentcc-user-id`
(or `metadata.agent.user_id`) when sent, else the body's `user`, else the
key's owner, as before. The key owner's own user budget still applies when
the request names another user, so naming a user does not step around it;
one request is charged once to each of those users. A user id longer than
64 bytes keys its Redis counter by a hash.

**C55. An organization's Model Database overrides apply to its requests.** Settings > Org Config > Model Database used to be stored and pushed but not applied: prices came from the operator's
model database, and token limits and capabilities were checked against the global model database only. An org's
overrides are now merged on top of the gateway's model database for that org's requests. A field left blank keeps the
model database's value.

**Which entry applies.** An override keyed `gpt-4o` applies to `gpt-4o` and to `openai/gpt-4o`. An override keyed
`openai/gpt-4o` applies when the org's `openai` provider serves `gpt-4o`. The cost plugin, the validation plugin, model
"auto", `/v1/count_tokens`, `/v1/capabilities` and `/v1/models` all match entries this way.

**Prices: precedence.** Prices apply only to calls made with the org's own provider keys (BYOK):

1. An explicit Cost Tracking custom price (`cost_tracking.custom_pricing`, while cost tracking is on) wins.
2. Otherwise the Model Database override's input, output and cached-input prices apply, field by field. A blank field
   keeps the model database's price.
3. Otherwise the model database's price applies.

A call to a managed model is always billed at FutureAGI's managed catalog price. No org override changes a managed
price.

The Model Database tab no longer shows the Batch Input/Output per Token fields. No gateway path prices a call at batch
rates: gateway batch jobs call the provider's regular API, so a batch price had no effect. Values already stored are
kept as they are.

**Token limits** apply to every call of the org, BYOK and managed (they only narrow what the org's own traffic may do):

- **Max Output Tokens.** A request whose `max_tokens` or `max_completion_tokens` is above the limit is refused with
  400 `max_tokens_exceeds_limit`, and the message names the limit. A request that sets neither is sent with
  `max_tokens` set to the limit. We refuse instead of clamping because a silently shortened answer is worse than a
  clear error.
- **Max Input Tokens.** A request whose estimated input (about four characters per token) is above the limit is
  refused with 413 `input_too_large`, and the message names the limit. The org's limit is checked exactly, without
  the 1.5x margin the gateway allows on the model database's own limit.
- Under model "auto", the limits and switches of the model auto picks apply.
- `/v1/count_tokens` reports the org's Max Input Tokens as `max_context_tokens` and counts `remaining_tokens` against
  it.

**Capabilities.** Each capability is now a three-way choice: Default, On or Off. The old switch showed an unset
capability as off, and saving the model stored `false` for it.

- **Off** refuses a request that uses the capability with 400 `model_capability_error`, and the message names the
  switch: Function Calling (tools), Parallel Tool Calls, Vision (an image part), Audio Input, Audio Output, PDF Input
  (a file part), Streaming, Response Schema (a `json_schema` response format), System Messages (a system or developer
  message) and Reasoning (`reasoning_effort`, `reasoning` or `thinking`).
- **On** lets through a request the model database would refuse.
- **Default** keeps the model database's value.
- Prompt Caching has no request-side signal. It changes only what `/v1/models` and `/v1/capabilities` report.

A key's `/v1/capabilities` view shows the org's limits and switches on every model cell and in the per-provider
rollup. Prices are not shown there. The admin view (`/-/capabilities`) and a global key's view are unchanged.

**C56. Model `auto` prices your own models as you pay for them.** Auto used to read only the managed catalog and the bundled model database. As a result:

- A model on the org's own provider that was priced only through Cost Tracking or Model Database was refused with
  400 `no_auto_candidate` ("no price or capability data").
- Every model of a Together or Fireworks preset provider was refused the same way.

Now:

- **Own-provider candidates** are priced with the same precedence as the bill: Cost Tracking, then Model Database,
  then the gateway's model database. Auto ranks, and applies the price caps, at the price the call is billed at. The
  org's limits and switches count too.
- **Managed candidates** keep the catalog price. Only the org's limits and switches apply to them.
- **Preset provider ids** find their models under the model database's prefixes: `together` -> `together_ai/`,
  `fireworks` -> `fireworks_ai/`, `vertex` -> `vertex_ai/`, `google` -> `gemini/`, `x-ai` -> `xai/`. The provider's
  own `<provider>/<model>` entry is checked first, and the general entry last. `/v1/capabilities` uses the same
  lookup.
- **A model nothing prices** is still set aside, and the reason is recorded.
- **Console.** Under Models > Auto routing, How auto works states the price rule. In the candidate picker, each of
  your providers' models shows the price auto will use (Cost Tracking or Model Database), or says that auto skips it
  unless the gateway's model database prices it.

**C57. `/v1/models` lists only what the key can call.** `/v1/models` and `GET /v1/models/{id}` used to list the gateway's global registry to every caller, while chat refused
those models to customer keys. On a hosted gateway that exposed operator models, including Bedrock ARNs that contain
the operator's AWS account id.

Each customer (non-internal) key now lists and GETs only:

- the models of its org's own providers that hold credentials, narrowed by the key's provider and model ACLs and
  described as the org sees them (Model Database limits, prices and switches; Cost Tracking prices win);
- `auto`;
- the managed catalog, when the org has opted in (also under the key's ACLs), at FutureAGI's catalog prices with the
  org's Model Database token limits and capability switches applied, since those also apply to its managed calls.

No operator provider's model is listed. Any other id answers 404 `model_not_found`. A customer key without an org
lists only `auto`, because chat refuses it every operator model. Internal keys, license-authorized requests and
gateways without keys list as before.

This is a visible behaviour change for clients that list models with a customer key.

**C58. `route-hint` and `require` steer model `auto`.** These agent-context fields used to be validated and recorded, but auto ignored them. They can be sent as headers
(`x-agentcc-route-hint`, `x-agentcc-require`, or the `x-omega-` forms) or as `metadata.agent.route_hint` and
`metadata.agent.require`.

**route-hint**

- `cost`, `balanced` and `quality` set auto's preference for the request when no `x-agentcc-auto-preference` header
  is sent. The header wins, and both win over the org's `routing.auto.preference`.
- `latency` is refused under model "auto" with 400 `route_hint_unsupported`, and the message names the value. Auto
  ranks by price tier against the task. The only latency data it has is this node's recent per-model P50, which a
  model lacks until it has been called on the node, and which also depends on output length. A "fastest" ranking
  built on it would be arbitrary on a fresh node, so a clear refusal is safer than a hint that silently does
  something else.
- On a named model, route-hint changes nothing. It is accepted and recorded, as before.

**require**

- Accepts `tools`, `json_schema`, `vision`, `reasoning`, `audio` and `long_context` (a context window of at least
  128,000 tokens), as a comma-separated list.
- Auto sets aside every candidate that lacks a required capability. Capabilities are read from the org's view of the
  model, so its Model Database switches count. The decision reason says "requires ...".
- If no candidate remains, the request is refused with 400 `no_auto_candidate`, and the message names the
  requirement.
- In the console, the Auto routing tab's Preference card names route-hint, and How auto works lists the require
  filter.

**C59. Analytics refuses a granularity it cannot bucket by.**
`usage-timeseries`, `latency-stats`, `error-breakdown` and
`guardrail-trends` now bucket by `5m`, `15m`, `1h`, `6h` or `1d` (fixed
widths, aligned to UTC) as well as `minute`, `hour`, `day`, `week` and
`month`; no granularity is still `hour`. Any other value answers 400 naming
the granularity, where it was silently treated as `hour`. The analytics
endpoints that do not bucket (`overview`, `cost-breakdown`,
`model-comparison`, `guardrail-overview`, `guardrail-rules`) still ignore
it (F37).

**C60. Webhook payloads carry the error code.** Every webhook event's
payload now has `error_code`: the code of the gateway's error answer for
the request, or `""`. It is `""` when that code can be a provider's own:
the openai and azure adapters pass a provider's code through, and an error
answered as `provider_<HTTP status>` with a nonzero status (the provider's,
or 502 for some upstream failures the gateway reports itself) is left out
with them. Other provider errors keep their `provider_...` code: on this
release, the errors the anthropic, gemini, bedrock and cohere adapters
parse, the speech relays' refusals, and a provider that never answered
(`provider_0`). A provider's code never raises `budget.exceeded`.
A `budget.exceeded` payload also has `budget_level`, `budget_period`,
`budget_period_start` and `budget_action`, each `null` when the gateway's
refusal did not name it (F35).

**C61. Email alert fields.** An email alert's `thresholds` are checked when
it is saved: `error_rate_percent` above 0 and at most 100, `latency_ms` a
whole number from 1, `cost_usd` above 0, `window_minutes` a whole number
from 1 to 1440 and `min_requests` a whole number from 1; anything else
answers 400 (other keys are stored as sent and never read). Reads add
`last_error` and `last_error_at`, the last failed delivery, cleared by the
next email sent. `last_triggered_at` is the last alert email sent; Send test
neither sets it nor waits for the cooldown (F34).

**C62. `x-agentcc-config` is read, and a config the gateway cannot
apply is refused.** The header was accepted and ignored, even when it was
not JSON. It is now a JSON object of at most 16 KiB. Its keys are request
header names without `x-agentcc-`: `cache-ttl`, `cache-namespace`,
`cache-force-refresh`, `request-timeout`, `timeout`, `max-attempts`,
`retry-delay-ms`, `backoff`, `trace-id`, `session-id`, `session-name`,
`session-path`, `request-id`, `user-id`, `metadata`, `property-<name>`,
`provider-lock`, `complexity-override`, `auto-preference`,
`guardrail-policy`, `log-content` and the agent context fields (`run-id`,
`max-cost-usd`, ...). Each key sets its header unless the request sends that
header itself, and the value is then checked and applied as the header is:
a provider lock only to a provider the key may use, retry headers only
tighten the org's retries, a timeout only shortens. The Agent Command
Center SDK's nested GatewayConfig (`GatewayConfig.to_headers()`) is read
too: in its `cache` section, `ttl`, `namespace` and `force_refresh` apply
as the cache headers. The `retry`, `fallback`, `load_balance`,
`guardrails`, `routing`, `mirror` and `timeout` sections and the other
cache fields are not read; the response names them in
`x-agentcc-config-ignored` (for example `cache.strategy,retry`). A section
or field that is null asks for nothing. A string `timeout` is the
`x-agentcc-timeout` duration (`"30s"`); a numeric `timeout` is named there
and not applied. `cache-ttl` and `cache.ttl` take whole seconds or a
duration string (`"5m"`), and `request-timeout` whole milliseconds; a
number whose value is whole counts (`300`, `300.0` and `3e2` are all 300),
and a fraction such as `300.5` is refused. An unknown key, a value of
the wrong type, a section that is not an object, two keys that set the same
header, a duplicate key, more than 32 sections and cache fields to name, a
cache field name that is not 1 to 64 letters, digits, `_`, `-` or `.`, or
more than 16 KiB answers 400 `invalid_agentcc_config` naming it, before
authentication.

**C63. `x-agentcc-guardrail-policy` is read.** It is an alias of
`X-Guardrail-Policy`, the guardrail mode for the request (`log-only`,
`disabled` or `strict`) under which the gateway's config-file rules run (an
organization's checks ignore it, C18). Where the gateway has such rules, the
key must allow it (`allow_policy_override`; without it, 403). It takes a
mode, not policy ids. When both are sent,
`X-Guardrail-Policy` wins. Before, the alias was ignored, so a request that
sent it got the organization's checks unchanged. Where the gateway has
such rules, a request that sends policy ids in it is now refused (403, or
400 `invalid_policy` where the key allows overrides).

**C64. A provider's own client timeout answers 504.** When the HTTP
client timeout of an OpenAI-compatible, Azure or Bedrock provider (its
`default_timeout`) ends a call before the request's deadline, the request
gets 504 `gateway_timeout` ("provider request timed out"), as it does when
the request's deadline ends the call. Before, it got 502 `provider_0` with
a message that named the provider's URL. The default retry, failover and
circuit-breaker lists include 504. A retry or failover list that names
502 but not 504 no longer matches this timeout: turn on `on_timeout`, or
add 504. A circuit breaker now counts a provider timeout (504, or a
provider's 408 or 504) as a failure whatever its `on_status_codes`.
On an OpenAI-compatible provider, an answer whose body stops arriving
until a deadline ends it, or a stream whose first chunk does not arrive
before one, also gets 504 `gateway_timeout`; a provider that cannot be
reached at all still gets 502.

**C65. A request's own id is kept, and the gateway's stays.** A
client's `x-agentcc-request-id` (at most 255 characters) is logged as
metadata `client_request_id` and echoed as `x-agentcc-client-request-id`.
The response's `x-agentcc-request-id` is the gateway's own id, as before
(the client's was dropped). A longer value answers 400
`invalid_agentcc_header`.

**C66. An organization's rate limits apply as Org Config describes them.**
The org config's `rate_limiting` (Org Config > Rate Limiting) now counts and
limits the organization's chat completions, completions, Responses,
Anthropic Messages and Gemini (`/v1beta`) requests
(`/v1/messages/count_tokens` too, when an Anthropic-format provider serves
it):

- `global_rpm`: the organization's requests per minute on those routes,
  from every key together. Before, it was each key's own limit, so an
  organization with five keys got five times its limit.
- `global_tpm`: the organization's tokens per minute on those routes, every
  key together.
- `per_key_rpm`: each key's requests per minute, as before. A limit set on
  the key itself (`auth.keys` `rate_limit_rpm`) is used instead.
- `per_key_tpm`: each key's tokens per minute.
- `per_model_rpm`: each model's requests per minute from every key of the
  organization, counted by the model name the request sends.
- `per_user_rpm`: each end user's requests per minute from every key. On
  chat completions the user is `x-agentcc-user-id` (or
  `metadata.agent.user_id`), else the body's `user`; on completions and
  Responses it is the body's `user`. Anthropic Messages and Gemini requests
  name no user here, so it does not limit them; nor a request that names no
  user: the key's owner, which budgets fall back to, is not a user here.

A relayed speech session (N12) counts as one request against
`global_rpm` and `per_key_rpm`, and against `per_model_rpm` by the model
the session's URL names; a session whose URL names no model (Cartesia
synthesis, or a session on the vendor's default model) is not counted per
model. A session over one of them is refused at the WebSocket handshake
with 429 naming it, before the vendor is reached. A session adds no
tokens to `global_tpm` or `per_key_tpm`, but while other requests have
spent one of them, or the key's own `rate_limit_tpm` (C75), for the
minute, a new session that limit holds is refused the same way.

Embeddings (`/v1/embeddings`), images, audio (`/v1/audio/...`), rerank,
search, OCR, Assistants, Vector Stores, Files, video, realtime and
scheduled requests are not counted or limited by this section (Known
limits; the key's own and the gateway's limits apply to the Assistants,
Vector Stores and Files APIs, C80). An answer served from the response
cache is not counted against, or refused by, any rate limit.

Before, `global_tpm`, `per_key_tpm`, `per_model_rpm` and `per_user_rpm`
limited nothing. A token limit lets a request through while the minute's
tokens are under the limit, and when the request finishes it counts the
tokens its response reports, streams included. While a request the gateway
reads as chat messages runs (chat completions and completions, and Messages
or Gemini requests it translates for a provider of another format), it
holds an estimate: its messages at about 4 characters a token plus
`max_completion_tokens` or `max_tokens`. A request that failed with no
answer counts none, and a stream that ended without reported usage keeps
its estimate. One request can therefore take the minute over the limit; the
next one is refused. A request is counted against every limit, or, when one
refuses it, against none.

The refusal is 429. On chat completions, completions and Responses it is
`rate_limit_exceeded`, with `error.param` naming the field that refused it
(`global_rpm`, `global_tpm`, `per_key_rpm`, `per_key_tpm`, `per_model_rpm`
or `per_user_rpm`; a key's own limit is `rate_limit_rpm`, the gateway's
default per key `rate_limiting.global_rpm`), a message naming the limit and
its value, and `Retry-After`; a refused key limit there now carries the
same `param` and `Retry-After`. On Anthropic Messages and Gemini it is that
API's own error (`rate_limit_error`, `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`), whose message
names the field, its value and the seconds to wait. A successful chat
completions response carries `x-ratelimit-limit-requests`,
`x-ratelimit-remaining-requests` and `x-ratelimit-reset-requests` for the
tightest request limit and, when a token limit is set,
`x-ratelimit-limit-tokens`, `x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens` and
`x-ratelimit-reset-tokens`.

With Redis (`redis.enabled`), every replica shares these org-config RPM
and TPM counts, and each counter's key names its organization. A config-file
key's own `rate_limit_tpm` is separate and remains replica-local even with
Redis (C75, Known limits). A caller's `x-agentcc-metadata` or
body `metadata` cannot set or raise any of these limits. The gateway applies
them only while its own `rate_limiting.enabled` is on (the default); Org
Config > Rate Limiting shows whether this gateway reports rate limiting as
enforced.

**C67. `POST /-/batches` names the API key its items run as.** A batch
submit now takes, next to the admin token, the header
`x-agentcc-batch-key: <an API key>` (bare or `Bearer <key>`). Each item runs
as a `POST /v1/chat/completions` request authenticated by that key, so it
runs as the key's organization: its providers, model access, guardrails,
budgets, rate limits and credits, and the request log files the item under
the key, its own request id and the batch request's trace id. An item's
client address is the submit's, so an organization or key IP allowlist
applies to the address that submitted the batch. With request auth on (every
shipped config), a submit without the header answers 400
`batch_key_required`, and an unknown, revoked or expired key 401
`invalid_api_key`; nothing runs. With auth off a submit may leave it out and
runs as before; a key it names is still checked. `GET /-/batches/{id}` and
`POST /-/batches/{id}/cancel` take `org_id`: a batch is found only with its
own organization's id (and a batch submitted without a key only with no
`org_id`); any other answers 404 and leaves the batch running. Submit, get
and cancel answer with `org_id`, and submit and get with `key_id`; the key
itself is never returned. The 10 MiB body limit and the default concurrency
(10, capped at the number of requests) are unchanged. Batches still live in
the gateway's memory: a restart loses them, and a finished batch is kept for
an hour. So batches need a single gateway replica: get and cancel answer 404
on any replica but the one that accepted the batch, and a key made with
`POST /-/keys` on one replica is unknown to the others until their next
control-plane key sync, so a submit naming it there answers 401
`invalid_api_key`.

**C68. An organization's alerts say how serious they are.** An alert rule
now carries a severity, `info`, `warning` or `critical`, set in Monitoring >
Create Rule and in Org Config > Alerting. The gateway sends it with every
alert the rule fires: as `severity` in the webhook's JSON body, and as a
"Severity:" line in the Slack message, whose emoji follows it. A rule saved
without a severity is sent as `warning`. An alert from a rule in the
gateway's own `config.yaml` has no severity, so its webhook body has no
`severity` field. `severity` is a new field of an alert rule in the admin
contract. Before this release the platform dropped it before the push.

**C69. An organization's provider health is the organization's own.**
`GET /agentcc/gateways/{id}/providers/` takes each provider's `status` from
the organization's request logs of the last 24 hours: `unhealthy` when 50%
or more of its requests failed, `degraded` at 10% or more, both counted
from 5 requests; with fewer it is `healthy`. A guardrail block (403 with a
triggered check) and a request the operator's managed models served are
not counted at all: not as a request, a failure or in the latency. `status_reason` says which rule applied (for example
`fewer than 5 requests in 24 h`), `healthy` is `status != "unhealthy"`, and
`circuit_state` is `"n/a"`. Before, the action merged the gateway's
`/-/health/providers`, which is the operator's monitor, by the bare
provider id: an organization's `openai` showed the operator's `openai`
breaker, and a half-open breaker (the gateway writes `half-open`) never read
as degraded. A provider the config push leaves out has `pushed: false`,
`status: "unhealthy"` and a reason such as
`not pushed: unsupported credential key organization` (C73) or
`not pushed: the stored credential cannot be decrypted`.

**C70. Only an Owner or Admin's health check re-pushes every
organization's config.** Any member may still run
`POST /agentcc/gateways/{id}/health_check/` and gets the result. Its side
effect, pushing every organization's active config to the gateway (at most
once per 5 minutes), now runs only when an Owner or Admin of the
organization checks, and `org_configs_pushed` says whether this check ran
it; before, any member's click, a Viewer's included, ran it. Every check,
passed or failed, records its time and outcome for the organization: list,
retrieve, `health_check` and `config` return `last_health_check` (ISO 8601,
null when none is recorded) and `last_health_check_status` (`healthy` or
`unreachable`). The record is kept in the platform's cache; after the cache
is cleared it reads as no check recorded until the next one.

**C71. `GET /agentcc/gateways/{id}/config/` carries the gateway's own
settings.** It now adds the `server`, `logging` and `batch` blocks and the
`org_sections_enforced` list of the gateway's `GET /-/config`, unchanged.
Nothing else from `/-/config` is copied; a block the gateway does not report
is absent, as it is when the gateway cannot be reached or refuses the read.

**C72. `test-playground` reads a guardrail outcome as the gateway sends
it.** In `POST /agentcc/gateways/{id}/test-playground/`, `blocked` is true
for a 403 whose `error.type` is `guardrail_error`, and `warned` for a 2xx
with `x-agentcc-guardrail-triggered: true`. The new `guardrail_action`
(`warn` or `log`) and `triggered_checks` (the check names) come from
`x-agentcc-guardrail-action` and `x-agentcc-guardrails-triggered`; they are
null and empty when the gateway does not send them.

Before, `warned` was set only on status 246 and `blocked` on 403 or 446. The
gateway sends neither 246 nor 446, so a check that warned read as a pass,
and any 403 (a key refused the model, say) read as a guardrail block.

**C73. A provider credential with a key the gateway does not take is
refused.** `POST /agentcc/provider-credentials/`, its `rotate` action and the
console's `update-provider` answer 400 naming each such key (for example
`organization` or `api_secret`). The legacy `access_key`, `secret_key` and
`region` still map to `aws_access_key_id`, `aws_secret_access_key` and
`aws_region`. Before, the save answered 201 and the config push logged and
skipped the provider, so it never reached the gateway. A provider already
stored with such a key shows as not pushed (C69); rotating its credentials
without the key repairs it.

**C74. Request-log dates, export, guardrail feedback and custom property
defaults.**

- `started_after` and `started_before` on `GET /agentcc/request-logs/`, its
  search, sessions and export read an ISO 8601 offset (`Z` or `+05:30`; send
  `+` as `%2B` in a query string). A value with no offset is read as UTC,
  as before: it is never refused. The console now sends the offset, so its
  date filter matches the local times the table shows.
- `GET /agentcc/request-logs/export/` validates its filters as the list
  does: a value it cannot read answers 400 instead of being dropped (which
  widened the export to every log). 0 matching rows answers 400
  `export_empty`; more than 10,000 answers 400 `export_too_large` with the
  count. A new `max_rows` (1 to 10,000) streams the first rows in the
  `ordering` sent (newest `started_at` first when none is sent) instead of
  that refusal. The
  console's Export shows the count and the 10,000-row cap before it
  downloads, and the server's message when it refuses. Times in the file
  are UTC.
- Guardrail feedback keeps one answer per request, check and reviewer:
  `GET /agentcc/guardrail-feedback/?mine=true` lists your own answers;
  `PATCH /agentcc/guardrail-feedback/{id}/` changes `feedback` and `comment`
  only (403 `feedback_not_yours` for someone else's answer, 400
  `feedback_target_fixed` for a change of request or check); a second POST
  for the same request and check updates your answer. The summary counts
  each reviewer's latest answer once, so an edited answer no longer counts
  twice.
- A custom property's Default is not applied anywhere (the gateway and the
  request logs never fill it in), so a new non-null `default_value` answers
  400 `property_rule_not_enforced`. A Default saved before stays readable
  and may be kept as it is or cleared with `null`. Required and Allowed
  Values are unchanged: `POST /agentcc/custom-properties/validate/` checks
  them; the gateway does not apply them to requests.

**C75. A config-file key's `rate_limit_tpm` limits its tokens.** A key
defined in the gateway's config file (`auth.keys`) is held to its
`rate_limit_tpm`: once the tokens its answers reported in the current
minute reach it, the key's next request gets 429
`token_rate_limit_exceeded`. Checking the limit charges nothing; each
answer's reported tokens are charged when it finishes, so one request can
take the key past its limit, and an answer served from the response cache
is charged nothing. This window is the key's own, apart from its request
limit, and is counted on each replica (Known limits). Before,
`rate_limit_tpm` was read and limited nothing. Keys made through the
platform cannot carry it (C22); the organization's `global_tpm` and
`per_key_tpm` (C66) hold every key of the organization, one without a
limit of its own included.

**C76. A routing alias sends its target's model and keeps its fallback
chain.** When the model a request names has routing targets
(`routing.targets`) whose target sets `model_override`, the provider
receives that override, streamed or not, whether or not the alias is also
listed among the provider's models, and an alias with a single target is
routed like one with several. A `model_fallbacks` chain configured under
the alias's name runs when its targets fail. A single-target alias whose
only provider is unhealthy is refused, and nothing is sent upstream.

**C77. Chat answers keep the provider's own fields; Gemini runs its own
tools.** A chat completion, streamed or not, keeps every field the
provider sent that the gateway's response does not name (for example
Perplexity's `citations` and `search_results`, or a provider's own `usage`
counters); a field the gateway names keeps the gateway's value. On a
Gemini provider:

- a tool Gemini runs itself, written as `{"google_search": {}}` (or
  `googleSearch`, `url_context`, `code_execution`,
  `google_search_retrieval` with its config as written), reaches Gemini
  beside the caller's functions;
- a grounded answer that is not streamed carries its sources as
  `url_citation` annotations on the message, beside its
  `grounding_metadata`;
- a tool Gemini cannot serve is refused with 400 `unsupported_tool` before
  the provider is called, unless the request also has a tool Gemini
  serves: then only the served tools are sent, so a model alias or failover
  group that spans providers keeps working.

**C78. An error message carries no credential from a URL.** In an error
the gateway answers in the OpenAI, Anthropic or Gemini error format, a
URL's password and its credential query parameters (`key`, `api_key`,
`apikey`, `access_token`, `token`, `password`, `secret`, `sig`,
`signature`, `x-goog-api-key`, `subscription-key`) read `REDACTED`; the
rest of the message is unchanged. A Gemini API key travels in the
`x-goog-api-key` header, never in the URL. It is not sent across a redirect
to another origin, on any later hop of it included, and a redirect from
`https` to `http` is refused. Every provider format the gateway supports
is tested to keep its key out of its errors.

**C79. A stream carries its usage once, where the request asks for it.**
Streams on `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/completions` guarantee:

- A request that sets `stream_options: {"include_usage": true}` gets
  OpenAI's contract: exactly one chunk with empty `choices`, right before
  `[DONE]`. It carries the billed usage, and on a managed key the billed
  cost.
- A request that sets neither `stream_options.include_usage` nor the
  `x-agentcc-include-metadata` header gets no chunk with empty or null
  `choices`, so the usual loop over `chunk.choices[0].delta.content`
