  reaches `[DONE]`. The billed usage rides on the last chunk that has
  choices, the one carrying `finish_reason`, as Mistral's API sends it.
  The gateway holds that finish chunk until the provider's stream has
  ended and the request is metered (the cost, the credits, the request
  log and an organization's output checks run first), then writes it with
  the usage. With `n` above 1 it holds each choice's finish chunk and puts
  the usage on the last one it writes. No other chunk waits, except the
  other choices in a chunk that carries a finishing choice: that chunk is
  held whole.
- `x-agentcc-include-metadata: 1` (or `true`) asks for the one final chunk
  as well, on both endpoints, and that chunk then carries
  `agentcc_metadata` beside the usage.
- On `/v1/chat/completions`, a managed stream whose provider sent no usage
  is billed on the gateway's estimate, and that estimate, with the billed
  cost, is the usage the client sees, in either shape.
- The usage a provider sends is metered and never forwarded, on whatever
  chunk it rides: its usage chunk, its finish chunk, Bedrock Converse's
  metadata chunk (one empty choice and the usage, after the finish chunk)
  or every chunk (Gemini). The client gets the usage once, where the
  first two bullets put it.
- A stream that a guardrail blocks carries none of the answer, including
  its finish chunks (C25). The usage chunk is sent only when the request
  asked for it. A passing stream that ends at the request's deadline or on
  a provider error keeps its error event; a finish chunk held for usage
  goes out just before that event. A disclaimer goes out
  when the provider's stream ends, as before, and the held finish chunk
  follows it. When the request's timeout (`x-agentcc-request-timeout`,
  `x-agentcc-timeout`, the organization's or the model's timeout) ends a
  stream after the provider's finish chunk, the held finish chunk still
  goes out, with the usage when one is known by then, and the stream
  ends there without `[DONE]` or an error event, as before.
- A chunk with empty or null `choices` that a provider sends anywhere in a
  stream (its usage chunk, or Azure's first chunk with
  `prompt_filter_results`) is metered and not forwarded, so the fields
  only it carries, such as Azure's `prompt_filter_results`, do not reach
  the client.

The gateway still asks the provider for usage on every chat stream, and
meters, logs and bills every stream on it the same way, whatever the client
asked. The `agentcc` 1.0.0 and `@agentcc/client` 1.0.0 SDKs never set
`stream_options`. They get the usage on the finish chunk:
`get_final_completion().usage`, `getFinalCompletion().usage` and the
`usage` stream event carry it. Two limits: a provider stream that never
sends a `finish_reason` gives a client that did not ask no usage, because no
chunk can carry it; and on `/v1/completions` a client that did not ask gets
the usage when the provider sends it. Before, every chat stream ended with
two chunks with
empty `choices` (the provider's usage chunk and the gateway's own final
chunk), whatever the request asked, and the OpenAI SDK loop raised
`IndexError` in Python or `TypeError` in TypeScript at the end of every
stream. Streams on `/v1/messages`, `/v1beta` and `/v1/responses` keep their
own event formats and are unchanged.

**C80. The Assistants, Vector Stores and Files APIs run the gateway's
pipeline.** Before, a request on these APIs ran only key authentication,
the IP rules and, on the routes C35 reads, the checks on the request: it
had no request log entry and no rate limit, and a key's allowed models did
not apply to it. Now each request runs the pipeline as a request to a model
endpoint does:

- **A key's allowed models and access groups** apply to the four requests
  that name a model: creating and updating an assistant (its model), and
  creating a run or a thread and run (the run's model override). A key that
  may not use the model gets chat's answer for the same key and model,
  before the provider is called: 403 `model_not_permitted` with
  `metadata.reason` `key_model_denied` for its `allowed_models`, and chat's
  403 `permission_denied` for a model its access groups do not hold. An
  alias the key's access groups define is sent as the model it stands for.
  A key's allowed providers applies as C1 says.
- **The model is read as OpenAI reads it**: the member named exactly
  `model`, the last one where the name comes twice. The provider gets that
  one `model` and no other. Only an `openai/` prefix, in any letter case,
  is stripped (`openai/gpt-4o` is sent as `gpt-4o`), as chat strips the
  prefix that names the provider it routes to. Any other name with a `/`
  (another prefix, as in `gpt-4o-mini/gpt-4o`), and `openai/` alone, is a
  name OpenAI does not serve: it is refused with 403 `permission_denied`
  (chat's answer, for a key held to its organization's providers, for a
  model none of them serves), after the key's access groups are checked
  and before the provider is called. Before, any prefix was stripped after the
  check, so a key whose access group holds `gpt-4o-mini*` could name
  `gpt-4o-mini/gpt-4o` and have `gpt-4o` sent. A body chat refuses as
  invalid JSON (one that is not a JSON object, or that has a member named
  `model`, in any letter case, that is not a string, or one named `stream`
  that is not a boolean) gets chat's
  400 `invalid_json` on those four requests and on submitting tool outputs,
  before the provider is called. Before, a key allowed only `gpt-4o` that
  sent `{"model":0,"model":"gpt-4o-mini"}` passed its allowed models, and
  the provider got the body as sent, which OpenAI reads as `gpt-4o-mini`;
  and `{"stream":0,"stream":true}` was relayed as JSON. An empty body
  still goes on as `{}`.
- **Rate limits**: the key's own `rate_limit_rpm` (for a key without one,
  the gateway's `global_rpm`, which is only that default) and its
  `rate_limit_tpm` apply, as on embeddings, images, audio and OCR. A
  request over the request limit gets 429 `rate_limit_exceeded`. Once the
  key has spent its `rate_limit_tpm` for the minute (on requests that
  report tokens; these APIs report none), a request gets 429
  `token_rate_limit_exceeded`. A refused request never reaches the
  provider. The organization's `rate_limiting` section does not count
  these APIs (C66).
- **Request log**: each request the pipeline runs for an organization's API
  key has a request log entry, with the status the client got, the model it
  names (none for a list, a retrieval or a file) and its operation
  (`assistants_operation`, `vector_stores_operation` or `files_operation`).
  That includes run polls (`GET /v1/threads/{id}/runs/{id}`), lists and
  retrievals, and a request the pipeline refuses (a rate limit, a check on
  the request). A request refused before the pipeline (a body chat refuses,
  a model OpenAI does not serve, or a model or provider the key may not use)
  has no entry, as on chat. A streamed run is logged when its stream ends.
- **Each of these requests is a metered gateway request.** As on the model
  endpoints, each request log entry becomes one `gateway_request` usage
  event, and these requests count toward the organization's monthly
  `gateway_requests` quota; a paused or over-quota organization is refused
  on them. An SDK helper that polls a run (`create_and_poll`) makes one
  metered request per poll. Before, these APIs made no usage event.
- **Managed credentials never serve them.** The Assistants and Vector
  Stores APIs are served with the organization's own OpenAI key or, for an
  internal key and on a gateway with auth off, the operator's. When the
  gateway's `openai` provider is managed (`managed: true`), they answer 501
  `not_supported` to every key, an internal one included, before any
  provider call. The Files API calls no provider.

**C81. The gateway's MCP admin routes answer for one organization.**
`GET /-/mcp/status`, `/-/mcp/tools`, `/-/mcp/resources` and
`/-/mcp/prompts` take the organization as the `org_id` query parameter,
and `POST /-/mcp/test` as the `org_id` field of its body, and answer from
that organization's servers only. Without `org_id` they answer 400
`missing_org_id`; for an organization the gateway holds no config for, 404
`org_not_found`. `GET /-/mcp/tools?org_id=<id>&vs=<vs_id>` lists one
virtual server's tools, and a virtual server the organization does not
have is 404 `virtual_server_not_found`. The config file's servers answer
under the organization `mcp.static.org_id` names (U24). The platform's
MCP admin API sends `org_id` on every call.

**C82. The key admin API and the key sync take an agent key's scope and
budget.** `POST /-/keys`, `POST /-/keys/sync` and the gateway's own key
sync now take three more reserved metadata names from the platform,
besides `org_id` and `allow_policy_override`: `scopes`, `budget_limit_usd`
and `budget_period`. The platform sets them only on the agent keys it
mints for Omega EE's scoped agent-key provisioning, and they only narrow a key. `PUT /-/keys/{id}`
still refuses a change to any reserved name, and a create that sends
another reserved name is still refused 400 `reserved_metadata`.

**C83. The MCP contracts' additive parts.** In
`api_contracts/gateway/agentcc-admin.schema.json`:

- `MCPCredentialSecret` takes `in` (`header`, `query` or `url_variable`)
  and `name`, which say where the gateway places the secret, and `parts`,
  up to 7 more secret parts (`MCPCredentialSecretPart`: `in`, `name`,
  `value`) for a vendor whose credential has more than one. Without `in`
  and `name` a secret goes in the header `header` names (`Authorization`
  when unset), as before. A placement the gateway cannot apply exactly as
  stated is refused at push and at the admin `PUT` with 400
  `mcp_credential_placement_unsupported`, whose `param` names the field.
  These values are push-only: never stored in an org config or returned
  by a read.
- `MCPServerOrgConfig` takes `catalog_ref`
  (`<app-id>/<provider-id>@<version>`, the connector catalogue record a
  server was added from; absent on a server added by hand) and
  `url_variables` (the organization's values for the record's
  organization-scoped URL variables, a record only: the gateway never
  renders `url` from it). A save that moves a server's `url` to another
  scheme, host or port while it keeps a stored credential is refused with
  400 `mcp_credential_origin_changed`: enter the credential again, or drop
  it. A change of path or query keeps it. A URL that does not parse names
  no origin, so a change to or from one is a move.
- `POST /-/mcp/probe` refuses `credential_id` with 400
  `invalid_probe_request`: the platform's probe resolves a stored
  credential and sends it inline as `auth`, only to the URL its server is
  configured with, and answers 400 `mcp_probe_url_mismatch` otherwise.
  `tools_hash` is the hex sha256 of the gateway's canonical tool list. A
  probe that succeeds also returns `tools` (`MCPProbeTool`), one entry per
  listed tool in the order listed: `name`, and when the server states them,
  `title`, `description` and the hints `read_only_hint`,
  `destructive_hint`, `idempotent_hint` and `open_world_hint` (each kept
  only when it is a JSON boolean). A probe that fails has none (N17 reads
  them).

In `api_contracts/gateway/examples/`: an `mcp-tool-call-v1` record's
`server_id` and `upstream_tool` are empty when the call named an unknown
or hidden tool (`error_code` `unknown_tool`), and an `mcp-denial-v1`
answer's `executed` is true once the call's request was written to the
upstream, whatever came back, and false when the call never left the
gateway, so do not retry a non-idempotent call whose `executed` is true.

**C84. The checkout status route answers only a Checkout Session id.**
`GET /agentcc/managed-credits/checkout/{session_id}/` reads a Stripe
Checkout Session id: `cs_test_` or `cs_live_` followed by at least 24
letters or digits, the id Stripe returns to the checkout page. Any other
value gets 404 with code `checkout_session_not_found`, in the API's error
envelope, and the response does not repeat the value. This answer comes
before authentication and permission checks, so a caller without a session
and a Member get it as well; before, they got 401 or 403, and an Owner or
Admin got the route's usual answer. A percent-encoded
id is read as the id itself (`cs%5Ftest%5F...` is `cs_test_...`); a value
that is still encoded after that is another value and gets 404. An id of
the served shape is answered as before. The console reads the route only
with the id Stripe returns, so it is not affected.

### New

**N1. Attempts in Request Logs.** Each upstream try is recorded as an
attempt, with its provider, model, outcome, price source and billing mode.
The Request Logs drawer lists a request's attempts, and the column picker
has an **Agent & billing** group. Attempts follow the content mode (N4). The
records come from new database tables (U6). Run ids show as plain text,
because the Runs page is not in this release (N7).

**N2. `model: "auto"`.** On `/v1/chat/completions`, send
`"model": "auto"` and the gateway chooses a model from the providers your
key can reach. It first sets aside models that cannot serve the request:
missing tool, structured-output or image support, a context or output limit
that is too small, a price above your caps, an open circuit, or the key's
model and access-group limits. It then scores the prompt as a simple,
standard or complex task and ranks the rest by how well their price tier
fits that task and your preference (`cost`, `balanced` or `quality`). The
next two models in the ranking become fallbacks. The response headers
`x-agentcc-auto-model` (the model auto chose, before any fallback),
`x-agentcc-auto-tier` and `x-agentcc-auto-reason` explain the choice, and
the request log records the top five of the ranking.
`x-agentcc-auto-preference` overrides the preference for one request. Set
the org defaults in the console, on **Gateway > Models > Auto routing**, or
in the org config's `routing.auto` (`preference`, `candidates`,
`max_input_per_mtok`, `max_output_per_mtok`).
If no model qualifies, the answer is 400 `no_auto_candidate`, with the
reasons.

Auto ranks the models your providers serve by how well their price tier
fits the task and your preference. No benchmark shows that it picks better
models than a fixed choice, and its scoring may change between releases.
[Known limits](#known-limits) says what else moves its ranking today.

**N3. Retry headers.** `x-agentcc-max-attempts` (tries per target, the first
call included: 1 to 5), `x-agentcc-retry-delay-ms` (0 to 60,000) and
`x-agentcc-backoff` (`constant`, `linear` or `exponential`) tune one
request's retries. They can only tighten the org's own retry settings,
never loosen them. A malformed value gets 400 `invalid_retry_header`.

**N4. Content mode and retention (API only).**

- The content mode decides what the gateway's request log keeps: `full`
  (today's behaviour, and the default), `metadata` (no request or response
  bodies and no request headers) or `none` (as `metadata`, and also no error
  text, no guardrail messages and none of your own metadata keys; attempts
  keep only their error class and status). Requests are still logged and
  billed in every mode.
- Set it per organization (`privacy.content_mode` in the org config), per
  key (the key's `log_content` field) or per request (the
  `x-agentcc-log-content` header). The most restrictive of these and the
  gateway's `privacy.default_content_mode` wins, and an unknown value counts
  as `none`.
- It governs the request log and restricts MCP tool-span bodies. MCP full-content
  capture separately requires admin consent `privacy.trace_content: true` and
  `otel.include_bodies`; it exports tool inputs and outputs to the organization's
  collector and masks known credential formats. Other sensitive content may still
  be exported. It does not change what reaches the provider or what the response
  cache stores. It is not a zero-data-retention mode.
- `privacy.retention.request_log_days` and `privacy.retention.attempt_days`
  (1 to 36,500) set how long request logs, outcomes and attempts are kept. A
  daily job (`agentcc-log-retention`) deletes older rows. With no value set,
  rows are kept, as today. Managed-credit ledger entries are never deleted.
- There is no console page for these settings yet.

**N5. Policy rollouts (API only).** The org config's `routing.rollout`
sends a percentage of traffic to a candidate routing config, sticky by
session, key or request. Each request log records the policy version and
whether the request took the stable or the candidate config.

**N6. Routing strategies for routes in the gateway's config file.**
`cost_optimized` now ranks targets by catalog price when no model database
prices them, and `adaptive` weighs each target by that model's own health.

**N7. Console.**

- **Gateway > Models.** On a deployment that offers no managed models (the
  hosted config for this release offers none, H1), the page shows no
  managed-models card and one tab, **Auto routing**. Its subtitle reads:
  Tune how model "auto" chooses between the models your providers serve. A
  link to the catalog tab opens Auto routing. Where managed models are
  offered, the page adds the managed card and a **Catalog** tab, which opens
  first.
- **Hidden pages.** Playground, Capabilities, Policies, Runs and Billing &
  Credits are not in the navigation, and their URLs open the not-found page.
  MCP tools and Integrations are in the navigation, under Providers, Tools &
  Keys.
- **Guardrails.** The Overview's Stage column shows where the gateway runs
  each check: After LLM only for data leakage and hallucination checks, the
  two that read the answer (C25). It used to show the stage saved with the
  rule, which never reaches the gateway. When a listed check reads the
  answer, a note says on which requests it does (chat, completions,
  Anthropic Messages, Gemini and Responses, streamed or not, C30), that it
  holds a streamed answer until a blocking check passes and sends none of
  a blocked answer, and that a background Responses request is refused
  when such a check would block it (C31). The
  edit dialog no longer offers a stage. The Rules
  dialogs no longer offer DynamoAI Guard's `MODEL_RESPONSE` text type, Tool
  Permissions' Apply To, MCP Security's Validate Outputs, Aporia's Policies
  (which the gateway never sent; they offered hallucination and RAG
  validation) or IBM Granite Guardian's groundedness criterion: those checks
  read the request only. Aporia's description now says it checks the
  request with the Aporia project's guardrails. Saving a check again
  changes only the fields the admin edited. The dialog gives the stored
  check back as stored apart from those fields: settings the form no longer
  shows (such as these), settings it shows with a default when absent, text
  it would trim, and the keys' order. A guardrails section an older console
  stored as a checks map stays that map, and update-config gets only the
  checks the admin changed, so a check stored there without an action or a
  threshold still runs as the gateway ran it: as log, at threshold 0. A
  section stored as rules, or as the guardrail policy sync's list, is saved
  as rules, as before, and a check stored there without an action or a
  threshold keeps the defaults it ran with (block, 0.8). Before, a re-save
  added `action: "block"` and `confidence_threshold: 0.8` to a check stored
  without them, and saving any edit turned a checks map into rules with
  block and 0.8 for every check stored without them. So a check that ran as
  log started to block, and a data leakage check stored without a threshold
  stopped blocking an answer that matches only one of its patterns (scored
  0.7). It also wrote defaults such as MCP Security's
  `max_calls_per_request: 10`. The Test tab no longer says the prompt caused
  every block.
- **MCP tools.** Under Providers, Tools & Keys, the page has seven tabs:
  Overview, Servers, Virtual servers (N15), Tool calls (N16), Credentials
  (N14), Guardrails and Try a tool. Registry, Connect, Trust, Approvals,
  Resources and Prompts are not shown, and a link to one opens the
  Overview. A list the gateway could not return says it could not be
  loaded from the gateway, never that it is empty.
- **MCP turned off.** On a deployment that runs with MCP off
  (`mcp.enabled: false`), the MCP tools page shows "MCP is turned off for
  this deployment" instead of its tabs (C21). The Integrations page shows
  the same state instead of its apps, with no Connect or Custom MCP server
  action, since every app connects through the gateway's MCP; an add sent
  to the API then answers 404 `gateway_mcp_disabled` and stores nothing.
- **Integrations.** Under Providers, Tools & Keys, next to Providers, the
  page lists the apps of the connector catalogue that the organization can
  add, and adds one (N17).
  Its Custom MCP server button opens the MCP tools page's Servers tab,
  which adds any MCP server by its URL.
- **Providers > Routing.** "Retry on Status Codes" and "Retry on Timeout"
  now save the retry settings (`routing.retry.on_status_codes`,
  `routing.retry.on_timeout`); before, the retry list saved the failover
  list. "Failover on Status Codes" saves `routing.failover.on_status_codes`.
  Each list says what it drives. Which upstream statuses a list matches is
  in F38.
- **Routing strategy (Providers > Routing, Org Config > Routing).** An
  unset `routing.strategy` shows as "None: first provider by ID", what the
  organization's keys run (C47, C48); before, both controls showed Round
  Robin. Choosing None clears a stored strategy. Providers > Routing saves
  the strategy only when it was changed; before, saving any routing field
  there stored `round_robin`.
- **Guardrails tab: Fail Open and Mode (Org Config > Guardrails).** The two
  controls are read-only and show how this gateway runs an organization's
  checks, from `GET /-/config` `guardrail_pipeline` (N8): "Set by this
  gateway, read-only: it runs your checks in turn and stops at the first
  block, and a check that errors or times out blocks the request [lets the
  request through]. This organization's own Mode and Fail Open are saved but
  not applied yet." (or that guardrails are off on this gateway). Before,
  they edited the organization's `fail_open` and `pipeline_mode`, which the
  gateway stores and does not read. Stored values are kept; Timeout (ms)
  stays editable. The Guardrails analytics tab no longer shows an Avg
  Latency card: the gateway records no per-check latency, so it always read
  0 ms.
- **Providers > Cache.** The Cache Configuration card shows only Enabled and
  Default TTL, what the gateway applies for an organization's cache, and
  says when this gateway runs no response cache ("Off on this gateway") or
  does not report it; the backend, max entries, semantic and edge lines are
  gone (never applied for an organization; stored values are kept).
- **Managed models and auto routing.** A save the platform stored and the
  gateway did not apply (`gateway_synced: false`) shows "Saved, but the
  gateway did not apply it: <reason>" as a warning, never the "Managed
  models enabled" or "Auto routing saved" toast.

**N8. `GET /-/config` reports the gateway's settings and the org
sections it enforces.** Besides `server.port`, `server.host` and the
counts, the answer (admin token) carries, with no secret:

- `server`: `read_timeout_ms`, `write_timeout_ms`, `idle_timeout_ms`,
  `max_request_timeout_ms`;
- `logging`: `level`, `request_logging`, `include_bodies`, `content_mode`
  (`privacy.default_content_mode`, `full` when unset);
- `batch`: `storage: "memory"`, `default_max_concurrency: 10` (what a
  submission without its own `max_concurrency` gets) and
  `max_body_bytes: 10485760` (the submit body cap);
- `org_sections_enforced`: a sorted list drawn from `alerting`, `budgets`,
  `cache`, `ip_acl`, `rate_limiting` and `tool_policy`, each present only
  when this gateway installed the plugin that reads it (`cache` only with
  the gateway's own cache, `rate_limiting` only with `rate_limiting.enabled`).
  A section missing from the list does nothing on this gateway;
- `org_sections_not_enforced`: a section this gateway does not enforce for
  a reason the console states, with that reason: `ip_acl` on a gateway with
  neither `server.trusted_proxies` nor `server.trusted_hops` is
  `"client IP unknown (trusted_proxies not set)"`; absent when there is
  none;
- `guardrail_pipeline`: how this gateway runs an organization's guardrail
  checks: `enabled` (`guardrails.enabled`), `fail_open` (the gateway's
  `guardrails.fail_open`, which an org check's error or timeout follows)
  and `mode` (`sequential`: checks run in turn and the first block stops
  the rest). An organization's own `fail_open` and `pipeline_mode` are
  stored and not read yet; the console's Guardrails tab shows these values
  read-only in their place.

**N9. Request properties and the session name and path are logged.**
`x-agentcc-property-<name>: <value>` is `"<name>": "<value>"` in
`x-agentcc-metadata` (the name lower-cased, at most 64 characters; the value
at most 1,024): it is logged and exported as one of your dimensions on every
route that reads metadata, under the same blocklist, so a property never
sets `org_id`, `key_type`, `cost` or another gateway-owned key.
`x-agentcc-session-name` (at most 255 characters) and
`x-agentcc-session-path` (at most 1,024) are logged as `session_name` and
`session_path`. A property wins over the same key in `x-agentcc-metadata`,
and `x-agentcc-request-id`, `-session-name` and `-session-path` win over a
property of their key. A longer value answers 400 `invalid_agentcc_header`. Browsers may send these
headers: CORS allows every documented request header, and a preflight that
asks for property headers is answered with their names.

**N10. `x-agentcc-latency-ms` on every response.** Errors (a refused
key, an unknown model, a bad body, an unknown route), embeddings,
`/v1/messages` and the models list now carry it beside
`x-agentcc-request-id` and `x-agentcc-trace-id`. `x-agentcc-provider` and
`x-agentcc-model-used` are on responses a provider served
(`x-agentcc-model-used` not on embeddings), and `x-agentcc-timeout-ms` where
the route resolved a timeout (not on `/v1/messages`).

**N11. Guardrail outcome headers.** When a check triggered without
blocking, the answer carries `x-agentcc-guardrail-action` (`warn` when any
check warned, else `log`; a check that rewrote the request counts as `log`)
and `x-agentcc-guardrails-triggered` (the checks' names, sorted,
comma-separated), beside `x-agentcc-guardrail-triggered: true`. A block
stays 403 with error type `guardrail_error` and carries neither. Browsers
can read both.

**N12. Deepgram and Cartesia streaming speech, relayed.** The gateway
serves each vendor's own WebSocket API under the vendor's name:
`/deepgram/v1/listen` and `/deepgram/v1/speak`, `/cartesia/tts/websocket`,
`/cartesia/stt/websocket` and `/cartesia/stt/turns/websocket`. Point the
vendor's SDK at the gateway's base URL and give it a gateway key, which the
gateway reads wherever that SDK sends one (`Authorization: Token` or
`Bearer`, `X-API-Key`, or the `api_key` query parameter). The gateway
connects to the vendor with the provider configured for it
(`api_format: deepgram` or `cartesia`, see `config.example.yaml`), sends
the vendor that provider's key and never the client's, and relays frames
unchanged.

- With request auth on (`auth.enabled`), only an internal key opens a
  session, since the platform's credential serves it: any other key gets
  403 and a request without a valid key gets 401, before the vendor is
  reached, and the key's IP allow list applies. With request auth off the
  gateway checks no key on these routes, so any caller that reaches it
  opens a session on the platform's credential. A request from a browser page
  (one with an `Origin` header) gets 403 either way.
- The key's model list and access groups apply to the model in the URL
  and, on Cartesia synthesis, to the model each request names. A session
  whose URL names no model, and every Cartesia synthesis request with
  text that names none (also after an earlier request of the session
  named one), leave the model to the vendor: a key with a model list is
  refused them (403, or the request is refused and the connection
  closed), and access groups admit them only when one of the key's groups
  admits every model of that vendor (`*`, or a pattern such as
  `deepgram/*`).
- A query that names `model`, `encoding`, `sample_rate` or `channels`
  more than once gets 400 `ambiguous_parameter` before the vendor is
  reached, so the vendor receives only the values the gateway checked and
  metered. Other parameters may repeat and travel as sent.
- Usage is metered from what the client sends: seconds of raw audio for
  transcription (so a transcription needs a raw `encoding`, a
  `sample_rate` and, for more than one channel, `channels`, or gets 400
  `unmeterable_audio`), and characters of text for synthesis. It is priced
  at the session's model's price in the model database, per second or per
  character. A session whose model has no price, or that names no model,
  is recorded unpriced (`cost_source` `unpriced`), with no cost.
- A session counts against the organization's rate limits as C66 says
  and, once open, keeps relaying past the request timeout ceiling (C23)
  until either side closes it or the relay's own idle and session limits
  end it: a side that sends neither a message nor a ping answer for 10
  minutes ends it, and no session runs longer than 2 hours.

**N13. Each organization's own MCP servers.** With MCP on, the gateway
keeps one set of upstream connections per organization, built from the
servers in the organization's config (`mcp.servers`), which an Owner or
Admin saves on the MCP tools page's Servers tab. `/mcp` serves a key the
servers of the key's own organization and no other's ([MCP on the gateway](mcp.md)):

- A key lists and calls only its organization's tools, named
  `<server>__<tool>` (`mcp.separator`). Two organizations may each save a
  server with the same id: each one's keys reach only their own, and each
  call lands only on the caller's organization's upstream. A session one
  key opened answers 404 to another organization's key (C15).
- The upstream receives the server's own credential (N14) and nothing of
  the caller's: not its key, not its agent headers, and not the gateway's
  `io.futureagi/*` `_meta` keys.
- The gateway connects to upstreams of MCP versions 2026-07-28 and
  2025-06-18 over Streamable HTTP and 2024-11-05 over HTTP+SSE
  (`transport: sse`), reads every page of a tool list, and relists when an
  upstream says its tools changed. One `/mcp` endpoint serves clients of
  2026-07-28 and 2025-06-18 alike.
- An upstream address is dialled through the gateway's guarded egress
  path: a loopback, private, link-local or cloud-metadata address is
  refused (`egress_refused`) unless `mcp.egress.private_allow` lists it,
  and a cloud-metadata address is refused even then.
- The request that applies a newly saved config waits up to 3 s for its
  new servers' first connect. A server that does not connect is reported
  with its last error and retried, from 1 s apart up to every 5 minutes. A
  change to the organization's access policy alone reconnects nothing.
- An organization's servers are served while MCP is on for the
  organization (`mcp.enabled` in its config, which an Owner or Admin turns
  on from the MCP tools page); a server saved with `enabled: false` is not
  connected.
- An organization whose MCP config the gateway cannot evaluate has every
  call refused (`policy_unavailable`); none is let through.
- `GET /-/mcp/status?org_id=<id>` reports the organization's servers, each
  with its health and last error, and `org_enabled` (C81).

**N14. The MCP credential vault.** An MCP server's credential (a bearer
token, or an API key sent in a header, a query parameter or a variable of
the server's URL) is stored encrypted in the MCP credential vault, and the
organization's config holds only a reference to it
(`credential: {mode, credential_id, state}`). The platform adds the secret
to the push it sends the gateway, and nowhere else: never to a config
version, a read or a log. The gateway's admin reads of an organization's
config (`GET /-/orgs/{id}/config`, `/-/orgs/configs`) show every MCP secret
as `****`.

- `GET /agentcc/mcp/credentials/` lists the organization's credentials
  without a value, to any member. Only an Owner or Admin creates one
  (`POST`), revokes one (`DELETE /agentcc/mcp/credentials/{id}/`) or
  rotates one (`POST .../{id}/rotate/`), and a credential is never read
  back. The MCP tools page's Credentials tab is this list.
- Only an active credential is sent to the gateway: a revoked one is not
  sent again.
- `POST /agentcc/mcp/probe/` (an Owner or Admin, 10 a minute per
  organization) tests a server through the gateway with its stored
  credential, sent only to the URL that server is configured with, and
  answers whether it connected, its MCP version, its tool count and the
  hash of its tool list.
- A config write that carries an MCP secret is refused (F13), and so is a
  save that moves a server with a stored credential to another origin
  (C83).

**N15. Virtual servers.** An organization's config can define virtual
servers (`mcp.virtual_servers.<id>`), each served at `/mcp/v/<vs_id>` to
that organization's keys only; another organization's key gets 404, and
`/mcp?vs_id=` selects nothing. A virtual server composes the tools of the
organization's servers it lists (`members`): `tools.include` and
`tools.exclude` globs narrow them, `overrides` rename, retitle, redescribe
or hide one tool, and names are `<member>__<tool>` (`naming: prefixed`,
the default) or the tool's own (`flat`), never two the same, at most 64
characters, in a stable order. `access` names the keys, agents and users
that may use it, and its rules narrow what each may list and call; a deny
always wins. A virtual server that names no key, agent or user is open to
every key of its organization. The MCP tools page's Virtual servers tab
edits them.

**N16. One record for every tool call.** Every `tools/call` through
`/mcp` or a virtual server is recorded once, whatever its outcome:
`success`, `is_error`, `denied` (with its code, such as `tool_denied` or
`unknown_tool`), `timeout` and the rest. The record (`mcp-tool-call-v1`)
names the key, the organization, the server, the virtual server, the tool
and its upstream name, the agent context, the outcome and error code, the
latency, the sizes and `billing_mode`; it carries the call's arguments and
result only under content mode `full`, and never a key, a bearer or the
session id. Every result a call returns carries
`_meta["io.futureagi/tool_call"]` with that record's `tool_call_id`.

- `GET /agentcc/mcp/tool-calls/` lists the organization's calls, newest
  first, 50 to a page (`limit` up to 100), filtered by `run_id`,
  `agent_id`, `api_key_id`, `server_id`, `tool` or `outcome` (each a comma
  list), `billing_mode`, and `from` and `to` (ISO 8601).
  `GET /agentcc/mcp/tool-calls/{id}/` is one call. The MCP tools page's
  Tool calls tab shows them.

**N17. Apps from the connector catalogue.** The gateway ships a catalogue
of apps (`agentcc-gateway/catalog/connectors`), and the Integrations page
(`GET /agentcc/connectors/catalog/`) lists the ones an organization can
add: apps whose vendor runs a remote MCP server that the organization
connects to with its own key. An Owner or Admin adds one with that key,
which the MCP credential vault stores and never shows again (N14):

- The app becomes a server of the organization's (with its `catalog_ref`,
  C83) and gets a virtual server of its own at `/mcp/v/<vs_id>` (N15).
- Its tools come from the vendor's live tool list, read with the
  organization's own key through the connection probe. A tool the vendor
  marks read-only (`readOnlyHint: true`) is allowed on the app's virtual
  server, and every other tool is denied there. The first list is the
  app's baseline, returned as `baseline` (`tool_count`, `tools_hash`).
- An add that cannot be made writes nothing: 400
  `connector_credential_rejected` (the vendor refused the key), 409
  `connector_no_tool_allowed` (the vendor marks no listed tool read-only),
  409 `connector_tool_listing_not_applied` (the app takes its key some other
  way than in one header), and 502 `connector_tool_listing_failed`,
  `connector_tool_listing_not_supported` or `gateway_unreachable` when the
  list cannot be read.
- Any other MCP server is added by its URL on the MCP tools page's Servers
  tab.

**Scoped agent keys. Omega EE agents call the gateway with scoped agent keys.** The
contract is `omega-ee-attach/v1`
([omega-ee-attach.md](connectors/omega-ee-attach.md)). An Owner or Admin
issues the organization's Omega EE service credential
(`POST /agentcc/mcp/service/credential/`; its secret is shown once, and it
can be rotated and revoked). With it, Omega EE mints one agent key per
workspace (`/agentcc/mcp/service/agent-keys/`) and ensures a virtual server
over the organization's servers
(`/agentcc/mcp/service/virtual-servers/ensure/`), whose address it gets
back (U26) and which only its bound key reaches; other keys get 404.

- An agent key calls `/mcp` and the model endpoints
  `POST /v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/embeddings` and `/v1/responses`, on the
  organization's own models, and nothing else: any other route of the
  gateway or the platform answers 403 `key_scope_denied` before it runs.
- It spends at most its workspace's budget (an Owner or Admin sets it at
  `/agentcc/mcp/service/workspaces/{id}/agent-key-policy/`, else the
  platform's default) per UTC day, week (from Monday) or month. Every model
  call counts at its cost, a streamed `/v1/responses` call as the same
  call unstreamed, and a stream that ends before reporting its usage on an
  estimate of what it sent and received (the prompt, and the streamed text
  at about 4 characters a token), marked `usage_estimated`. On a chat
  stream with no usage from the provider, the usage the gateway reports at
  the end of the stream is that estimate. A key with no budget is priced as
  before (F3).
  Once the period's spend reaches
  the budget, the next call answers 402 `agent_key_budget_exhausted`
  before the provider is called, with `limit_source` `agentcc_key_limit`,
  `scope` `key:<id>` and `resets_at` the end of the period. Its contract
  is `omega-ee-attach/v1` (`gateway_key_budget_error`): the body has
  error-402-v1's shape and metadata, but `agent_key_budget_exhausted` is
  not in error-402-v1's list of codes, so a client that checks a 402's
  `code` against that list accepts this code as well.
- A scope or budget the gateway cannot read allows nothing. Agent keys
  live 90 days, and an organization holds a capped number of live ones
  (409 `agent_key_cap_reached`). Every mint, rotation and refusal is
  written to the organization's audit log, with the workspace and Omega EE
  as the actor.

**N19. OpenRouter's routing fields.** A chat request may send these
OpenRouter fields, on the org's own keys and on Future AGI models alike:

| Field                                                                                                                                                         | What the gateway does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `models`                                                                                                                                                      | An ordered fallback list. When the request's model fails with a rate limit or an upstream error, each listed model is tried in turn; each try is judged, held and billed as its own attempt, and a model the key may not use is skipped. The list is never sent upstream. |
| `provider.order`                                                                                                                                              | Upstream provider slugs to try first, in that order.                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `provider.sort`                                                                                                                                               | `price`, `throughput` or `latency` (or `cost`, `tps`, `ttft`): the providers are ranked by that figure.                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `provider.allow_fallbacks`                                                                                                                                    | `false` keeps the request on the providers `provider.order` names, or, with no order, on the first-ranked one.                                                                                                                                                            |
| `provider.only`, `provider.ignore`, `provider.max_price`, `provider.zdr`, `provider.data_collection`, `provider.quantizations`, `provider.require_parameters` | As before (G10).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

The per-attempt statement for `models` covers chains of token-priced models; a
chain that mixes catalogue-priced and token-priced models is off in this
release and is not offered.

The organization's `routing.fallback_enabled` switch also controls the
caller's `models` chain. An explicit `false` leaves the primary request
unchanged but never installs or tries that list, for streaming and
non-streaming chat alike; an upstream failure is returned rather than
rescued by a caller-listed model. The list is still validated and stripped
from the upstream body. `true` enables the list; an unset switch preserves
caller fallbacks even when the organization has no stored chains. The
request's effective routing configuration, including a rollout candidate,
decides the switch. This does not change provider failover, retries, or the
eligibility and credit checks each permitted model hop must pass.

To OpenRouter on the org's own key the provider object is sent as the
caller wrote it, and OpenRouter applies it. On Future AGI models the
gateway applies `order`, `sort` and `allow_fallbacks` to the providers it
pins the call to, from the catalogue's prices, throughput and latency; a
`provider.sort` the catalogue has no figures for, an order or sort on a
model with no list of its providers, or `sort.partition: "none"` gets 400
`provider_preference_unavailable`. `allow_fallbacks: false` with an order
that names none of the model's providers gets 404 `no_provider_matches`.
Every other routing field the gateway reads (`fallbacks`,
`provider.preferred_max_latency`, `provider.preferred_min_throughput`,
`providerOptions.gateway.*`, `preset`, `caching`) still gets 400
`routing_field_not_yet_supported`, and Future AGI models still refuse
`plugins`, `route` and `transforms` (400 `unsupported_routing_field`).

### Fixed

**F1. Two requests no longer share a request id.** The gateway made each
request and trace id from a pool of random sources seeded with the clock.
After a garbage collection emptied the pool, requests that arrived at the
same moment could get the same ids. Managed credit holds and settlements are
keyed on the request id, so a managed request's settlement could be refused
as already settled and its spend left unrecorded, and the platform's request
log keeps only the first entry it receives for a request id. Every id now
comes from one crypto-random source per gateway process, and ids made in the
same millisecond never repeat. Earlier releases have the bug, FutureAGI's
hosted gateway included, until they run this one.

Work the gateway starts itself had no ids at all. An A2A task, each
`/-/batches` item and each run of a scheduled job (which this build does
not run, U4) ran with an empty request id and trace id, so all of them
shared one. With managed credits and A2A both on, an organization's managed
A2A tasks after its first were refused at settlement as already settled
(the ledger settles a request id once, and remembers it for seven days),
and their spend went unrecorded. Each such run, a scheduled job's retry
included, now gets its own ids from the same source. An A2A task's run
carries the trace id of the A2A request that started it (the
`x-agentcc-trace-id` on that request's response), a task sent with
`returnImmediately` too, but a request id of its own, not that request's
`x-agentcc-request-id`. A `/-/batches` item's run
carries the batch request's trace id the same way, and each result of
`GET /-/batches/{id}` names the item's own `request_id`, the id its entry in
the request log is filed under.

**F2. A starting gateway reports ready only once it knows the keys made in
the app.** When the gateway syncs keys from a control plane
(`control_plane.url` with `sync_on_startup` or a `sync_interval`, as Helm and
docker-compose set it), `/readyz` now answers 503 until its first key sync
has loaded the keys made in the app. `/healthz` and `/livez` answer 200 from
the start, as before. Before, a new replica reported ready at once while its
first key sync was still running (it retries from 2 s, doubling to 30 s, and
the app can spend minutes on a first boot), so during a rollout, a scale-out
or a restart it took traffic and answered every key made in the app 401
`invalid_api_key` until that sync finished. The wait reaches only a readiness
probe that reads `/readyz`, as the Helm chart's does: a probe on `/healthz`
or `/livez` still sends traffic to a replica that has not loaded the keys,
so point it at `/readyz`. A gateway with no control plane,
or whose control plane syncs no keys (no `sync_on_startup` and no
`sync_interval`), is ready at once, as before: nothing would end the wait.
If the app cannot be reached when a replica starts, that replica stays out
of rotation until it can; replicas already serving are not affected. With
`sync_on_startup` off and a `sync_interval`, the first key sync, and so
readiness, comes one interval after start. The first list can be empty (the app
lists no key until one is made): it counts, also on a replica that already
holds a key made on it (`POST /-/keys`) or pushed to it one by one
(`POST /-/keys/sync`) before the list came; an empty list keeps such a key.
Before, such a replica stayed out of rotation until the app listed a key. The wait covers keys only: org
settings, which load in the same sync, can still arrive after the replica
reports ready. An app whose database has no key table yet (a new install
before its bootstrap job has migrated it) answers the key list with 503
`migrations_pending`, and that counts as an empty first list: no key has
been made. Without it, a Helm install with bundled datastores never finished
under `helm install --wait`, which runs the post-install bootstrap job only
once the gateway reports ready. The answer never changes the keys
a replica holds, and any other failed answer still keeps it out of rotation.

**F3. `/v1/responses` streams are priced.** A `/v1/responses` stream is
now priced from the usage its last event reports (`response.completed`, or
`response.incomplete` or `response.failed` for a response that stopped
early), as the same response is priced when it is not streamed, and the
request takes the model that event names. Before, a stream was never
priced: its cost was 0, it counted toward no budget, a managed key's
prepaid balance was not debited for it, and the request log recorded no
usage for it. A `/v1/responses` request with `background: true` that would
be paid from prepaid credit (a managed key's own balance) is now refused
before the provider is called, with 400 `usage_unavailable`, streamed or
not. A background response goes on after its stream or its queued answer,
and its usage never passes through the gateway, so it cannot be priced.
Send it without `background`. Before, it was sent, and served unpriced. The
refusal comes after the key is authenticated, as the gateway's other
refusals of a request do: a managed key without access to the model gets
403, not this 400, and a revoked or expired key gets 401 from the key check
in front of every `/v1` route, as before.
Organization managed credits do not reach `/v1/responses` in this release
(managed models serve chat completions only); the refusal covers them too.
The gateway reads a stream's last event within 10 MiB of line. A stream
paid from prepaid credit whose last event is longer (a `response.completed`
that carries base64 images can be) has no usage the gateway can read: it is
charged what a hold for it is, never 0. That is its prompt as the gateway
estimates it and its `max_output_tokens`, or without one the most a hold
assumes (the model's maximum output, at most the organization's
`default_max_tokens_estimate` or the gateway's
`managed.reserve_default_output_tokens`, 4096 by default), priced at the
model's card as any usage is, so the request's cost, which the request log
records, is the amount the managed key is debited. The log marks
the request `usage_estimated`, with `usage_unreadable:
final_event_over_limit` in its metadata, and the gateway logs a warning.
Before, such a stream cost 0 and the managed key was not debited. What is
still not priced is in [Known limits](#known-limits).

**F4. The Guardrails page edits a section stored as a checks map.** An older
console stored an organization's guardrails as a checks map (N7). On such a
section, the Overview's switch and its edit dialog answered "The gateway
cannot accept this config. guardrails.rules: Extra inputs are not
permitted" and saved nothing: they wrote a rule beside the map, which the
gateway's config contract refuses. They now change the check in the map.
The switch sets its `enabled`. The dialog sends only what the admin changed
(`action` or `confidence_threshold`), and every other setting the check is
stored with is kept. A check the switch turns on that the map does not hold
yet is added with block and 0.8, as a new rule is. The Rules tab and the
Overview's edit dialog now show a check of such a map stored without an
action or a threshold as the gateway runs it, log at threshold 0. The Rules
tab showed it as block at 0.80, and both dialogs opened on block, so
choosing Block saved nothing and the check kept logging; it is now an edit,
and is saved. A section stored as rules, or as the guardrail policy sync's
list, is shown and saved as before.

**F5. An organization guardrail config never reads the gateway's
environment.** A `${VAR}` in a credential or `base_url` of a guardrail an
organization configures used to be expanded against the **gateway's own**
process environment, and the check then sent that value to the configured
URL. An organization that set a `futureagi` or external-provider check with
`api_key: "${AGENTCC_ADMIN_TOKEN}"` (or any other variable the deployment
passes to the gateway) and a `base_url` of its own received the gateway's
host-environment value. Now a guardrail built from organization config takes
every credential, URL and setting exactly as written. The one environment
value it still reads is `FI_BASE_URL`, the operator's address for a
`futureagi` check that names no `base_url`, which is the operator's setting,
not the organization's, and holds no secret. A `${` in a `futureagi` check's
`api_key`, `secret_key` or `base_url`, or in any top-level setting of an
external-provider check, is a configuration fault: no call is made, and with
action `block` the request gets 403 `content_blocked` naming the check and
the field, never the value (as C3). With action `warn` or `log` the failure
is warned or logged, and the request goes on.

The console and the control plane refuse such a value first, with a 400
that names the field: on every save that sends a guardrail check (org
configs in each shape, update-config, update-guardrail, guardrail policies),
on a save that would switch on a check whose stored value holds one or
change anything else about such a check (its endpoint, provider or action,
say), and on activating a version with such a check switched on. A save
that pushes such a check exactly as the active version does goes ahead (the
check itself keeps failing closed at the gateway until it is fixed), and
switching a check off is never refused for the value it holds. Where the
switch is depends on how the organization's guardrails are stored: U10
lists each case, including a config written by a guardrail policy, where
the console's on/off switch does not switch a check off. A guardrail
policy's check config must be a JSON object: a string, list, number or
boolean answers 400 (an absent or null config still means none). Anywhere
else in a guardrail config (a blocklist word such as `${jndi:`, a pattern, an
expression, a webhook header, a check name) `${` is plain text: it saves, and
the gateway runs it as written. A save that does not change guardrails (a
budget, an MCP server) is never refused. A rule in the gateway's own
`config.yaml` is operator-trusted and still expands `${VAR}` (U5).

When a `futureagi`, external-provider or webhook check's call fails, its
message no longer carries the URL or the address the gateway dialed. Before,
it echoed both, so an organization learned the operator's evaluation host
(for a `futureagi` check that names no `base_url`) or egress proxy. The
gateway's log keeps the full error. Earlier releases have the environment
read, FutureAGI's hosted gateway included, until they run this one. Before
upgrading a self-hosted gateway, see U10.

**F6. The request log never stores a credential a caller sends in a
header.** The gateway, when it builds a request's log entry, and the
platform, when it stores it, kept only a few header names out. The Google
GenAI SDKs send their key in `x-goog-api-key`, which the gateway reads as
the gateway key on `/v1beta`, and the request log stored it in clear in
`request_headers` (with `include_bodies: true` and content mode `full`,
FutureAGI's hosted defaults). Any member of the organization, a Viewer
included, could read it on the request's detail and use it. Every other
credential header a caller sends (`Proxy-Authorization`,
`X-Amz-Security-Token`, a provider's or a guardrail service's key) was
stored as sent too. The request log now keeps the name of every credential
header with the value `***`: the headers the gateway reads a key from, the
headers a provider or guardrail service takes a key in, and any header
whose name reads as a credential (a token, a secret, a password, an API
key, a cookie, a header whose last word is `key` or `auth` such as
`X-OpenAI-Key`, `x-key` or `Helicone-Auth`, and every `X-Portkey-` header).
A name names a token when `token` is in any of its words (`X-Access-Token`,
`X-Access-Token-V2`, `slack_token_prod`, `X-CSRFToken`), except where
`token` is followed by `s` (a count of tokens, such as `prompt_tokens` or
`X-Ratelimit-Remaining-Tokens`), by `iz` (a tokenizer: `Tokenizer`,
`tokenize`), or by `-` or `_` and one of `count`, `budget`, `limit`,
`usage`, `used`, `remaining`, `total`, `max` or `min` (such as
`X-Token-Count` or `token_budget`). A last word `key` after a word that
names a lookup key (`cache`, `idempotency`, `dedup`, `dedupe`,
`deduplication`, `partition`, `sort`, `routing`, `lookup`, `primary`,
`foreign` or `public`, as in `Idempotency-Key` or `cache_key`) is not one
either, and neither is a bare `key`. The trace export never exports them
either. The platform masks them again on its own, in `request_headers` and
`response_headers`, whatever a gateway sends, and no longer stores headers
sent as anything but an object. A request's detail shows a row stored
before this release with those values masked too; they stay in the
database until U11's scrub masks them. Earlier releases have
the bug, FutureAGI's hosted gateway included, until they run this one.

**F7. No guardrail check gets a caller's credential.** Every check got the
request's metadata as it was, and it holds the caller's `Authorization`
header, which the gateway reads the key from. A webhook check sent it, the
caller's gateway key included, with the client's address and the prompt,
to the URL its config names; an expression check could read the key and
test it. Every check now gets a copy without the key and without any entry
whose name reads as a credential by F6's rule (a caller's own dimension such
as `session_token`, `access_token_2` or `tenant_key` included; one that
counts tokens, such as `token_budget` or `token_usage`, is kept): the
gateway config file's rules and an organization's checks, before and after
the provider, and the streaming checker's. A webhook still receives the
request, the client's address, the key's id, name and owner and the
request's other dimensions. An async job
keeps no credential in its metadata either; its run holds the key in
memory until it has run, to authenticate it again.

**F8. A native Google API call sends Google the organization's key.** On
`/v1beta`, through a provider with the native Google format, the gateway
forwarded every `X-Goog-*` header the client sent, after the provider's own
key. The client's `x-goog-api-key`, which is its gateway key there,
replaced the organization's Google key, so Google got the client's gateway
key instead. The gateway no longer forwards a credential header: the
provider sends its own key on `generateContent`, `streamGenerateContent`,
`countTokens` and `embedContent`, and the client's other `X-Goog-*` headers
(`X-Goog-Api-Client` and the like) are forwarded as before.

**F9. Only an organization's Owner or Admin can change its guardrail
policies.** A guardrail policy's checks are merged into the organization's
config and pushed to the gateway, and any member, a Viewer included, could
create, change, delete, apply or sync one through
`/agentcc/guardrail-policies/`. Anyone but an Owner or Admin now gets 403,
as for every other change to the gateway's config, and nothing changes.
Every member can still list and read them. The console does not use these
endpoints.

**F10. A guardrail webhook, external check or FutureAGI eval check an
organization configures cannot reach the operator's internal network.** A
webhook guardrail (its `url`), an external-provider guardrail (its
`endpoint`, `base_url` or `region`) and a FutureAGI eval guardrail (its
`base_url`) were dialled with no address guard, so an organization member
who can set a check could point one at `127.0.0.1`, a private or LAN
address, `169.254.169.254` or another cloud-metadata address and make the
gateway connect there and POST the request content (for a FutureAGI eval
check, with its API key and secret), following redirects. Those checks now
dial through the gateway's guarded egress path, the same one MCP upstreams
use: a loopback, private, link-local or cloud-metadata address is refused
after DNS, on every attempt, and every redirect hop is re-checked; a redirect
to another origin carries none of the check's keys. A FutureAGI eval check
that names no `base_url`, the built-in default, or exactly the gateway's
`FI_BASE_URL` goes to `FI_BASE_URL`, the operator's own evaluation backend,
as before, with no listing (U12). A self-hosted
deployment reaches a guardrail service on a private or LAN address only when
the operator lists it in `mcp.egress.private_allow`; a check that names a
refused address returns a call failure, so the request is handled under the
check's action (refused when it blocks). The gateway's own `config.yaml`
guardrail rules are operator-trusted and keep a direct client, so an
operator check on a private host keeps working without being listed. A
guardrail that names a non-http(s) URL, a URL with no host, a URL carrying a
user or password, or one with a control character is refused when it is
saved, naming the field.

**F11. An organization's alert channel cannot reach the operator's internal
network.** An org's alert channel (a webhook or Slack URL) was dialled with
no address guard, so an organization admin could set one to a loopback,
private or cloud-metadata address and, when a rule fired, make the gateway
POST the alert there, following redirects — a blind probe of the operator's
network. Org alert channels now dial through the same guarded egress path,
with the same `mcp.egress.private_allow` exception for a self-hosted LAN
collector. The operator's own `config.yaml` alert channels keep a direct
client. A channel URL that is not a well-formed http(s) URL is refused when
it is saved, naming the field.

**F12. An org-config infrastructure secret is never shown to a reader.**
Before, the cache backends' Redis password, S3 secret access key, Azure
connection string and SAS token and the semantic cache's vector-store API
keys, the A2A agents' tokens, the audit-sink and alert-channel webhook
headers, and the MCP servers' auth were stored in clear in the org config and
returned verbatim by the config and org-config read endpoints and Settings >
Full Config to every member of the org, a Viewer included. They are now stored
encrypted and returned as a mask with a `secrets_set` flag, and decrypted only
for the push to the gateway, which still receives the real values. An MCP
server's credential leaves the config: it is kept in the MCP credential vault,
and the config holds a reference to it (N14). A secret is
write-only: a save that leaves it blank, or sends back the mask, keeps the
stored value; the console's secret field offers Replace and Remove (Remove
sends null and deletes it). A kept secret goes only to an origin (scheme, host
and port) it is already stored for: a save that moves its host to another
origin is refused `secret_origin_changed` and the secret must be entered
again. A read-back mask keeps the secret stored for that leaf's origin, so one
value stored for two hosts (a `Content-Type` header on two alert channels)
saves at each. A URL the platform cannot read
(it does not parse) names no origin: a secret is kept there only while that
URL is left exactly as stored. Every spelling the gateway contract accepts
for a secret field is a secret too: `secretAccessKey`, `connectionString`,
`sasToken` and `apiKey` as well as the snake_case names, and the
`azureBlob` and `managedTools` sections as well as `azure_blob` and
`managed_tools`. Provider keys and guardrail-check credentials were already
encrypted and were not affected. Migrations 0047 and 0050 encrypt the rows
saved before this release (U13), and 0056 moves the MCP ones into the vault
(U25).

**F13. An MCP server secret is never written into an org config.** A config
write (`POST /agentcc/org-configs/`, update-config, the MCP tools page's
server actions, or activating a version) that would put an MCP server
credential into the config as a value (`auth.token`, `auth.key`,
`credential.secret` or a managed-tool secret), a mask included, is refused
400 `secret_in_config`, naming the path, and nothing is saved. A write that
changes a credential reference the vault owns is refused 400
`mcp_credential_vault_owned`. The Servers tab's dialog
(`update-mcp-server`) and `/agentcc/mcp/credentials/` store the credential
in the vault (N14); a config with no MCP secret saves. A read-back mask
(`__encrypted__`, alone or with its fingerprint) sent there as a secret is
refused 400 too; to keep a stored credential, send no `auth`. Each stored
credential is bound to the origin of the URL its secret was entered with:
the push and the probe send it only to its server at that origin, and
activating a config version that puts its server anywhere else, or that
names a credential bound to none, is refused 400
`mcp_credential_origin_changed` with nothing pushed; enter the credential
again with its server.

**F14. Removing an organization's last guardrail policy switches its checks
off.** Deactivating or deleting the last guardrail policy that held a check
stored a guardrails section the gateway refuses (`enabled: false` beside an
empty checks list), so the push failed (`gateway_synced: false`), the gateway
kept running the old checks, and every later save that does not touch
guardrails (a budget, the cache) answered 400 until a
guardrails save repaired the section. The removal is now pushed as an empty
guardrails section, the gateway stops running those checks, and later saves
go ahead. A section an earlier release stored that way, or a rules editor
save with every rule removed, is pushed the same way: no repair save is
needed after the upgrade.

**F15. The Guardrails page's switch and edit work on guardrails a policy
wrote.** When a guardrail policy sync last wrote an organization's guardrails
(a checks list), the on/off switch (toggle-guardrail) and the edit
(update-guardrail) answered 200 and the gateway kept running the check as it
was. They now change the check in the policy it came from, or, for a check no
policy holds, in the console's own policy, so the gateway runs the change and
later policy syncs keep it. A new credential typed in the edit is stored
encrypted in that policy. The same refusals apply as on the other shapes
(U10): a check whose stored credential is a `${VAR}` can be switched off, not
on. A checks list no policy wrote is changed as a list.

**F16. A guardrail policy's check needs a name.** A policy check whose name
was not a string (a number, a list, an object, null) or was empty saved with
200; a number then made every later org-config save answer 400, a list or an
object made every policy sync fail, and an empty one was silently never
pushed. Creating or changing such a policy now answers 400 naming
`checks[i].name`, and nothing is saved. A policy saved before this release
with such a name is not changed: until it is fixed or deleted, a number there
still makes every org-config save answer 400, and a list or an object still
makes every policy sync fail.

**F17. A change to another organization's guardrail policy answers 404.** A
`PATCH`, `PUT`, `DELETE` or `apply` of a guardrail policy id another
organization owns, or of an unknown id, answered 400 with the model's name;
it now answers 404, as reading it does. Nothing crossed organizations before
or after: the other organization's policy is never changed, decrypted or
pushed.

**F18. Only an organization's Owner or Admin can change its shadow
experiments.** A shadow experiment names a share of the organization's
traffic to mirror to another model and provider (on this release the gateway
mirrors nothing for it: mirroring comes only from a self-hosted gateway's
config file, `routing.mirror`, and an org config's `routing.mirror` is
refused, C5), and pausing, resuming or completing one pushes the
organization's config, yet any member, a Viewer included,
could create, change, delete, pause, resume or complete one through
`/agentcc/shadow-experiments/`. Anyone but an Owner or Admin now gets 403, as
for every other change to the gateway's config (F9), and nothing changes.
Every member can still list them, read one and its stats. The console's
Experiments page, which is not in the navigation on this release, shows these
actions disabled, with "Owner or Admin only", to anyone but an Owner or Admin
(F23).

**F19. An organization's stored response is kept under its own id.**
Stored `/v1/responses` were kept one per id across every organization, and
a save was refused when another organization's unexpired response held the
id. The id comes from the upstream provider, which an organization may
configure, so one organization could keep another from storing, and then
reading back, its own response (its `GET` answered 404). The store is now
keyed by organization and id: the same id is stored, read, deleted and
expired separately for each organization, and no organization can read,
replace or delete another's.

**F20. Prometheus label values are escaped.** `/-/metrics` wrote label
values as they came. A model name a caller chose or an upstream echoed
could close its label set with a double quote and a line feed and write a
series of its own, and two label sets that differed only by a comma or an
equals sign inside a value were counted as one series. Label values are now
escaped as the Prometheus text format defines (backslash, double quote,
line feed), and such label sets are separate series. `/-/metrics` needs the
admin token and is served only when `prometheus.enabled` is set.

**F21. Model-hub provider keys and secrets are stored encrypted, not
base64-encoded.** Before, the model hub's provider keys (Settings, API keys,
text and JSON keys), custom-model credentials and the secrets a dataset's
vector-database and API-call columns use were stored as base64 of the first
16 characters of `SECRET_KEY` followed by the value: anyone who could read the
database, a dump or a backup could decode every organization's keys. They are
now stored as Fernet ciphertext under `INTEGRATION_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, the way the
gateway's provider credentials and F12's secrets are. The server decrypts a
key only to use it (a provider call, a dataset column, a Hugging Face load) and
to build its mask. Every response shows the same mask as before, never the
key or its ciphertext. A key this deployment
cannot decrypt is listed as "cannot be decrypted, enter this key again", and a
call that needs it fails with an error naming the key and
`INTEGRATION_ENCRYPTION_KEY`; no other key, FutureAGI's own included, is used
in its place. A stored ciphertext typed into a key field is stored as typed
and treated as a key that cannot be decrypted; it never decrypts to the key it
came from. Migration `model_hub` 0125 encrypts the keys saved before this
release (U15). Without a valid `INTEGRATION_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (unset, or set to
something Fernet refuses, such as a placeholder) the keys stay in the old
encoding and keep working, as before, and the server logs a warning that names
the variable and the fix (U15).

**F22. An alert channel URL that carries a credential is never shown to a
reader.** A Slack incoming-webhook URL is its channel's credential, and so
is a webhook URL with a token in its path or query. Such a URL is now stored
encrypted, returned as a mask with a `secrets_set` flag on every org-config
read (Settings > Full Config, `org-configs/`, `active/`, the diff and the
write answers), and decrypted only for the push and the gateway's bulk sync,
which still receive the real URL. Which URLs count: a `slack` channel's URL;
any channel URL that does not parse, or has a user or password, a query or a
fragment; and any URL with a path segment that is not a short lowercase word
(`alerts`, `hooks`, `on-call` stay readable; a digit, an upper-case letter,
a `%` or more than 24 characters make it secret). Such a URL is write-only:
a blank or the read-back mask keeps it, a new URL replaces it, and null
removes it. A blank keeps the channel's own URL even after an earlier
channel was removed, and two channels that share a name each keep their own.
Another secret's mask is not accepted as a URL, nor a URL's mask as another
secret (refused with 400). Migration 0051 encrypts the URLs saved before
this release (U13). In the console, the Alerting tab shows a stored one as
dots with Replace, and Monitoring says it is stored and hidden.

**F23. The console disables what only an Owner or Admin may change.** The
platform refuses anyone but an organization's Owner or Admin every change to
the gateway's config, its API keys and its shadow experiments (F9, F18). The
console now shows those controls disabled, with "Owner or Admin only", to a
Member, a Viewer or a user whose role has not loaded: Add Provider and a
provider's Edit and Remove; API keys' Sync, Create Key, Edit and Revoke Key;
shadow experiments' New, Pause, Resume, Complete and Delete; Activate in the
config version history; MCP tools' Add server, a server's Edit and Remove,
and Try a tool's Run; the managed-models switch;
the Guardrails page's switch, Edit, Save & Activate and Run Test; the Org
Config editor's Save & Activate; Budgets' Set Budget, Remove and the
Enforce budgets switch; Settings > Batch Jobs' Submit Batch Job and a
running batch's Cancel (F41); Fallbacks' Save & Apply and Providers >
Routing's Save Routing Config; Monitoring's Create Rule, Add Channel and
each rule's and channel's Delete. Auto routing
is read-only for them too (its own note says edit access is
needed). Every read stays open. Add Provider used to follow a project
permission that Members hold; it now follows the organization role.

**F24. A provider URL whose address carries a loopback or metadata IPv4
address in an IPv6 form is refused.** The platform's address check judges a
NAT64 (`64:ff9b::/96`), 6to4 (`2002::/16`), IPv4-compatible (`::a.b.c.d`) or
Teredo (`2001::/32`) address by the stricter of its own class and the IPv4
address it carries, and GCP's IPv6 metadata address `fd20:ce::254` is never
allowed. So a provider `base_url` whose address carries a loopback or
cloud-metadata address is refused even with
`AGENTCC_ALLOW_PRIVATE_PROVIDER_URLS=true`; one that carries a private
address still saves with that setting, as before. A NAT64 prefix an operator
chose (such as `64:ff9b:1::/48`) is not read.

**F25. Provider blocks in `config.example.yaml` start as written.** The
Perplexity block (type only) stopped the gateway at start-up
(`base_url is required`), and so did the azure, azure-ad, groq, mistral,
together, huggingface, fireworks, deepinfra, cerebras, xai and openrouter
blocks. Each now states `base_url` and `api_format`; Perplexity also states
`api_path_prefix: ""`, so chat goes to
`https://api.perplexity.ai/chat/completions`.

**F26. An IPv6 address that carries an IPv4 address is checked as that
IPv4 address.** NAT64 (`64:ff9b::/96`), 6to4 (`2002::/16`),
IPv4-compatible (`::a.b.c.d`) and Teredo (`2001::/32`) addresses were
classified as public whatever IPv4 address they carry, so on a network with
DNS64/NAT64 an org callback or alert channel whose name resolved to
`64:ff9b::a00:5` reached `10.0.0.5`. The egress guard (org guardrail
callbacks and alert channels), the provider `base_url` guard and Bedrock's
dialer now refuse such an address as they refuse the IPv4 address in it.
An IPv4 range in `mcp.egress.private_allow` does not open the IPv6 form of
an address in it: list the name or the IPv6 range. A NAT64 prefix of the
operator's own choosing is not read.

**F27. Set Budget turns budgets on.** A budget saved from Budgets > Set
Budget was stored but never enforced: the push left the organization's
budgets off unless it had switched them on in Org Config. Now budgets are
on when any level has a limit above 0 and the organization never chose; an
explicit off stays off; removing the last level turns them off. The Budgets
page shows the same switch, "Enforce budgets", as Org Config > Budgets.
From the gateway's `org_sections_enforced`, the page says "Not enforced on
this gateway" when that gateway does not run the budget plugin, and
"Enforcement unknown" when the gateway does not report it.

**F28. Throttle throttles.** "When Limit Exceeded: Throttle" behaved as
Warn. Now, past the limit, the budget admits its "Requests per minute"
(`throttle_rpm`, a whole number from 1, default 1) in each clock minute on
each gateway replica, as the console says, and refuses the rest with 429
`budget_throttled` and `Retry-After` (the seconds to the next minute);
under the limit every request is admitted. A request
that another level refuses takes no throttle slot. `throttle_rpm` is a new
field of a budget level and of the organization budget in the admin
contract.

**F29. The Alert Threshold reaches the gateway.** Set Budget's Alert
Threshold (%) was dropped, so the warning always came at 80% of the limit.
Now it is the budget's `warn_threshold` (on a team, user, key or tag
budget, its `alert_thresholds`): from that share of the limit, each
request's log carries `org_budget_warning`. The dialog takes a percentage
above 0 and up to 100; a stored value outside that range is not sent.

**F30. The Organization or Hard Limit budget saved last is enforced.**
With both set, the Organization budget always won, so a later Hard Limit
save was ignored. Each save now carries the time it was made (`saved_at`),
the one saved last is enforced whole, and the Budgets page marks the other
"Not in force". Budgets saved before this release enforce what they did
before.

**F31. Budget bars show real spend.** The bars read a `spent` value that
nothing writes, so they always showed $0.00. Each organization-level bar
now shows the organization's spend for that budget's period from the
request logs: `GET /agentcc/spend-summary/` also answers a signed-in
console user now, with their own organization only (the gateway's admin
token still reads every organization). Team, user, key and tag budgets are
listed one per entry; their spend is counted by the gateway and is not
shown on the page. Roles & Access no longer shows "Auth Enabled: No" (the
console never received that setting); it says how the gateway identifies a
request.

**F32. Saving an organization's config no longer resets its budgets.**
Every save of an organization's config cleared that organization's budget
counters on the gateway, so each budget started again from $0 after any
change. The counters are kept now, also when the config is removed; each
still resets at the start of its period.

**F33. A budget set partway through a period counts the period's spend so
far.** The gateway counted an organization's spend only while its budgets
were on, and its start-up seed skipped an organization whose budgets were
off, so a budget set below what the organization had already spent this
period (Set Budget turns budgets on) admitted requests until that much more
was spent, while the Budgets page's bar showed it exceeded. The gateway now
counts every organization's spend at the organization level, whether its
budgets are on, off or not set, and each team, user, key and tag budget an
organization configures, on or off; its start-up seed covers every
organization. The Budgets page says that the gateway checks each limit
against its own count, which can be lower than the bar (see Known limits).
Set Budget's limit field now names the period the gateway applies (the
organization's Budget Period in Org Config > Budgets) instead of "Monthly".

**F34. Email alerts are sent.** An email alert was saved and counted
against the plan's email-alert limit but never sent: only Send test reached
a mail provider. Now each active alert is sent through its own provider
(SMTP, SendGrid or Resend). Error Occurred, Guardrail Triggered and Budget
