Exceeded are recorded when the gateway's request log reaches the platform,
and the email is started on Temporal, never on the request that delivered
the log. Error Rate Spike, Latency Spike and Cost Threshold are checked
every minute against the organization's own request logs over the alert's
window (`window_minutes`, default 5): the error rate and the p95 latency
only with at least `min_requests` requests (default 5), against
`error_rate_percent` (default 5) and `latency_ms` (default 5000); spend
against `cost_usd` (default 10). Each alert sends at most one email per
`cooldown_minutes`; events that arrive inside the cooldown are sent
together in the next email, with how often each happened. A threshold that
stays crossed is sent again after each cooldown. A failed send is recorded
on the alert (`last_error`, shown on the Email Alerts card), logged with the
alert's id, kept and retried on the next minute's check, or sooner when the
organization's next request event is recorded; it never fails the log
delivery.

**F35. Budget Exceeded is produced.** Webhooks and email alerts offered
Budget Exceeded, and nothing produced it. Now a request the gateway refused
for a budget (error code `budget_exceeded`, `org_budget_exceeded` or
`budget_throttled`, from the gateway's own error, never from the caller's
metadata) produces it, once per organization per budget level per budget
period (the refusal's `budget_exceeded_level` and `budget_period_start`),
or, when the refusal names no level, once per error code per UTC day.

**F36. Webhook retries run.** Retry on a webhook event only set it back to
pending, and no worker ever delivered pending events, so a failed delivery
was never tried again. Now a schedule delivers due events every 30 s,
waiting 30 s after the first failed attempt and doubling the wait after
each, up to the event's `max_attempts` (5); Retry starts the delivery at
once, off the request. One event is never sent twice by two workers at the
same time.

**F37. Analytics charts are bucketed at the range's size.** The console
asks for 5-minute buckets up to 6 h, 15-minute up to 24 h, hourly up to 7
days, 6-hour up to 30 days and daily beyond, and every one of them was
answered with hourly buckets (a 1 h range had 2 points, 30 days 721). Each
now gets its own bucket size (C59).

**F38. Retry, failover and circuit-breaker status lists match the
provider's own status.** A provider adapter answers a provider's 5xx as 502,
and the lists were matched against that 502 only: a list naming the
provider's code (503, 500, 529) never matched an outage, and only a list
naming 502 matched any provider 5xx. A list now matches the status the
client gets or the provider's own (kept beside the 502 for OpenAI-compatible
and Azure providers and on every unparsed error; read from the error code
for Cohere, Bedrock, Anthropic and Gemini). Lists that name 502 match as
before, and the default lists are unchanged. "Retry on Timeout"
(`routing.retry.on_timeout`) and failover's `on_timeout` now act on a
provider timeout (504 `gateway_timeout`, or a provider's 408 or 504);
before, an error with a status was never checked against `on_timeout`. A
circuit breaker counts a provider timeout as a failure whatever its
`on_status_codes`.

**F39. The response cache never sends its Redis password in plaintext when
`tls` is set.** With `cache.redis.tls: true` the gateway connected without
TLS and sent `AUTH` with the password in clear. Every connection is now TLS
or fails (U19).

**F40. Console batch jobs run as your organization.** Settings > Batch
Jobs sent the batch to the gateway with the admin token alone, so under
request auth every item ended `invalid_api_key: Invalid or missing API key`
and no provider was called; with auth off the items ran on the gateway
operator's own provider key with no organization. The console now mints a
key for your organization for each batch (named `console-batch-<id>`,
listed with your API keys, owned by the user who submitted it, expiring 24 h
after it was made) and the gateway runs every item as that key (C67). The
key is revoked as soon as the batch is seen completed, failed or cancelled,
and in any case 24 h after the batch was submitted. A batch's status and
results are read and cancelled only for your organization. Console batch
jobs need a single gateway replica (C67; the Helm chart runs one by
default): with several, a submit can be refused and a batch's status can
answer "Gateway error ... 404". Each item's client address is the console
server's, so an organization IP allowlist (on a gateway that enforces it,
U16) must include that address; otherwise every item of a console batch
answers 403.

**F41. Only an organization's Owner or Admin can submit or cancel a batch
job.** Submitting or cancelling a console batch spends the organization's
credits on its providers, and any member, a Viewer included, could do it.
Anyone but an Owner or Admin now gets 403 and nothing reaches the gateway.
Every member can still follow a batch's status and results, and Check
Health stays open to every member. Batch jobs never ran before this release
(F40), so no member loses a batch that worked.

**F42. Webhooks subscribed to Batch Completed receive it.** The Webhooks
page offered the Batch Completed event, but nothing produced it. The first
time the console or the `agentcc-batches` schedule (U20) sees a batch
completed, failed or cancelled, every active webhook of the organization
subscribed to `batch.completed` receives one event, once per batch:
`{"event": "batch.completed", "batch_id", "org_id", "status", "total",
"created_at", "completed_at", "summary"}`, where `summary` is the gateway's
(`total_cost`, `total_input_tokens`, `total_output_tokens`, `completed`,
`failed`, `cancelled`). `status` is the gateway's `completed` or
`cancelled`, or `failed` for a batch the gateway no longer holds (it
restarted, or the finished batch's hour passed) 24 h after it was
submitted; that event has no `summary`, and adds `"outcome": "unknown"` and
an `error` saying so. Delivery and retries are the webhook's usual ones.
The console shows such a batch as failed, and stops polling it, as soon as
its page reads it after those 24 h; a finished batch whose results the
gateway no longer holds shows the status it finished with, without results,
instead of "Gateway error ... 404".

**F43. An organization's alert rule no longer fires on every request.** A
rule saved without a cooldown fired its channels on every request past its
threshold. Now, after a rule fires, it waits its cooldown before it can fire
again, while its condition still holds. A rule saved without a cooldown, or
with one that is not a duration, waits 15 minutes. `0s` is honoured: the rule
fires on every request past its threshold. A config push (a save in any
section) no longer restarts the cooldown of a rule whose name is unchanged.
Monitoring > Create Rule has a Cooldown field (it starts at 15m), and the
Alert Rules table shows each rule's cooldown, or "15m (default)".

**F44. A Monitoring alert rule says "Active" only when this gateway runs
it.** The Status chip said Active for every rule that was not disabled. It
now reads which org config sections the gateway reports it enforces
(`org_sections_enforced` in `GET /-/config`): Active when that list includes
`alerting`; "Not enforced on this gateway" when it does not; "Enforcement
unknown" when the gateway does not report the list; "Alerting off" while
the organization's alerting switch is off.

**F45. Monitoring's Live Metrics cards open the Analytics tab they name.**
Error Rate, Avg Latency and Cost opened the Usage tab. Each card now opens
its own tab (Usage, Errors, Latency, Cost). The request card is labelled
"Requests (24h)", the count it shows; it was labelled "Request Rate".

**F46. "Gateway Connected" is ticked only when the gateway is healthy.**
The Overview's Getting Started step was ticked whenever the platform listed
a gateway, which it always does, even when the gateway was unreachable. It is
now ticked only when the platform's last health check of the gateway
succeeded. While the gateway is not healthy, the Overview offers Check Health
to every member, and the check reports its real result ("Gateway healthy",
or "Gateway unreachable" with the reason).

**F47. Settings shows the gateway's own settings.** The Settings cards
read blocks the config action never returned, so every gateway showed
dashes for its timeouts, "Request Logging: Disabled" and "Last Health Check:
Never". They now show the gateway's read, write, idle and maximum request
times, its request logging, body logging and content mode, the
organization's last health check with its outcome, and the org sections
this gateway enforces (C70, C71); a value the gateway does not report
reads "Not reported". The Batch API card says batches live in the gateway
node's memory (a restart loses them), that concurrency is set per
submission (10 when a submission sets none) and that a submission may be up
to 10 MiB. Shutdown Timeout and the log format, which no gateway reports,
are no longer shown.

**F48. Provider Health shows each provider's own health.** Its chip was
Healthy for every provider (C69). The table now says how the status is
derived, shows why each row has its status, labels latency as the 24-hour
average (it said P50) and has no circuit breaker column. A provider the
config push leaves out reads "Not pushed" with the reason. Org Config >
Providers no longer offers per-organization overrides it had no field for;
it links to Providers > Provider Config, where each provider's Edit dialog
is, and shows each provider's status and reason.

**F49. The Guardrails Test tab says what happened.** A check that warned
showed "Request passed all guardrails", a block showed "BLOCKED (446)", a
provider's 429 or 500 showed a green OK, and Recent Tests showed every test
that was not a block as OK. The tab now shows Blocked (403); Warned or
Logged, with the check names when the gateway sends them; Passed; or Error
with the HTTP status and the gateway's message, in the result and in Recent
Tests. Its help text names 403 `guardrail_error` and the
`x-agentcc-guardrail-*` headers instead of 246 and 446. The Guardrails Logs
tab colours each request by the strongest action its checks took (block,
warn, log).

**F50. A malformed URL stored under a name two entries share no longer
locks a save out.** The checks that refuse a save introducing a malformed
alert channel or guardrail callback URL let a URL stand when the same name
already holds it unchanged. They remembered one URL per name, so with two
alert channels or two guardrail checks of the same name, the first one's
unchanged malformed URL (saved before those checks existed) read as new, and
every gateway save of the organization answered 400, saves that touch
neither alerting nor guardrails included. Each name now holds every URL
stored under it. A new malformed URL under a shared name is still refused,
naming its own field, and another name never vouches for one.

**F51. An organization keeps its last good config when the platform cannot
build a new one.** When the platform cannot build one organization's
config for the gateway's sync, it still serves every other organization's
and names that one in `unbuilt_org_ids`; the gateway keeps the config it
already holds for each organization named there. An organization that is
neither served nor named is dropped, as before.

### Present but switched off

- **Managed models and credits.** The code to serve models with FutureAGI's
  own upstream keys, hold and settle prepaid credit, and answer 402 is in
  this release, but nothing turns it on. No shipped config marks a provider
  `managed: true`. Without one, the managed admin routes answer 404
  `managed_models_disabled`, and the console offers no managed models (N7).
  Do not mark a provider `managed: true` in this release: settled
  managed spend does not reach the billing ledger yet.
- **Managed tools.** `tools.enabled` defaults to false, and a managed tool
  call answers 503 `managed_capability_unavailable`.
- **Settings that nothing reads yet.** `security.*`,
  `telemetry.overhead_header`, `responses.hollow.*`, `runtime_tokens.*` and
  `managed.upstream_key_mode` are parsed and have no effect.
- **Audit sinks other than stdout, and `cluster.redis_url`.** The audit log
  is written to stdout only (JSON lines; ship them to a SIEM with your log
  collector). An `audit.sinks` entry of type `file` or `webhook` is
  accepted and writes nothing, and the audit events carry no hash chain.
  Cluster membership is per node (`GET /-/cluster/nodes` lists the node
  that answers), and `cluster.redis_url` is not read; replicas share rate
  limits, budgets, credits, key revocations and key rotations through the
  `redis` block instead. The gateway starts with either set and names each
  in one startup warning.

### Known limits

- **Releases are not signed yet.** The release workflow on this branch adds
  an SBOM, checksums, a keyless signature and a SLSA provenance
  attestation, but no release has run it yet
  ([supply-chain.md](security/supply-chain.md#what-the-release-workflow-does-ci-only)).
- **MCP full-content capture is a separate opt-in.** It exports tool inputs and
  outputs to the organization's collector and masks known credential formats;
  other sensitive content may still be exported. MCP body export is off by
  default, requires admin consent plus `otel.include_bodies`, and respects
  restrictive content modes and retention. This MCP guarantee does not describe
  model-request span bodies or caller metadata on other tracing paths.
- **What a check on the answer reads.** It reads the answer's text on the
  five routes in C30. It does not read the output of other APIs that return
  model text: audio transcriptions and translations, OCR, the Assistants API
  and Realtime. An organization's `data-leakage-prevention` and
  `hallucination-detection` read a plain-text answer only. They do not read
  an answer whose content mixes text with images or audio, a model's
  reasoning, or Gemini's thought summaries. On a stream a check reads the
  answer when the stream ends. A blocking check holds the stream until then
  (C25): the client gets the response's headers at once and the answer only
  once it is complete and has passed, and a stream over 10 MiB is refused.
  A check that does not block holds nothing and reads the answer's first
  2 MiB. Tool calls in a stream are not assembled. The streaming checker,
  which reads a chat stream as it goes, runs only the rules in the gateway's
  config file; in stop mode it holds the stream too, and stops the
  provider's stream as soon as a rule blocks. A rule that rewrites the
  answer (PII masking at the post stage) cannot rewrite an answer passed
  through to the provider's own API, which the client gets as the provider
  sent it (C25, C26, C30). On the APIs
  whose answer is not model text (C35) there is no answer to withhold: a
  check on the answer in block mode that triggers there is recorded as
  logged.
- **What a held stream costs.** Until its checks have run, a held stream
  (C25) keeps in memory up to 10 MiB of the response's frames (the held
  frames) and up to 10 MiB of the answer assembled for the checks (the
  capture). A stream past either limit is refused with `answer_unavailable`,
  or `stream_blocked` when the streaming checker's own check blocks it.
  Neither refusal releases the withheld content.
  On chat, the streaming checker also keeps the text it has read, and
  neither limit bounds that text. There is no gateway-wide limit on what
  held streams keep together, so many long answers held at once grow the
  gateway's memory by up to about 20 MiB each for the held frames and the
  capture, plus, on chat with the streaming checker on, the text the
  checker has read. Nothing is sent while a stream is held, not even
  keep-alive comments, so a client with a short idle-read timeout may give
  up on a long answer.
- **What a check on the request reads.** It reads the request's text on
  `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/completions` and the routes in C32 and C35
  (the console's Guardrails page lists them), and on async, batch and A2A
  requests, which are chat requests. Each batch item runs through the chat
  handler as the submitted `x-agentcc-batch-key`, including that key's
  organization and its guardrails (C67, F40). With request auth disabled,
  a submission without a batch key runs with no organization, so only the
  config file's rules apply to its items. It does not read Realtime,
  which answers 501 in this release. On a transcription, a translation and
  OCR the input itself (the audio, the document) is not text: a check that
  would block or rewrite such a request refuses it (C35). On the other
  routes it reads text only: not images, audio, PDFs or other files inside
  the request, which are neither read nor refused, and not a
  model's reasoning that a request sends back (Anthropic thinking blocks,
  Gemini thought parts, Responses reasoning items and their summaries, a
  chat message's `reasoning_content` and `thinking_blocks`). It does not read what
  is stored at the provider and named by id: the earlier turns a Responses
  `previous_response_id` or `conversation` names, an `item_reference`, a
  stored prompt's own text, files and images by id, or Gemini
  `cachedContent`. A `/v1/completions` `suffix` is not read, nor Gemini
  `executableCode` (code sent to run) or a Vertex AI countTokens
  `instances` list. In the result of a tool the provider runs, and in a
  block or item of a type the gateway does not know, it reads the fields
  that hold text in the providers' APIs (`text`, `title`, `output`,
  `content`, `stdout`, `stderr`, `logs`, `lines`); text under a field of
  another name is not read, nor what the provider sends encrypted (a web
  search result's page content). A rewrite of the request (C33) that runs
  across two fields of one block, or across two prompts of a list, refuses
  the request rather than send it. In a tool call it reads the arguments,
  not the tool's name, up to 64 levels of nesting; a check that would block
  or rewrite a request whose arguments are nested deeper, or begin with more
  than 64 `[` or `{` (free text included), refuses it (C36).
  In a body it passes through or proxies as sent, a value it walks on its
  own (a block or item of a type it does not know, a tool's result, a
  Gemini function response, blocks in blocks) is read up to 64 levels deep;
  a check that would block or rewrite a request holding one nested deeper
  refuses it (C36). `prompt-injection` does not read assistant
  messages, and in system and developer messages counts only the signs of
  text someone else wrote, not instruction wording (C37);
  `system-prompt-protection` and `language` read the user's messages only;
  `input-validation`'s length rules count message content, not tool calls'
  arguments.
- **`mask` runs as `log` on a check that cannot rewrite the request** (C34).
  An organization's check of any type other than `pii-detection` that holds
  the action `mask` (saved by an older console, which offered it for every
  check, or through the API) runs as `log`: it neither masks nor blocks. On
  a self-hosted gateway whose config file has a rule with the same name as
  an organization's check, the organization's check sets that rule's action
  and threshold instead of running on its own; there `mask` runs as `log`
  too, and whether the rule rewrites the request is set by its own
  `remediation` in the config file.
- **An organization's other checks read the request only.** PII, content
  moderation, secrets, keyword blocklist, validation, FutureAGI and
  external provider checks set in an organization's config never read the
  answer.
- **A credential is known by its name.** A key sent in a header whose name
  does not read as a credential (`X-My-Header`, say) is kept in the request
  log as sent, and exported to traces when the trace header allowlist names
  that header (F6). A caller's own metadata dimensions are kept in the
  request log (content mode `none` drops them) and exported to traces as
  sent, whatever their names: only a guardrail check's input and an async
  job's metadata leave out one whose name reads as a credential (F7).
- **A guardrail webhook receives the request.** A webhook check still sends
  the URL its config names the request, the client's address, the key's
  id, name and owner and the request's other dimensions (F7). Through the
  platform, only an organization's Owner or Admin can set that URL (F9).
- **The platform checks a callback URL's shape, the gateway checks its
  address.** On save the platform refuses a guardrail or alert URL that is
  not a well-formed http(s) URL with a host and no user, password or control
  character (F10, F11); it does not judge the address, so a host name that
  resolves to a private address saves. What the URL may connect to is decided
  at dial time by the gateway's egress guard against `mcp.egress.private_allow`
  (F10, F11), so a check pushed straight to the gateway, bypassing the
  platform, is still refused the address. A FutureAGI eval check's call to
  the gateway's own `FI_BASE_URL` is operator configuration and is not
  guarded; any other `base_url` an organization sets is (F10, U12).
- **The gateway's admin API returns an organization's credentials to its
  token holders.** `GET /-/orgs/{id}/config` on the gateway's admin API
  returns an organization's whole config in clear, its cache, A2A, audit
  and alerting credentials included (provider credentials and MCP secrets
  are masked there, N14), to whoever holds the gateway admin token. That token is
  operator scope: keep it to the people who run the gateway.
- **Which alert URLs are secret is read from their shape** (F22). A token
  in a URL's host name, or a token that is a short lowercase word in its
  path, is not detected, and the URL stays readable; a plain URL that the
  rule takes for a secret is masked and still delivered.
- **Browsers send only three agent headers by default**: `x-agentcc-user-id`,
  `x-agentcc-session-id` and `x-agentcc-trace-id`; the others need
  `cors.allowed_headers` (C7).
- **No async for organization keys** (C16).
- **What `model: "auto"` does not do** (N2): no benchmark shows that it picks
  better models than a fixed choice. Do not rely on it to steer away from a
  failing provider. Its ranking also lowers a model for latency and errors,
  using what this gateway has recorded for that provider name across every
  organization's calls, so other organizations' traffic can change which of
  your models auto picks. A candidate whose recorded calls all failed takes
  no error penalty at all.
- **Mirroring copies only the operator's own traffic.** On a self-hosted
  gateway whose config file sets `routing.mirror`, only a request made with
  an internal key or license authorization is copied to the mirror target,
  unbilled, on the gateway's own provider credentials. A request made with
  an organization's key is never copied, and config load refuses a rule
  that targets a managed provider (MIXED-HOP-GUARD-1).
- **An IP rule is only as reliable as the client address** (U3, C17).
- **The platform still prices a log entry that has no gateway cost from
  its metadata** (C40). When an entry reports no cost and no
  `cost_source`, the platform prices it from `audio_seconds`,
  `input_characters`, `images_generated` and `quality` in its metadata. A
  gateway of this release never lets a caller set those names; a gateway
  before this release does, so an entry from one can be priced on a
  caller's numbers.
- **Some `/v1/responses` requests are not priced** (F3). A stream that ends
  before its last event (the client went away, or the provider's stream
  broke) has no usage to price, so a managed key is not debited for it. A
  background response sent with an organization's own provider credentials
  is not priced either: it counts toward no budget, and neither does a
  stream on such credentials whose last event is over 10 MiB (prepaid
  credit is charged the hold for one, F3). A response that is not streamed
  is read up to 10 MiB: a longer one is cut there, so its usage cannot be
  read and it is not priced on any key, and the client gets the cut body
  with 200.
- **Per-key rate limits and IP allow lists are not offered yet for keys
  made through the platform** (C22). The gateway reads only `log_content`
  from such a key. On a key defined in the gateway's own config file
  (`auth.keys`), `rate_limit_rpm`, `rate_limit_tpm` and `allowed_ips` apply.
  A key's `rate_limit_tpm` is counted on each replica even with Redis (with N
  replicas a key can use up to N times its limit), and it is checked before a
  call and charged with the call's tokens after it, so one request can take a key past
  its limit before the next is refused (429 `token_rate_limit_exceeded`).
  The organization's `per_key_rpm` and `per_key_tpm` (C66) apply to every
  key of the organization, platform keys included.
- **What a token limit counts** (C66). The tokens of the response that
  served the request, the usage it is priced on: an attempt that failed
  before a retry or fallback is not counted. A request holds an estimate
  while it runs only when the gateway reads it as chat messages (chat
  completions and completions, and Messages or Gemini requests translated
  for a provider of another format); a Responses request, or a Messages or
  Gemini request passed to a provider of its own format, holds none and
  counts its reported usage when it finishes. Without Redis each replica
  counts on its own.
- **An organization's rate limits do not cover every route** (C66). They
  count and limit chat completions, completions, Responses, Anthropic
  Messages and Gemini (`/v1beta`) requests, and the relayed speech sessions
  (one request each, counted per model only by a model the session's URL
  names; a session adds no tokens, and is refused while a token limit that
  holds it is spent). Embeddings (`/v1/embeddings`), images,
  audio (`/v1/audio/...`), rerank, search, OCR, Assistants, Vector Stores,
  Files, video, realtime and scheduled requests are not counted against
  them and are never refused by them. `per_user_rpm` limits no Anthropic
  Messages or Gemini request: those routes read no end user.
- **A cached answer is not rate-limited** (C66). An answer served from the
  response cache is not counted against, or refused by, any rate limit: the
  cache answers before the rate limit is checked.
- **A cache hit on `/v1/completions` through an OpenAI-compatible provider
  is answered 500.** Such a provider gets the legacy request as written.
  Its answer is stored, but a later request that hits the entry is answered
  500 `internal_error` ("no response from provider") without calling the
  upstream, and without the cached answer. Entries are keyed by the chat
  form of the request, not by its route, so an entry a matching
  `/v1/chat/completions` request stored is hit the same way. A
  `/v1/completions` request translated for any other provider is served
  from the cache. This needs a response cache the gateway's operator turned
  on and an organization that turned its own on; the hosted gateway's cache
  is off (H2).
- **An organization's settings reach the other replicas at their next
  sync.** A change saved in the console is pushed to one gateway replica,
  which applies it at once. Additive or relaxing changes reach every other
  replica within the control-plane sync interval
  (`control_plane.sync_interval`: 60 s by default in `docker-compose.yml`
  and Helm; at the gateway's own default of 0 there is no periodic sync,
  and the other replicas keep the old settings until they restart). In this release a restrictive
  change also reaches the other replicas only within the sync interval;
  it does not reach every replica at once. Key revocations are separate: they reach every replica that
  shares the gateway's Redis at once (C19).
- **A budget's throttle is counted on each gateway replica.** Past the
  limit, each replica admits `throttle_rpm` requests a minute, so N replicas
  admit up to N times that. The spend the limit is checked against is shared
  through Redis when the gateway has one.
- **The gateway checks a budget against its own count of the spend.** The
  Budgets page's bars read the request logs; the gateway counts spend as it
  answers, and when it starts it reads this period's spend from the request
  logs for its default budget period (monthly unless the gateway's config
  sets another). Its count can be lower than the bar in these cases (the
  page says it can be lower after a restart or a change of period):
  - After a restart, a budget over another period (a daily or weekly
    budget on a monthly gateway, or a monthly budget on a daily one)
    counts from the restart. The logs count
    spend by key id and by the body's user or the key's owner; key budgets
    count by key name and user budgets by the request's user (C54), so a
    key budget, and a user budget for a user named only in
    `x-agentcc-user-id`, is not seeded either. The organization level is
    seeded for every organization, its budgets on or off.
  - A budget whose period changes can count less than the new period's
    spend until that period next starts: the gateway counts the
    organization level in its current period only.
  - A team, user, key or tag budget added partway through a period counts
    from when it is added (or from the next restart, for one the seed
    covers).
  - Gateway replicas that share no Redis each count only the spend they
    answer, on top of their start-up seed.
  - On a gateway with Redis, in the period this release is deployed, an
    organization whose budgets were off before the deploy counts the spend
    seeded at that period's first gateway start plus what it spends after
    the deploy; the spend between the two is not counted until the next
    period.
- **An alert rule's cooldown is per gateway replica** (F43). Each replica
  keeps when a rule last fired in its own memory, so with N replicas a rule
  can fire up to N times in one cooldown, and a restart forgets it. The
  request that fires an alert waits for the channels to answer (each one up
  to 10 seconds) before its response is sent.
- **Chat parameters the Anthropic, Gemini and Bedrock adapters do not send.**
  A chat request translated for one of these providers loses these fields,
  with no error or header to say so: on Anthropic and Bedrock, `n`, `seed`,
  `presence_penalty`, `frequency_penalty`, `logit_bias`, `logprobs`,
  `top_logprobs`, `user`, `service_tier`, a `response_format` of type
  `json_object` (only `json_schema` is sent) and a request for extended
  thinking (`thinking`, `thinking_budget` or `reasoning_effort`); on Gemini,
  `n`, `seed`, `presence_penalty`, `frequency_penalty`, `logit_bias`,
  `logprobs`, `top_logprobs`, `user` and `service_tier` (`json_object`,
  `json_schema`, `thinking_budget` and `reasoning_effort` are sent).
  Requests to OpenAI-format providers carry them as sent
  (`TestR7iChatParametersThisAdapterDoesNotSend` in each of the three
  adapters; `TestR7fJSONObjectAndThinkingThisAdapterDoesNotSend` for
  Anthropic and Bedrock, `TestR7fJSONFormatsAndThinkingThisAdapterSends` for
  Gemini).

### Proof

Go tests run with `go test ./...` in `agentcc-gateway`. `sc/NN` is a
scenario script in `agentcc-gateway/scripts/scenarios/`, and a `W…` name is
a gate script in `scripts/scenarios/gates/`; both run the real gateway
binary against a mock upstream and need Redis (`make scenarios`). Django
tests are in `futureagi/agentcc/tests/`, and frontend tests sit next to
their components in `frontend/src/sections/gateway/`.
